name: AWS Clean Rooms
one: Two companies compare their customer data without either one handing the data over.
like: Two people each hold a sealed guest list. A trusted clerk in a locked room counts how many names appear on both lists, tells you the number, and shreds everything else.
what: You and a partner each put a dataset in, agree in advance on exactly which queries are allowed, and only the agreed results come out. Neither side can download or browse the other side's rows. It is mostly used by advertisers and media companies to measure campaign overlap. Setting up the agreement and the query rules is slow, and both sides need an AWS account, so it is not something a small team picks up casually.
when: Two firms need a joint answer but legally cannot share raw records
Advertiser and publisher measuring the same audience
Partner analytics where a contract or privacy law blocks a data copy
nope: If you own both datasets, just put them in S3 and query with Amazon Athena
For simply selling or buying a dataset, use AWS Data Exchange
For matching messy records you own, use AWS Entity Resolution
eg: A retailer and a TV network want to know how many people who saw an ad later bought the product, without the retailer revealing its buyer list.
pay: Per compute unit while a query runs, plus storage. The surprise is the cryptographic option, Clean Rooms ML and differential privacy cost noticeably more than plain queries.

name: AWS Data Exchange
one: A shop inside AWS where you buy or sell data sets and keep them updated automatically.
like: A magazine subscription. You pay, and new issues arrive on your doorstep without you asking each time.
what: Sellers list data products, weather history, stock prices, health statistics, and buyers subscribe. The data lands in your own S3 bucket, or is queryable through Redshift or an API, and refreshes when the seller publishes an update. A lot of the free listings are public data you could fetch yourself. It only makes sense when you want billing, licensing and delivery handled in one place.
when: Buying a commercial data feed and wanting it delivered into your account
Selling data to other AWS customers with billing handled for you
Replacing a manual quarterly file download from a vendor
nope: For free public data, check the AWS Open Data Registry or the source directly, it costs nothing
For sharing data with one named partner, use S3 cross-account access or Lake Formation sharing
For a joint analysis where neither side may see the other's rows, use AWS Clean Rooms
eg: A lender subscribes to a weekly postcode-level property price file and it appears in S3 every Monday.
pay: The subscription price the seller sets, often thousands per year, plus normal S3 storage and transfer. The catch is that subscriptions can auto-renew.

name: AWS Entity Resolution
one: Works out which records in different files are the same person or company.
like: Merging two address books where one says Rob Smith, 12 High St and the other says Robert Smith, 12 High Street. A careful assistant marks them as one person.
what: You point it at data in S3 and it matches records using rules you write, a built-in machine learning matcher, or a third party service. It hands back groups of records that look like the same entity, with a confidence level. It does not clean your data or store a master record for you, you still decide what to do with the matches. This is a narrow tool, most teams solve this with SQL or a library until the data gets genuinely large and messy.
when: Joining customer records across systems with no shared ID
De-duplicating a marketing list before a campaign
Building a single customer view from several sources
nope: If your records share a reliable ID, a plain SQL join is cheaper and exact
For fixing formats, blank fields and typos, use AWS Glue DataBrew or Glue first
For matching across two companies who may not share data, use AWS Clean Rooms
eg: A hotel group finds that one guest exists three times because of two email addresses and a misspelt surname.
pay: Per record processed each time you run a matching job. Re-running a large list often, or matching against a paid third party provider, is where the bill grows.

name: AWS Glue DataBrew
one: A point-and-click tool for cleaning up messy data without writing code.
like: Find-and-replace in a spreadsheet, but it remembers every step you took and can repeat them on next month's file.
what: You load a sample of a file, see the columns, and click through fixes, trim spaces, split a name column, fill blanks, standardise dates. It saves the steps as a recipe and runs that recipe over the whole dataset. It has around 250 built-in transformations. It is deliberately limited, anything unusual is easier in a Glue script, and the visual editor gets slow with very wide tables.
when: A non-programmer needs to clean a recurring file
Exploring an unfamiliar dataset to see how dirty it is
Building a repeatable cleanup before loading into a warehouse
nope: If you are comfortable in Python or SQL, plain AWS Glue or Athena is faster and cheaper
For streaming data, this only reads files, use Managed Service for Apache Flink
For tiny one-off files, a spreadsheet or a short script is less effort
eg: A finance analyst turns a monthly supplier CSV with inconsistent date formats into a clean file for the warehouse.
pay: Per half hour of interactive session while the editor is open, plus per node-hour when a job runs. People forget the session is billed while they sit and think.

name: AWS Glue
one: Cleans and moves data between places.
like: The kitchen prep station. Wash, chop and arrange before the cooking starts.
what: Glue extracts data, transforms it and loads it somewhere useful. Its catalogue records what your data looks like so Athena and Redshift can read it. It is serverless, so nothing to run.
when: Messy data from several sources
Preparing data for analysis
nope: A single simple copy job. A script may be enough.
pay: Per data processing unit hour.
eg: Nightly job turning raw CSV exports into clean Parquet for Athena.

name: AWS Lake Formation
one: Decides who is allowed to see which tables, columns and rows of your data in S3.
like: A library where some shelves are open to everyone, some need a staff pass, and a few books have certain pages taped over.
what: It sits on top of the AWS Glue Data Catalog and lets you grant permissions in database terms, this team may read this table but not the salary column, instead of writing S3 bucket policies. Athena, Redshift Spectrum, EMR and Glue then honour those grants. It is genuinely fiddly, it layers on top of IAM rather than replacing it, and mixing the two is the usual source of confusion and denied queries.
when: Many teams share one data lake and need different access
You must restrict specific columns or rows, such as hiding personal data
Sharing catalogued tables with another AWS account
nope: One team, one bucket, use plain IAM and S3 policies, this is overkill
For a business-facing catalogue people browse and request access through, use Amazon DataZone
If your data lives in a database rather than S3, use that database's own permissions
eg: Analysts can query the orders table but the card number column comes back blank for everyone outside the payments team.
pay: The service itself is largely free. You pay for the query engines and storage underneath, and for the extra compute when it filters rows and columns for you.

name: Amazon Athena
one: Run SQL directly on files sitting in S3.
like: Reading the files in your cupboard without first moving them into a filing system.
what: Athena queries CSV, JSON or Parquet files in S3 using normal SQL. Nothing to set up. Store data as Parquet and partition it, or queries get slow and expensive.
when: Occasional analysis of files
Log analysis
You do not want a data warehouse yet
nope: Fast dashboards many people refresh all day. Use Redshift.
pay: Per TB of data scanned. Bad file formats cost real money here.
eg: Asking how many orders came from Gujarat last month, straight from log files.

name: Amazon CloudSearch
one: An old search box service for websites, now closed to new customers.
like: A card index at the back of a shop. It finds things fine, but the shop stopped ordering replacement drawers.
what: This is a legacy service. AWS closed it to new sign-ups in July 2024 and adds no new features, though existing customers can keep running it. It powered site search, type a word, get ranked results with facets and suggestions. If you meet it today it is in an old system, and the official path forward is Amazon OpenSearch Service. Nobody starting now should learn it.
when: You inherited a running CloudSearch domain
Planning the migration off it
nope: For any new search feature, use Amazon OpenSearch Service
For product search on a site, a hosted option like Algolia or OpenSearch Serverless is less work
For looking through logs, use OpenSearch or CloudWatch Logs Insights
eg: A ten year old support site whose search box still runs on a CloudSearch domain nobody has touched.
pay: Per search instance hour, whether anyone searches or not. The surprise is a forgotten idle domain quietly billing for years.

name: Amazon Data Firehose
one: Takes a constant trickle of records and drops them into storage for you, in batches.
like: A funnel with a bucket under it. Drips go in continuously, and every so often the full bucket is carried off to the store room.
what: Formerly called Kinesis Data Firehose. You send it records and it buffers them for a set time or size, then writes them to S3, Redshift, OpenSearch or a partner like Splunk. It can compress, convert JSON to Parquet, and call a Lambda to tweak each record. It is fully managed with no shards to size, but it is one way and near real time, not instant, there is always a buffer delay of at least a minute or so.
when: Shipping application or clickstream logs into S3 without writing a loader
Feeding a dashboard index in OpenSearch
Converting streaming JSON into Parquet for cheap querying
nope: If several different apps must read the same stream, or you need replay, use Kinesis Data Streams
If you need results in well under a second, the buffer makes this the wrong tool
For moving whole database tables, use AWS DMS or Glue, not a stream
eg: A mobile app sends every screen view, and an hour later those events are sitting in S3 as tidy Parquet files.
pay: Per GB ingested, rounded up per record to 5 KB. Lots of tiny records cost far more than the raw byte count suggests, and format conversion is billed on top.

name: Amazon DataZone
one: A catalogue where staff can find the company's data and ask for permission to use it.
like: A staff intranet directory. You search for what you need, see who owns it, and click a button to request access.
what: It gives each team a project space, publishes datasets with business descriptions, and runs a request and approval flow for access, with Lake Formation doing the actual enforcement. AWS has folded it into Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio, so newer accounts often meet it under that name rather than as DataZone. It solves an organisational problem, not a technical one, so it only pays off in a company with many teams and real governance rules.
when: A large company where people cannot find what data exists
Formal approval trails are needed for data access
Standardising business definitions across departments
nope: Under a few teams, a shared document and Lake Formation grants do the job
For the technical table metadata itself, that is the AWS Glue Data Catalog underneath
For enforcing permissions, that is Lake Formation, DataZone just requests them
eg: An analyst searches the portal for customer churn, finds the owning team, requests access and gets it approved in a day.
pay: Per active user per month plus metadata storage and API calls. The user count is the part that grows unnoticed as people are added and never removed.

name: Amazon EMR
one: Big data processing with Spark and Hadoop.
like: Hiring a hundred workers for one week to sort a mountain of paperwork.
what: EMR runs Spark, Hive and Hadoop clusters for heavy processing. It is powerful and needs real expertise. Most teams should try Athena or Glue first.
when: Terabytes of data
You already have Spark jobs
nope: Anything Athena can answer.
pay: Per instance hour plus an EMR fee.
eg: Reprocessing five years of raw logs in one run.

name: Amazon FinSpace
one: A data store built for finance firms, now being shut down.
like: A specialist trading-floor filing room. Useful to a handful of banks, and the landlord has given notice.
what: AWS has ended support for Amazon FinSpace, effective 7 October 2026, and stopped taking new customers a year earlier. It stored and analysed financial time series data, with a Managed kdb Insights option for firms already using the kdb+ database. It was always a niche service for capital markets. Unless you work at a hedge fund or bank that already runs it and is migrating off, you can safely ignore it.
when: You already run FinSpace and must plan the exit before October 2026
Understanding an existing kdb+ workload in AWS
nope: For time series data generally, use Amazon Timestream or Parquet in S3 with Athena
For a normal analytics warehouse, use Amazon Redshift
Do not start anything new here, the service is ending
eg: A trading desk holding years of tick data in FinSpace now has to move it to S3 and rebuild the queries.
pay: Per environment hour plus storage, and it was expensive. Migration effort before the end date is the real cost now.

name: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams
one: A pipe that holds a stream of events for a while so several programs can read them.
like: A conveyor belt past several workstations. Each worker reads items as they pass, at their own speed, and the belt keeps them for a day before they fall off the end.
what: Producers write records, consumers read them independently, and each keeps its own place in the stream. Records stay for 24 hours by default and up to a year if you pay for it, so you can replay. Order is guaranteed only within a shard, not across the whole stream, which is the thing people get wrong. You either manage shard counts yourself, provisioned mode, or let it scale on demand.
when: Several different systems need the same live event feed
You need to replay recent events after fixing a bug
Ordering matters per user or per device
nope: If you just want events landing in S3, use Amazon Data Firehose, far less work
For a work queue where each message is handled once and then deleted, use Amazon SQS
If you need Kafka APIs or existing Kafka tooling, use Amazon MSK
eg: Every card swipe goes into a stream, read at once by the fraud checker, the ledger, and the analytics loader.
pay: Provisioned mode bills per shard hour whether data flows or not, plus per record unit. On-demand is simpler but costs several times more per GB, and long retention adds another charge.

name: Amazon Kinesis Video Streams
one: It takes video from cameras and stores it so software can watch it back or analyse it.
like: A CCTV recorder in a shop back office, except the tape room is rented and never runs out.
what: Kinesis Video Streams ingests video from many devices, timestamps it, keeps it for as long as you set, and lets programs read it frame by frame for machine learning or playback. It also has a WebRTC mode for live two way viewing of a camera. It is a pipe and a recorder for machines, not a streaming service for an audience; there is no encoding, packaging or player for viewers.
when: Fleets of cameras, doorbells, dashcams or drones
Feeding video into machine learning such as Rekognition
Letting an app view a camera live from anywhere
nope: Streaming to an audience, use IVS or MediaLive
Storing a handful of finished video files, use S3
Simple motion clips from one camera, an off the shelf camera service is far cheaper
eg: A logistics firm streams dashcam footage from its trucks and runs automatic checks on hard braking events.
pay: Per gigabyte ingested, per gigabyte stored per month and per gigabyte consumed. Long retention across many cameras is what makes the bill climb.

name: Amazon Kinesis
one: Handles data that never stops arriving.
like: A conveyor belt running all day. You take things off as they pass.
what: Kinesis takes continuous streams of events and lets several consumers read them in order. Unlike a queue, data stays for a set window so more than one reader can process it.
when: Clickstreams, sensor data, live logs
Real time dashboards
nope: A handful of events per day. Use SQS or EventBridge.
pay: Per shard hour, or per GB with on demand.
eg: Every page view on a site, flowing in live for a real time counter.

name: Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink
one: Runs code that does sums over a live stream of events, like a running total per minute.
like: A shop assistant with a tally counter, keeping a rolling count of customers per hour rather than counting at closing time.
what: This was renamed from Amazon Kinesis Data Analytics in 2023. It runs Apache Flink applications, in Java, Scala, Python or SQL, and handles the servers, checkpoints and restarts. Flink is good at windows, counting events per five minutes, and at joining two streams. It is also genuinely hard, the concepts of state, watermarks and late data take real learning, and the service is expensive to leave running.
when: Continuous aggregations, averages or counts over a live stream
Detecting a pattern across events, such as three failures in a minute
Joining two streams as they arrive
nope: For simple per-record work, a Lambda on the stream is far cheaper and simpler
If a five minute delay is fine, land the data with Firehose and query with Athena
For plain delivery with no computation, use Amazon Data Firehose
eg: A delivery app keeps a live count of orders per city per minute and raises an alert when one city stalls.
pay: Per Kinesis Processing Unit hour, and the application runs continuously, so you pay around the clock. Durable state storage and the mandatory extra unit for orchestration catch people out.

name: Amazon Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka
one: AWS runs Apache Kafka for you so you do not have to babysit the servers.
like: Hiring a managed office building instead of buying one. Same offices, someone else fixes the boiler.
what: Kafka is the industry standard event log. MSK runs the brokers, patching and monitoring, in two forms, provisioned, where you pick broker sizes, and Serverless, which scales itself. It is real Kafka, so your existing clients, Connect plugins and tools work unchanged. Note that AWS manages the infrastructure, not your topics, partitions or consumer lag, which are still your job and still the usual source of pain.
when: You already use Kafka and want to stop running brokers
You need Kafka-only features such as Connect, compaction or exactly-once semantics
Moving an on-premises Kafka estate to AWS
nope: Starting fresh on AWS with no Kafka history, Kinesis Data Streams is simpler and cheaper to run
For a simple task queue, use Amazon SQS
For fan-out notifications, use Amazon SNS or EventBridge
eg: A retailer lifts its on-premises Kafka cluster into AWS and its dozens of existing producers keep working untouched.
pay: Per broker hour plus storage, billed continuously, and a small cluster across three zones costs real money every month even when idle. Cross-zone data transfer is the line people do not expect.

name: Amazon OpenSearch Service
one: A search engine you can point at your logs or your website content.
like: The index at the back of a book, rebuilt automatically every time a page changes.
what: It runs OpenSearch, the open source fork of Elasticsearch, and gives you full text search, filters, dashboards and vector search for AI features. It is very commonly used for log search. Two flavours exist, managed clusters, where you size and pay for nodes, and Serverless, which scales itself but costs more at small scale. It is not a database, do not treat it as your only copy of the data, reindexing from a real source is a normal part of running it.
when: Searching logs across many services
A search box over products, documents or articles
Vector or semantic search for a retrieval AI feature
nope: For occasional queries over files in S3, Athena is much cheaper than a running cluster
As the primary store for your records, use RDS or DynamoDB and index into OpenSearch
For simple metric alarms, CloudWatch is enough
eg: An engineer types an error message and finds every occurrence across twenty services in the last week.
pay: Per instance hour plus storage, running all the time. The classic surprise is Serverless, which has a minimum capacity floor that costs a few hundred dollars a month even with no traffic.

name: Amazon Redshift
one: A warehouse built for asking big questions of big data.
like: A library with a proper index, built for research rather than for borrowing one book.
what: Redshift is a data warehouse. It answers analytical queries over billions of rows fast. It is not for running your app. You load data into it from S3 or your database.
when: Business intelligence dashboards
Reporting across years of data
nope: The live database behind your app
Small data. Athena is cheaper.
pay: Per node hour, or per unit with Serverless.
eg: A dashboard showing revenue by city by month across four years.

name: Amazon SageMaker
one: The place to build, train and run your own machine learning models on AWS.
like: A fully equipped workshop you rent by the hour, with tools, benches and a delivery van, instead of building in your garage.
what: A large umbrella of tools, not one thing: notebooks for experimenting, managed training jobs on rented GPUs, endpoints that host a trained model behind an API, plus pipelines, a feature store and a model registry. Confusingly, it now also covers Canvas for no-code models and a unified Studio that includes data and analytics tools. You need to know some ML. It gives you infrastructure, not answers.
when: Training or fine-tuning your own model
Hosting a model you already have behind an API
Team workflows where experiments and models must be tracked
nope: Using an existing large language model, call Bedrock and skip all of this
Common tasks like text or image recognition, the ready-made AI services are far less work
A one-off experiment, a single EC2 GPU instance or Colab is simpler and cheaper
eg: Fine-tuning a model on your own product photos, then hosting it as an endpoint your app calls.
pay: Per instance-hour for notebooks, training and endpoints, at a premium over raw EC2. The classic bill shock is a notebook or endpoint left running all month doing nothing.

name: AWS AppSync
one: A managed GraphQL API.
like: One waiter who brings exactly the dishes you asked for, in one trip.
what: AppSync serves a GraphQL API backed by DynamoDB, Lambda or your own database. It supports real time subscriptions and offline sync, which suits mobile apps.
when: You use GraphQL
Real time updates
Mobile apps that go offline
nope: You are happy with REST. API Gateway is simpler.
pay: Per million queries, plus real time minutes.
eg: A chat screen that updates live without polling.

name: AWS B2B Data Interchange
one: It turns the old-fashioned trading files big companies exchange into JSON your software can read, and back again.
like: A translator between two companies who insist on writing to each other in a 1980s telex format.
what: It handles EDI, the standard format retailers, logistics firms and hospitals use for purchase orders and invoices. You define trading partners and mapping templates, and it converts X12 EDI into JSON or XML on the way in, and back to EDI on the way out. It supports X12, so EDIFACT and HL7 users are mostly out of luck. Only relevant if a partner forces EDI on you.
when: A large retailer will only send you orders as X12 EDI
Replacing an ageing in-house EDI translator
You already handle files in S3 and want the parsing managed
nope: Nobody is asking you for EDI, then you do not need it, use a normal API
You need EDIFACT or HL7 or full partner communications with AS2, a specialist EDI vendor covers more
eg: A supplier receives an 850 purchase order from a supermarket chain and it arrives in their order system as plain JSON.
pay: Per transaction processed plus a small charge per active trading partner. Low volumes are cheap, so the real cost is the mapping setup work.

name: AWS Express Workflows
one: A fast, cheap mode of AWS Step Functions for very high volume, short jobs.
like: A quick checkout lane at the shop. It moves a lot of people fast, but it is not a different shop.
what: This is not a separate AWS service. Express Workflows are one of the two workflow types inside AWS Step Functions. When you create a state machine you pick Standard or Express, and you cannot change it later. Express runs for up to five minutes, has no limit on state transition rate, and is priced by the number of runs, how long they take, and the memory used. Standard runs up to one year and is priced per state transition. Express does not keep an execution history of its own, so you must turn on Amazon CloudWatch Logs to see what happened. Express is at-least-once for the async kind, so a run can happen more than once. The sync kind is at-most-once and returns the result to the caller. Because of this, Express suits steps that are safe to repeat, like writing a record to Amazon DynamoDB. Standard is exactly-once and suits steps that must not repeat, like taking a payment.
when: High volume event processing, like IoT or streaming data, where each run finishes in seconds
Short data transform steps that are safe to run twice
A small chain of steps behind an API call, using the sync mode, so the caller gets the answer back
Cutting Step Functions cost when you run millions of short workflows
nope: Do not use it for work that takes more than five minutes. Use a Standard workflow.
Do not use it for anything that must run exactly once, like charging a card. Use a Standard workflow.
Do not use it if you need human approval steps or long waits. Express does not support the callback or job-run patterns.
Do not use it if you need Distributed Map or Activities. Those are Standard only.
Do not go looking for it as a product to sign up for. You get it by choosing the type when you make a Step Functions state machine.
eg: A sensor sends readings every second. An Express workflow cleans each reading, checks it against a rule, and writes it to DynamoDB. Millions run a day and each takes under a second.
pay: You pay per run, plus the run time and the memory it used. There is no charge per step, unlike Standard workflows. Logs sent to CloudWatch cost extra. Check the Step Functions pricing page for current rates.

name: AWS Step Functions
one: Draws your multi step process as a flowchart that actually runs.
like: A checklist that ticks itself, remembers where it stopped, and retries the step that failed.
what: Step Functions coordinates several Lambdas or services in order, with branches, retries and waits. It remembers state, so a long process survives failures. You can see exactly which step failed.
when: A process with several steps
Steps that must retry
Anything that takes minutes or days
nope: A single function call.
pay: Per state transition. The Express type is cheaper for high volume.
eg: Order, then payment, then invoice, then email, with a retry if payment times out.

name: Amazon AppFlow
one: A managed way to move data between business apps like Salesforce or SAP and AWS, without writing the plumbing.
like: A courier between two offices that do not speak the same language. You say what to send and how often, and it goes.
what: Amazon AppFlow is a real AWS service. It copies data between software as a service apps and AWS. On one side you have apps like Salesforce, SAP, ServiceNow, Slack or Zendesk. On the other side you have AWS stores like Amazon S3 and Amazon Redshift. You set up a flow: pick the source, pick the target, map the fields, and pick when it runs. It can run on a schedule, on an event in the source app, or when you press run. It can filter rows, mask or drop fields, and combine data before it lands. Traffic can stay off the public internet using AWS PrivateLink. You do not build or run any connector code yourself.
when: Pulling Salesforce or SAP records into Amazon S3 for reporting
Feeding SaaS data into a data lake or warehouse on a schedule
Pushing AWS data back out into a business app so sales or support teams see it
Small to medium data syncs where you do not want to maintain custom API code
nope: Not for moving data between AWS databases. AWS Database Migration Service or AWS Glue fit better.
Not for app to app data that is already in your own systems and needs heavy transformation. AWS Glue gives more control.
Not for real time streaming. AppFlow runs flows, it is not a stream.
Not useful if your source app has no AppFlow connector. Check the supported list first, or write your own integration.
If you need complex joins or business logic in the middle, do that after landing the data, not in AppFlow.
eg: A company copies new Salesforce opportunities into Amazon S3 every hour, then reports on them in Amazon Athena next to their billing data.
pay: You pay per flow run, plus per GB of data processed. Prices differ by connector type. There is no monthly fee for keeping a flow that does not run. Check the AppFlow pricing page.

name: Amazon EventBridge
one: A router for events between services.
like: A post office that reads the address and delivers only to the right houses.
what: EventBridge takes events and sends them to targets based on rules you write. AWS services and some SaaS tools publish into it. It can also run things on a schedule, like a cron.
when: Many events with rules about who cares
Scheduled jobs
Reacting to AWS events
nope: A single simple hand off. SQS is simpler.
pay: Per million events. Scheduled rules are free.
eg: Run a report every night at 2am IST.

name: Amazon MQ
one: It runs ActiveMQ or RabbitMQ for you, so old applications keep talking the way they already do.
like: Keeping the same post room in a new office building, because everyone already knows how to address the envelopes.
what: It is a managed broker for standard protocols such as JMS, AMQP, MQTT and STOMP. The whole point is compatibility: you move an existing message-based application to AWS without rewriting its messaging code. It runs on fixed broker instances, so it does not scale automatically the way SQS does, and you still pick versions and maintenance windows.
when: Lifting an on-premises app that uses JMS or AMQP
You need a protocol SQS and SNS do not speak
Strict message ordering or transactions from an existing broker
nope: Writing something new on AWS, use SQS and SNS or EventBridge, they scale on their own and cost less
Very high throughput streaming, use Kinesis or MSK
eg: A logistics firm moves a Java application that uses JMS queues into AWS without touching the messaging code.
pay: Per broker-hour plus storage, whether or not any message flows. A redundant multi-zone deployment doubles it, and idle brokers are the usual waste.

name: Amazon Managed Workflows for Apache Airflow
one: It runs Apache Airflow for you, so scheduled data pipelines have somewhere to live.
like: Hiring a caretaker for a machine you already own. Same machine, same controls, you just stop doing the maintenance.
what: Airflow is the common open source tool for scheduling data jobs written as Python DAGs. MWAA runs the scheduler, workers and web UI inside your VPC and handles version upgrades. It is still Airflow, so the quirks, the Python dependency conflicts and the learning curve all come with it.
when: Your team already writes Airflow DAGs
Daily data pipelines with dependencies between many steps
You want to stay portable rather than tied to an AWS-only workflow tool
nope: A handful of scheduled tasks, use EventBridge Scheduler with Lambda
Event-driven application logic rather than batch data jobs, use Step Functions
eg: A data team runs a nightly DAG that pulls from three databases, transforms in Glue, and loads into Redshift.
pay: Per environment-hour for the scheduler and web server, plus workers and storage. The surprise is the base cost, roughly 350 dollars a month for a small environment even if no DAG ever runs.

name: Amazon Simple Notification Service
one: Sends one message to many listeners at once.
like: A WhatsApp group broadcast. One post, everyone in the group sees it.
what: SNS publishes a message to a topic. Everything subscribed gets a copy: queues, Lambda functions, emails, SMS. SQS is one to one, SNS is one to many.
when: One event must trigger several things
Alerts to a team
nope: You need a durable work queue. Use SQS.
pay: Per million publishes, plus SMS charges which are not cheap.
eg: A payment succeeds, so an email goes out, stock updates and analytics record it.

name: Amazon Simple Queue Service
one: A waiting line for tasks.
like: A ticket counter. Work is dropped in the queue and picked up when someone is free.
what: SQS holds messages until a worker takes them. If the worker crashes the message comes back. It protects you from traffic spikes. Standard queues can deliver a message twice, so your worker must handle that.
when: Slow work that should not block the user
Absorbing spikes
Separating parts of a system
nope: You need an instant answer back to the user.
pay: Per million requests. Very cheap.
eg: Order placed, a message goes in the queue, invoices are generated in the background.

name: AWS App Studio
one: Describe a business app in plain words and it builds a working one for you.
like: Telling a joiner "I need a cupboard with three shelves and a lock" and getting the cupboard, rather than the wood.
what: You type what the app should do, and it generates the data model, the screens and the logic, then hosts it for you. It is aimed at internal business apps, approvals, trackers, small workflows, built by people who are not developers. It is narrow: you cannot export the code to run elsewhere, styling is limited, and anything unusual needs a developer anyway. It sits opposite tools like Power Apps and Retool.
when: A small internal tool nobody has time to build properly
A non-developer team needs a form and a workflow on AWS data
Prototyping a process before committing engineering time
nope: Anything customer-facing or with real design needs, build a normal web app
Apps you may need to move off AWS later, there is no code to take with you
Heavy logic or integrations, a developer with Lambda and a frontend will be faster
eg: An operations team builds a leave request tracker that reads staff records and emails the manager.
pay: Per hour that someone is actively building, and per hour that published apps are used. Publishing an app many staff use all day is where the cost lands.

name: AWS Deep Learning AMIs
one: A ready-made server image with the AI tools already installed.
like: Buying a kitchen that already has the oven, pans and knives fitted, instead of an empty room you have to kit out yourself.
what: An Amazon Machine Image, a template you launch an EC2 server from, that comes with PyTorch, GPU drivers, CUDA and the usual Python stack preinstalled and tested together. It saves you a day of driver pain. It is not a managed service, so once the server is running you patch it, secure it and shut it down yourself, and the running server costs the same as any GPU instance.
when: You want a GPU box for training or experiments and do not want to install drivers
You need full control of the machine, SSH access included
You are testing on one instance before moving to something bigger
nope: If you want training runs, tuning and endpoints managed for you, use SageMaker AI instead
If you ship in containers, use Deep Learning Containers on ECS or EKS instead of a hand-kept server
eg: A researcher launches a g6 GPU instance from the Deep Learning AMI, fine-tunes a small model overnight, and terminates it in the morning.
pay: The AMI is free. You pay the normal EC2 GPU hourly rate plus storage, and the storage keeps billing after you stop the instance. Forgetting to terminate a GPU box is the classic bill shock.

name: AWS Deep Learning Containers
one: Prebuilt Docker images with PyTorch and its GPU parts already working.
like: A sealed meal kit. Everything inside is already measured and known to go together, so you just heat it.
what: Docker images AWS builds and keeps in its own registry, with PyTorch, the GPU libraries and AWS bits installed and version matched. You run them on ECS, EKS, SageMaker AI or plain EC2, and you can build your own image on top. They are just images, so nothing is managed for you, and AWS stops updating older framework versions, so you have to move up over time.
when: You run training or inference jobs as containers
You want the same image locally and in the cloud
You want to avoid matching CUDA to framework versions by hand
nope: If you want one server to log into and tinker with, the Deep Learning AMI is simpler
If you only call a hosted model through an API, you do not need containers at all, use Amazon Bedrock
eg: A team bases its training image on the AWS PyTorch GPU container, adds its own code, and runs it as a SageMaker training job.
pay: The images are free to pull. You pay for whatever runs them, the ECS, EKS, EC2 or SageMaker compute, plus ECR storage if you push your own version.

name: AWS DeepRacer
one: A toy race car game that taught people reinforcement learning, now shut down as an AWS service.
like: A driving school in a car park. The car was small and the stakes were zero, but you learned how steering works.
what: You wrote a reward function, trained a model in a simulator and raced a 1/18 scale car on a virtual or real track. It was a teaching tool, never a production service. AWS closed the DeepRacer console service in December 2025 and ended the racing league after 2024. The code now lives on as a solution you deploy into your own AWS account. Almost nobody needs this unless they are running a learning event.
when: You are running an internal training event on reinforcement learning
You want a hands-on way to understand reward functions
You already own the physical cars and want to keep using them
nope: If you want to actually learn modern machine learning for work, skip it and use SageMaker AI with real data
If you want a reinforcement learning system in production, build it yourself, DeepRacer was never meant for that
eg: A company ran an internal DeepRacer day in 2023 so its developers could feel what training a model is like.
pay: The hosted service is gone, so there is no service charge. Deploying the open solution yourself costs whatever the training compute and simulation instances cost, which is not trivial.

name: AWS Elemental Inference
one: A media focused machine learning capability. We could not confirm the current details.
like: A sign on a door we could not open to look inside.
what: This appears in the AWS icon set under media services. We could not verify what it currently is, or whether it is generally available, from an official AWS page during this research. It is deliberately left unconfirmed here rather than described from guesswork. Check the AWS media services documentation for the current position.
nope: Do not plan around this entry. Confirm with AWS first
pay: Not confirmed.

name: AWS HealthImaging
one: Storage for hospital scan images that keeps them fast to open.
like: A hospital film library where any X-ray can be pulled off the shelf in a second, however old it is.
what: It stores medical images in the DICOM format that scanners produce, and serves them back quickly enough for a radiologist to scroll through a study. It handles the storage and the fast retrieval. It is not a viewer and not a diagnosis tool, you still need viewing software on top, and it only makes sense if you work with DICOM imaging.
when: You run or build for a hospital, imaging centre or medical imaging vendor
You have a growing archive of scans that is expensive to keep on disk
You want to run AI models over imaging data
nope: If your images are ordinary photos or documents, use S3, it is far cheaper and simpler
If you need the clinical records rather than the pictures, use HealthLake
eg: A radiology group moves ten years of CT studies into HealthImaging so old scans still open in a few seconds.
pay: You pay for stored data, for each image set you import, and per request when images are read. Heavy viewing traffic, not storage, is what usually pushes the bill up.

name: AWS HealthLake
one: A place to put patient records so you can search and analyse them.
like: Taking filing cabinets of patient notes from different clinics and retyping them all onto one standard form, so you can finally compare them.
what: It stores health data in FHIR, the standard format healthcare systems use, and adds search plus export to analytics tools. It can pull structured facts out of doctors' free text notes. It is a narrow service for regulated healthcare work and it does not make you compliant on its own, you still sign a BAA and design your access controls.
when: You are building healthcare software that must speak FHIR
You need to combine records from several clinical systems
You want to run analytics or AI across patient data
nope: If you are not in healthcare, this is the wrong shape entirely, use a normal database
If you only need to store documents or images, use S3 or HealthImaging
eg: An insurer loads claims and clinical records into HealthLake to find patients overdue for a follow up.
pay: You pay for stored data and per request, and separately for the text analysis on notes. The data store runs continuously, so it costs money even on a quiet day.

name: AWS HealthOmics
one: Runs genetics analysis pipelines and stores the huge files they produce.
like: An industrial laundry. You hand over a very large load, machines you do not own do the work, and you get the finished result back.
what: It has three parts, storage for genome sequence files, workflows that run your existing WDL or Nextflow pipelines on AWS managed compute, and analytics tables over variant data. It does not write the science for you, you bring the pipeline. This is for genomics teams only and most engineers will never open it.
when: You process sequencing data and already have WDL or Nextflow pipelines
Your genome files are too big and too many to manage by hand
You want runs tracked and repeatable for regulators
nope: If your pipeline is not genomics, use AWS Batch or Step Functions, they are cheaper and more flexible
If you just need bulk file storage, S3 alone is fine
eg: A lab runs variant calling on a thousand samples as a HealthOmics workflow instead of babysitting its own cluster.
pay: You pay for sequence storage, for the compute a workflow run uses, and for analytics queries. Storage has an active and an archive tier, and pulling data back out of archive costs extra and is slow.

name: AWS HealthScribe
one: Listens to a doctor and patient talking and writes up the clinical note.
like: A very fast medical secretary sitting in the corner of the room taking notes.
what: HealthScribe turns a recorded consultation into a structured clinical note, with the transcript, the speakers separated, and sections like history and assessment. Every line it writes links back to the moment in the audio, so a clinician can check it. It is a drafting tool and the clinician still signs off. It supports English only.
when: Cutting the time doctors spend typing notes
Building a scribe feature into medical software
nope: General meeting notes, Amazon Transcribe plus a summariser is cheaper
Anything that decides treatment, it drafts, it does not diagnose
eg: A fifteen minute consultation comes back as a draft note the doctor edits in two minutes instead of ten.
pay: Per minute of audio processed. Long consultations add up, so most teams cap the recording length.

name: AWS Neuron
one: The free software kit that lets your model run on AWS's own AI chips.
like: A plug adapter for a different country. Your appliance works, but only once the adapter is in.
what: Neuron is the compiler, runtime, drivers and profiling tools for Trainium and Inferentia. It plugs into PyTorch and JAX so your code mostly looks normal. The honest limitation is coverage, a model or an operator only works if Neuron supports it, and support lags behind the newest research. Check the supported model list before you plan a migration.
when: You are moving training or inference onto Trainium or Inferentia
You need to profile why a model is slow on those chips
You want to write custom kernels for them using NKI
nope: If you are staying on Nvidia GPUs, you never touch Neuron, use CUDA
If your model is brand new or exotic, check support first, and expect to stay on GPUs if it is missing
eg: A team adds a few lines of torch-neuronx to their training script so the same code runs on Trn instances.
pay: Neuron itself is free. You pay only for the EC2 instances. The real cost is the days spent getting a model to compile and match its GPU accuracy.

name: AWS Panorama
one: A discontinued box that ran computer vision on existing security cameras.
like: A clever set top box wired into the CCTV, watching the feeds so a person did not have to. The maker has now stopped supporting it.
what: Panorama was a hardware appliance plus a service that took feeds from ordinary IP cameras and ran vision models on site, so video never left the building. AWS stopped taking new customers in May 2025 and ends support on 31 May 2026, after which the console and resources go away. Do not start anything new on it. AWS points people to SageMaker for the models and IoT Greengrass, EKS or ECS Anywhere for running them on site.
when: Only relevant if you already own appliances and are planning your exit before May 2026
nope: For any new on-site vision project, build the model in SageMaker AI and deploy it with AWS IoT Greengrass instead
If the video can go to the cloud, plain cloud inference on EC2 or SageMaker is simpler than edge hardware
eg: A factory used Panorama to spot missing safety helmets on its existing camera feeds, and is now moving that model to Greengrass on its own hardware.
pay: Moot now. It was appliance hardware bought up front plus a monthly charge per deployed model per device.

name: Amazon Augmented AI A2I
one: Sends the AI's unsure answers to a human to check.
like: A machine that sorts post, and drops anything with messy handwriting into a tray for a person to read.
what: You set a confidence score. If a model's answer scores below it, A2I puts that item in a queue with a simple review screen, and a human fixes or confirms it. The reviewers are your own staff, a vendor, or Mechanical Turk workers. It is a workflow tool, it does no AI of its own, and it only plugs neatly into a few AWS services like Textract and Rekognition.
when: Document or image AI where a wrong answer costs money
A regulator or auditor wants a human in the loop
You need the corrected answers as training data later
nope: Simple yes or no checking by a few staff, a small internal web page and a database table is less work
Text or chat review, most teams just build their own queue with SQS and a form
eg: An invoice scanner reads a total as 1,00O instead of 1,000 with low confidence, so it lands in a clerk's review queue.
pay: You pay per object reviewed, plus the worker cost if you use Mechanical Turk. The surprise is that the human time, not AWS, is the real bill.

name: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
one: Runs an AI agent as a live service, with memory and tools attached.
like: An office for a new assistant, with a desk, a filing cabinet, a locked key drawer and a phone line, rather than the assistant itself.
what: A set of separate pieces you can pick from: Runtime hosts your agent code in an isolated sandbox for long sessions, Memory stores short and long term notes, Gateway turns your APIs into tools the agent can call, Identity handles who the agent is acting for, plus a browser and a code interpreter it can use. You still write the agent. It is new, it moves fast, and the pieces are billed and used independently.
when: An agent that runs for minutes and needs to remember across sessions
You want your existing APIs exposed to an agent safely
You need the agent to browse or run code in a sandbox
nope: A single prompt and answer, call Bedrock directly
Short tool-calling flows, Lambda plus Step Functions is cheaper and easier to debug
eg: A support agent that remembers a customer's past tickets, looks up their order through your API, and holds a ten minute conversation.
pay: Per vCPU-hour and GB-hour while the agent is active, plus separate charges for memory records, gateway calls and web search. A parked agent that never sleeps properly is the usual surprise.

name: Amazon Bedrock
one: Use ready made AI models, including Claude, through one API.
like: A tap. The water treatment plant already exists, you just open the tap.
what: Bedrock gives access to foundation models from several providers without managing any servers. Your data is not used to train the models. It supports retrieval from your own documents and agents that take actions.
when: Adding AI to an app
Summarising, extracting, chatting, classifying
nope: A simple rule would do the job.
You need to train on your own data from scratch. Use SageMaker.
pay: Per thousand input and output tokens. Provisioned capacity is also available.
eg: Reading a scanned invoice and pulling out the amount and date.

name: Amazon CodeGuru
one: Reviewed your code and found slow spots in running apps, and is now mostly closed.
like: A picky senior colleague who read your pull requests and timed your app with a stopwatch, who has since left.
what: Two parts. Reviewer commented on pull requests. Profiler watched a running app and showed which lines burned CPU. As of November 2025 you cannot add new repositories to Reviewer, and AWS points people to Amazon Q Developer for reviews and Amazon Inspector for security scanning. Profiler and the security scanning bits live on under other names. Treat CodeGuru as a service on the way out.
when: You already have existing repository associations running
You want CPU profiling of a live Java or Python app
nope: New code review setups, use Amazon Q Developer or a normal linter and human review
Security scanning, use Amazon Inspector
eg: A team learned one logging call in a hot loop was eating a quarter of their CPU.
pay: Reviewer charged per hundred lines scanned per month, Profiler per sampled hour. Large monorepos made the line count bill jump.

name: Amazon CodeWhisperer
one: The old name for AWS code autocomplete, now folded into Amazon Q Developer.
like: A shop sign that was painted over. Same shop, new name.
what: CodeWhisperer suggested code in your editor as you typed. On 30 April 2024 it became part of Amazon Q Developer, which kept the inline suggestions and security scans and added chat, agents and AWS troubleshooting. The name CodeWhisperer no longer exists as a product, so if a tutorial or exam question uses it, read it as Q Developer.
when: Reading old documents or exam material that still uses the name
nope: Anything you are building today, install Amazon Q Developer instead
Broad agentic coding work, most people use a dedicated coding agent
eg: An old blog post tells you to enable CodeWhisperer in VS Code, and the plugin you actually install is Amazon Q.
pay: Nothing, it no longer exists. Q Developer has a free tier and a paid per user per month tier.

name: Amazon Comprehend Medical
one: Pulls medicines, doses, conditions and symptoms out of doctors' notes.
like: A nurse who reads a scrawled handover sheet and writes the drugs and doses neatly on a form.
what: You send free text from a clinical note and get back structured items: drug name, strength, frequency, condition, test results, plus links to standard medical codes like RxNorm and ICD-10-CM. It also finds personal health details so you can mask them. It reads English only, it extracts rather than diagnoses, and AWS is clear it is not a medical device, so a clinician still has to check the output.
when: Turning piles of clinical notes into searchable data
Stripping patient identifiers before research use
Coding notes for billing, with human review
nope: General business text, plain Amazon Comprehend is far cheaper
Anything that decides patient care on its own, it is not approved for that
eg: A note saying "pt on metformin 500mg BD" comes back as drug metformin, strength 500 mg, frequency twice daily.
pay: Per unit of 100 characters, with a minimum charge per request. Sending thousands of tiny requests instead of batching is what inflates the bill.

name: Amazon Comprehend
one: Finds meaning inside plain text.
like: A reader who highlights the names, places and mood in a letter.
what: Comprehend pulls out entities, key phrases, sentiment and language from text. It also detects personal data, which is useful for privacy work.
when: Sorting support tickets
Sentiment on reviews
Finding personal data in text
nope: Complex reasoning. Use Bedrock.
pay: Per unit of text processed.
eg: Flagging angry support messages so they are answered first.

name: Amazon DevOps Guru
one: Watches your AWS metrics and tells you when something looks wrong and probably why.
like: A caretaker who knows the normal hum of the building and rings you when a pipe sounds different.
what: It learns the normal pattern of your CloudWatch metrics, logs and events, then raises an insight when things drift, grouping related symptoms into one report with a likely cause and a suggested fix. It needs weeks of data before it is useful, it only sees AWS resources, and in practice many teams find the insights too vague and go back to hand-written alarms.
when: You run many AWS services and have no time to tune alarms
Nobody on the team knows what normal looks like yet
You want RDS-specific slow query diagnosis
nope: A small app with a handful of metrics, plain CloudWatch alarms are cheaper and clearer
Deep tracing of a request through microservices, use X-Ray or a proper APM tool
eg: It flags that a DynamoDB table started throttling twenty minutes before the checkout errors began.
pay: Per resource-hour analysed, plus per API call. The shock is that it charges for every resource in the account, so switching it on account-wide is expensive.

name: Amazon Elastic Inference
one: A retired way to bolt a slice of a GPU onto a normal server.
like: Renting a quarter of a power tool instead of the whole thing. The rental shop has since closed.
what: It let you attach a fraction of GPU acceleration to an EC2 instance or SageMaker endpoint, so you paid less than a full GPU for models that only needed a little help. AWS stopped taking new customers in April 2023 and has wound it down. Do not design anything around it. The modern answers are Inferentia instances, SageMaker serverless inference, or just a small GPU instance.
when: Nothing. It is retired
nope: Cheap inference today, use Inferentia (inf1/inf2) or SageMaker serverless inference
Occasional inference, use Lambda or a Bedrock model and skip servers entirely
eg: An exam question from 2021 offers it as the cheap way to run a PyTorch model, which is no longer the real answer.
pay: It billed per accelerator-hour alongside the instance. Not relevant now.

name: Amazon Forecast
one: Predicted future numbers from your past numbers, and is closed to new customers.
like: A shopkeeper's notebook that guesses next month's sales from the last three years, and the notebook is no longer sold.
what: You uploaded a history of dated values, plus extras like price and holidays, and it trained time series models and returned predictions with a range, not a single number. AWS closed it to new customers on 29 July 2024 and adds no new features. Existing users can still run it. New work goes to Amazon SageMaker Canvas, which does the same forecasting job.
when: You are an existing customer with pipelines already built
nope: Any new forecasting project, use SageMaker Canvas or a normal library like Prophet on a small instance
Forecasting a handful of series, a spreadsheet or simple script will do
eg: A retailer predicted per-store demand per product for the next six weeks to decide reorders.
pay: Charged for data storage, training hours and per thousand forecasts. Training runs on hundreds of thousands of series were the expensive part.

name: Amazon Fraud Detector
one: Scores an online action as likely fraud or not, using your own past cases.
like: A shop manager who has seen enough shoplifters to get a feeling about a particular customer at the till.
what: You upload historic events labelled fraud or legitimate, it trains a model, and you then send live events and get a score from 0 to 1000 plus an outcome from rules you write. It needs a decent volume of labelled history, roughly ten thousand events with at least a few hundred frauds, so a new business usually cannot use it. It scores, it does not block, your code has to act on the outcome.
when: Account signup abuse or fake reviews at reasonable volume
Guest checkout payment fraud where you have labelled history
You want rules and a model in one place
nope: Card payment fraud where your payment provider already screens, you would pay twice for the same check
A new product with no fraud history, start with hand-written rules
Anything where you must explain each decision precisely to a regulator
eg: A signup from a fresh email on a known hosting IP scores 890, so your code sends it to manual review.
pay: Per prediction, plus training and hosting hours. Scoring every page view rather than the few risky moments is the classic overspend.

name: Amazon Kendra
one: A search box for your company's documents that understands questions, not just keywords.
like: A librarian who answers "what is our parental leave policy" instead of handing you every book with the word leave in it.
what: It connects to sources like S3, SharePoint, Confluence and Salesforce, indexes them, and answers natural language questions with the passage and the source document. It respects the permissions of the source, so people only see what they may see. It is expensive, priced by the hour whether or not anyone searches, and since Bedrock Knowledge Bases arrived many teams pick that instead.
when: Enterprise document search across many systems with per-user permissions
You want answers with citations from internal files
Connectors matter more than cost
nope: A handful of documents, a Bedrock Knowledge Base or OpenSearch costs far less
Searching structured records in a database, that is SQL, not Kendra
Public website search, a small OpenSearch index or a hosted search tool is cheaper
eg: A support agent types "can a customer cancel after 30 days" and gets the exact clause from the contract PDF.
pay: Per index-hour, running around a thousand dollars a month for the Developer edition and much more for Enterprise, even at zero queries. That fixed hourly charge is the surprise.

name: Amazon Lex
one: Builds a chatbot or phone bot that works out what the caller wants.
like: A phone menu that lets you say "I want to change my flight" instead of pressing 4, then asks which flight.
what: You define intents (things a user might want) and slots (details to collect), and Lex handles the conversation, asks for missing details, and calls your Lambda to do the work. It is the engine behind Alexa. It is intent-based, so it handles defined tasks well and open-ended chat badly. Many teams now put a Bedrock model behind or beside it for the free-form parts.
when: Phone or chat flows with a fixed set of tasks
Call centre self-service in front of Amazon Connect
You need speech and text with one definition
nope: Open-ended conversation or reasoning, use Bedrock with a model directly
A simple FAQ, a search page or a Knowledge Base is less work to maintain
eg: A caller says "track my order 4471" and the bot reads back the delivery date from your database.
pay: Per text request and per speech request. Voice costs roughly four times text, and retries during a confused call are all billable.

name: Amazon Lookout for Equipment
one: Learns the normal readings of a machine and warns when they drift, and it is being shut down.
like: A mechanic who knows how your car normally sounds and says something is off before it breaks.
what: You feed it sensor history from an industrial machine, it learns normal behaviour with no failure labels needed, then flags abnormal periods and says which sensors drove the flag. AWS closed it to new customers and support ends on 7 October 2026, so do not start anything new on it. You need existing sensors and a data historian already in place.
when: Nothing new. Existing users should be planning a move
nope: Any new predictive maintenance project, use SageMaker anomaly detection or a vendor platform like your historian's own tooling
Sites with no sensors, you need hardware first
eg: A pump's vibration and temperature drift together for three days before a bearing fails.
pay: Charged for data ingest, training hours and per hour of inference scheduling. Not worth planning around now.

name: Amazon Lookout for Vision
one: Spotted defects in photos of products on a line, and has been discontinued.
like: A quality inspector on a conveyor belt who pulls off the cracked tiles. The inspector has been let go.
what: You gave it photos of good and bad parts, it trained a model, and it then judged new photos as normal or anomalous, optionally marking where the defect was. AWS stopped new customer access in October 2024 and ended support on 31 October 2025. It is gone. Build visual inspection on SageMaker with your own model, or use a specialist machine vision vendor.
when: Nothing. It is discontinued
nope: New visual inspection, train a small image model on SageMaker or buy a machine vision system
General image labelling, use Amazon Rekognition
eg: A line camera photographed each circuit board and the model flagged missing solder.
pay: It billed training hours and inference hours. No longer relevant.

name: Amazon Monitron
one: A sensor you stick on a motor that warns when it starts running badly, no longer sold to new customers.
like: A smoke alarm for a machine. You stick it on, it beeps on your phone when something changes.
what: An end to end kit: a battery powered vibration and temperature sensor, a gateway, a phone app and a service that learns normal and sends alerts. It was the no-expertise option for factories. AWS closed it to new customers on 31 October 2024 and stopped device sales in July 2025, honouring warranties and support for existing users. Do not plan new deployments.
when: Nothing new. Existing installs continue under warranty
nope: New condition monitoring, buy from a vibration sensor vendor with its own platform
Anything needing custom sensor types, Monitron only ever read vibration and temperature
eg: A sensor on a conveyor motor sends a phone alert that vibration has climbed out of its normal band.
pay: You bought the sensors and gateways, then paid a yearly per sensor fee. The recurring per sensor fee across hundreds of machines was the part people underestimated.

name: Amazon Nova
one: Amazon's own family of AI models, sold through Bedrock.
like: A supermarket's own-brand range sitting on the shelf next to the big names, cheaper, and fine for a lot of jobs.
what: A set of models rather than a service: Micro, Lite, Pro and Premier for text and reasoning, Canvas for images, Reel for video, and Sonic for speech in and speech out. They are notably cheap per token and fast. On hard reasoning and coding they generally trail the frontier models from Anthropic and others, so people often use Nova for high volume simple work and something stronger for the hard calls.
when: High volume classification, extraction or summarising where cost matters
You want image or video generation inside Bedrock
Low latency speech conversations with Nova Sonic
nope: Difficult reasoning, long code changes or agent work, pick a stronger model on Bedrock
Running outside AWS, Nova is Bedrock only
eg: Tagging a million support emails by topic with Nova Micro for a few dollars.
pay: Per million input and output tokens, at the cheap end of Bedrock. The surprise is not the token price but provisioned throughput, which bills by the hour whether you use it or not.

name: Amazon Personalize
one: Builds the "you might also like" list for your site from what your users actually did.
like: A shop assistant who remembers what you bought last time and points you at the aisle you probably want.
what: You send it user actions, item details and user details, it trains recommendation models, and you query it live for a ranked list for a given user. It handles new users and new items reasonably. It needs real scale to work, roughly a thousand users and tens of thousands of interactions minimum, and it is a black box, so you cannot easily explain any single recommendation.
when: A catalogue with many items and steady traffic
Personalised ordering of a feed or search results
You have interaction history but no ML team
nope: A small catalogue, "most popular" and "bought together" queries in SQL get you most of the benefit
A new site with no user history, there is nothing to learn from
Recommendations you must justify to a user or regulator
eg: A streaming site reorders the home page rows per viewer based on what they finished watching.
pay: Training hours, data ingest, and per thousand recommendation requests, plus an hourly charge for the minimum provisioned capacity on a live campaign. That idle hourly charge catches people.

name: Amazon Polly
one: Turns written text into a natural sounding voice.
like: A newsreader who will read anything you hand over.
what: Polly converts text to speech in many languages and voices, including Indian English and Hindi. Neural voices sound noticeably better than the standard ones.
when: Audio versions of lessons
Accessibility
Voice notifications
nope: You need a specific human's voice.
pay: Per million characters.
eg: Turning a written lesson into an audio file students can listen to.

name: Amazon Q
one: An AI assistant for AWS work, split into one for developers and one for business users.
like: A colleague who has read the whole manual and all your internal documents, sitting next to you.
what: Two different products under one name. Q Developer lives in your IDE, terminal and the AWS console, suggests code, scans for security issues and answers AWS questions against your account. Q Business connects to company systems like SharePoint and Slack and answers staff questions with citations, respecting each person's permissions. AWS has said the Q Developer IDE plugins end on 30 April 2027 in favour of Kiro, so expect more name changes.
when: Asking why an AWS resource is misconfigured, with account context
Inline code suggestions for AWS SDK work
An internal question-answering assistant over company documents
nope: General coding away from AWS, a dedicated coding agent is stronger
A custom chatbot in your own product, build on Bedrock instead
A small team wiki, Q Business has a high per user cost for what it gives
eg: You ask the console "why can't this Lambda reach my RDS instance" and it points at the missing security group rule.
pay: Q Developer is free for basic use, about 19 dollars per user per month for Pro. Q Business is roughly 20 dollars per user per month plus index charges, and it bills per assigned user even if they never log in.

name: Amazon Rekognition
one: Understands what is in a picture or video.
like: A person who can glance at a photo and tell you what is in it.
what: Rekognition detects objects, text, unsafe content and faces in images and video. Face features carry real privacy and legal weight, so check the law before using them on people.
when: Moderating uploaded images
Finding text in photos
Counting objects
nope: Reading a structured document. Use Textract.
pay: Per image or per minute of video.
eg: Automatically rejecting an uploaded profile photo that is not a face.

name: Amazon SageMaker AI
one: Build and train your own machine learning models.
like: A full workshop with tools, benches and machines, for making something custom.
what: SageMaker covers the whole machine learning lifecycle: prepare data, train, tune, deploy, monitor. It is for building your own model. If you just want to use an existing AI model, Bedrock is far simpler.
when: You have your own data and a real ML problem
You need a custom model
nope: You want to use a ready made model. Use Bedrock.
pay: Per instance hour for notebooks, training and endpoints. Idle endpoints are a classic waste.
eg: Training a model on your own sales data to predict next month's demand.

name: Amazon SageMaker Ground Truth
one: Gets humans to label your training data, and manages the whole labelling job.
like: Hiring a room of temps to go through a mountain of photos and circle every car, with a supervisor checking the work.
what: You point it at data in S3, choose a task type such as bounding boxes or text classification, and it builds the labelling interface and hands work to your own staff, a vetted vendor, or Mechanical Turk. It can auto-label the easy items with a model it trains as it goes and only send the hard ones to people. Quality management is still your job, and labelling instructions are where most projects go wrong.
when: Thousands of images or documents needing labels
Sensitive data that must stay with your own reviewers
You want active learning to cut the human labelling cost
nope: A few hundred items, label them yourself in a spreadsheet or a free tool
Text data a model can label well already, have an LLM do a first pass and spot-check it
eg: Labelling ten thousand shelf photos with boxes around each product before training a stock detector.
pay: Per labelled object, plus the workforce cost and the auto-labelling compute. A three-way agreement check triples the per-object price.

name: Amazon SageMaker Studio Lab
one: A free notebook for learning machine learning, with no AWS account, now closing to new users.
like: A free practice room at a music school. Anyone could book a slot, and the school has stopped issuing new keys.
what: You signed up with just an email, got a JupyterLab environment with a few free CPU or GPU hours per session and persistent storage, and no bill was possible. It was for students and learners, not production. AWS is closing new customer access from 30 July 2026, pointing people at SageMaker Studio instead. Sessions were always time-limited and could be interrupted.
when: Nothing new if you cannot already sign in
nope: Real work, use SageMaker Studio or a plain EC2 instance
Free notebooks today, Google Colab or Kaggle notebooks fill the same gap
eg: A student ran a PyTorch tutorial on a free GPU without giving a card number.
pay: Free, and it could not bill you. That was the whole point.

name: Amazon Textract
one: Pulls text and tables out of scanned documents.
like: A clerk who types up a scanned form into a spreadsheet, including the table.
what: Textract reads printed and handwritten text, and understands forms and tables, unlike basic OCR. It returns structured data with a confidence score for each field.
when: Invoices, forms, ID documents, receipts
nope: A clean digital PDF you can already read.
pay: Per page, more for forms and tables.
eg: Reading a scanned purchase order into your system.

name: Amazon Transcribe
one: Turns speech into written text.
like: A stenographer who types everything that is said.
what: Transcribe converts audio and video to text, with timestamps and speaker labels. It handles Indian English. Accuracy drops with heavy background noise or heavy code switching.
when: Subtitles for lessons
Meeting notes
Making audio searchable
nope: Very poor audio. Fix the recording first.
pay: Per second of audio.
eg: Auto subtitles on a recorded class.

name: Amazon Translate
one: Translates text between languages.
like: An interpreter who works instantly and never tires.
what: Translate converts text between many languages including Hindi and Gujarati. Quality is good for general text and weaker on specialised jargon unless you give it a custom glossary.
when: Multi language content
Translating user messages
nope: Legal or medical text where a mistake is serious. Use a human.
pay: Per million characters.
eg: Showing course descriptions in Gujarati as well as English.

name: Apache MXNet on AWS
one: AWS support for an old deep learning framework that is no longer maintained.
like: A car model the maker stopped producing. Some still run, but no parts are being made.
what: MXNet was an open source deep learning framework AWS backed heavily around 2016 to 2020, with prebuilt images, SageMaker containers and Deep Learning AMIs. Apache moved MXNet to the Attic in 2023, meaning it is retired with no further releases, and AWS has dropped it from newer Deep Learning Containers. It still turns up in old AWS tutorials and exam material. Nobody should start a new project on it.
when: Keeping an existing MXNet model alive long enough to port it
nope: Any new model, use PyTorch, which is what almost everyone uses now
Serving an old MXNet model long term, export it to ONNX and run it somewhere supported
eg: An old SageMaker notebook imports mxnet and fails on a current container image.
pay: The framework was free. You only ever paid for the EC2 or SageMaker compute under it.

name: PyTorch on AWS
one: Not a service, just the many ways to run the PyTorch framework on AWS.
like: A shop's sign saying we sell shoes. The sign is not itself a shoe.
what: PyTorch is open source software from the PyTorch Foundation for building and training neural networks. PyTorch on AWS is a marketing page, not something you can switch on or get a bill for. What it points to is real, the Deep Learning AMIs and Containers, SageMaker AI training jobs, GPU and Trainium instances, and the Neuron plugin. If you are looking for a service to enable, there is not one.
when: You are deciding where to run PyTorch training or inference on AWS
You want the AWS-maintained builds rather than installing everything yourself
nope: Do not look for a PyTorch service to turn on, pick SageMaker AI, EC2 or ECS and run PyTorch there
If you only want to call an existing model, you do not need PyTorch at all, use Amazon Bedrock
eg: A developer reads the page, then launches a Deep Learning Container on SageMaker AI to train a PyTorch model.
pay: Nothing for PyTorch, it is free and open source. You pay only for whatever compute and storage you run it on, and GPU hours are the bulk of it.

name: TensorFlow on AWS
one: Not a service. It is the ways you can run the TensorFlow library on AWS.
like: A page telling you which of the shop's ovens will bake your particular recipe.
what: TensorFlow is open source software from Google for machine learning. AWS does not sell it. This entry covers the routes to run it: on SageMaker, on a Deep Learning AMI, in a Deep Learning Container, or on a plain GPU instance you set up yourself. There is nothing here to switch on.
when: You already have TensorFlow code and need somewhere to run it
nope: If you want to use a ready made AI model, use Bedrock and skip all of this
If you are starting fresh, most teams now pick PyTorch
eg: A team lifts an existing TensorFlow training script onto a SageMaker training job without changing the code.
pay: Nothing for TensorFlow itself. You pay for whichever compute you run it on, and GPU instances are the expensive part.

name: Amazon Managed Blockchain
one: Runs blockchain networks so you do not have to operate the nodes yourself.
like: Renting a seat at a shared ledger that several companies all write into, with someone else maintaining the room.
what: Two separate things sit under this name. One creates and runs a private Hyperledger Fabric network between named members. The other gives you access to public blockchain nodes, mainly Ethereum and Bitcoin, so you can read and write without running your own node. Very few business problems actually need a blockchain, and a shared database with good audit logging solves most of them.
when: Several companies that do not trust each other must share one record
You need public chain node access without operating nodes
nope: Keeping an audit trail inside one company, an append only table with row level security is far simpler and cheaper
Anything where one organisation owns the data, a normal database is the honest answer
eg: Three logistics firms record container handovers on one shared ledger that none of them alone can rewrite.
pay: Per node hour and per GB of data written, or per request for node access. Idle nodes keep billing, which is the usual surprise.

name: AWS AppFabric
one: It pulls the activity logs out of your SaaS apps and puts them in one place.
like: Every shop in a mall keeps its own visitor book in its own format. AppFabric collects all the books nightly and rewrites them in one common format so security can actually read them.
what: You connect SaaS tools like Slack, Zoom, Okta or Asana, and AppFabric fetches their audit logs, converts them to the OCSF standard schema and drops them in S3 or sends them to a security tool. It is read-only plumbing for logs and user lists, not a way to control those apps. The catch is the connector list: if your app is not on it, AppFabric does nothing for you.
when: You run many SaaS apps and want their audit logs in one SIEM
Security asks who did what across tools
You want a user inventory across SaaS apps
nope: Your apps are not on the supported connector list, write to the vendor APIs or use your SIEM vendor's own connectors
You want to sync data or automate actions between SaaS apps, that is a job for EventBridge or an iPaaS like Workato
eg: A 300 person company sends Slack, Zoom and Okta audit logs through AppFabric into Splunk so one query can find every login from a new country.
pay: Charged per GB of log data ingested, plus the S3 storage and the SIEM ingestion cost on the other side. The SIEM bill is usually the bigger surprise.

name: AWS End User Messaging
one: It sends SMS, voice calls and phone push notifications from your code.
like: A post office counter that will send a text, place a recorded call or ping someone's phone for you, and handles the paperwork with the phone companies.
what: This is the SMS, MMS, voice and mobile push part of Amazon Pinpoint, renamed in 2024 and kept alive while the rest of Pinpoint is retired. It handles phone numbers, sender IDs, carrier registration and one-time passcodes. It sends messages, it does not decide who to message or track campaigns, that logic is yours. Note the API and SDK clients are still called pinpoint, which confuses people.
when: Sending one-time passcodes or login codes
Order and delivery alerts by SMS
Push notifications to your iOS or Android app
nope: You want email, use Amazon SES instead
You want campaign scheduling, segments and journeys, that was Pinpoint and it ends 30 October 2026, look at Amazon Connect outbound campaigns or a third party like Braze
eg: A food delivery app texts a six digit login code and later pushes a notification when the rider is two minutes away.
pay: Per message, and the price varies a lot by destination country. What surprises people is the per number monthly rental plus one-off carrier registration fees, for example US 10DLC registration.

name: AWS Supply Chain
one: It reads your existing ERP data and warns you when stock is about to run short.
