like: A shop manager who walks the stockroom every morning, checks what is arriving, and tells you which shelf will be empty on Thursday.
what: It connects to SAP, Oracle or flat files, builds a data lake of your inventory, orders and suppliers, and then runs demand forecasting, supply planning and risk alerts on top. It is a finished application, not a toolkit. Honestly, it is a niche product with few users, and its value depends almost entirely on how clean your ERP data is. Getting the data mapped in is most of the work.
when: You already run SAP or Oracle and want forecasting without a new full system
You want one view of inventory across warehouses
You need supplier lead time risk alerts
nope: You are small or your data lives in spreadsheets, a normal inventory tool or even Excel is cheaper and faster
You want to build your own supply chain logic, use Glue, Athena and SageMaker instead of a closed app
eg: A mid sized electronics maker sees an alert that a component's lead time doubled and a build slot in six weeks is now at risk.
pay: Priced per module per unit hour, so you pay for demand planning, supply planning and insights separately, plus data lake storage. The surprise is that turning on several modules multiplies the bill.

name: AWS Wickr
one: An end-to-end encrypted chat and calling app for organisations that need messages to stay secret.
like: A sealed envelope service where only the sender and the named receiver have a key, and the envelope can be set to burn itself after an hour.
what: Messaging, voice, video and file transfer with end-to-end encryption, plus expiry timers and optional compliant archiving for regulators. It is used mostly by government, defence and public safety, and there is a FedRAMP High and DoD authorised version. The free consumer app Wickr Me was retired at the end of 2023, so what remains is the enterprise product. Most ordinary companies do not need this.
when: Government, defence or law enforcement communications
Incident response chat that must stay out of the compromised systems
Work where message content is genuinely sensitive
nope: You just want team chat, Slack or Teams are far better tools for daily work
You want customers to talk to your business, use Amazon Connect or a normal support tool
eg: A security team runs its ransomware response in a Wickr room because the corporate email and Teams may be in the attacker's hands.
pay: Per user per month, with tiers. The surprise is the minimum user count on enterprise plans, you pay for the floor whether or not you fill it.

name: Amazon Chime SDK
one: Building blocks for putting video calls, audio and chat inside your own app.
like: Buying the engine and gearbox rather than the whole car, you still have to build the vehicle around it.
what: Gives you meeting sessions, audio and video streams, WebRTC clients for web, iOS and Android, live transcription, noise reduction and phone dial-in via SIP. You build the entire user interface yourself, which is a lot more work than people expect. It survives the shutdown of the Chime app, but the market is competitive and Twilio, Daily, LiveKit and Agora are common alternatives.
when: Your product needs calls inside it, like telehealth or online tutoring
You want call audio piped into transcription or an AI agent
You need meetings under your own brand
nope: You just want staff meetings, use a finished app like Zoom, not an SDK
You want a full contact centre with queues and agent screens, use Amazon Connect
eg: A telemedicine site opens a doctor patient video call in the browser with no app install, and records the audio for notes.
pay: Per attendee minute for meetings, extra per minute for recording, transcription and phone dial-in. The surprise is that a one hour call with five people is five attendee hours, not one.

name: Amazon Chime
one: Amazon's own video meetings app, which is being switched off.
like: A meeting room that the building owner has announced will be locked up for good, so nobody is booking it any more.
what: A Zoom style meetings and business calling product. It is retired: no new customers are accepted, and after 20 February 2026 you cannot schedule or host meetings or use Business Calling. Do not build anything on it. The separate Amazon Chime SDK is not affected and continues.
when: Nothing new, it is closing
Only relevant if you still have meetings or numbers to migrate off it
nope: Any new meeting need, use Zoom, Teams, Google Meet or Webex
Any new voice or video in your own app, use the Amazon Chime SDK
eg: An IT team exports its Chime Business Calling numbers and ports them to another provider before the February 2026 cutoff.
pay: Was per user per month plus per minute calling. Not worth planning around now.

name: Amazon Connect
one: A ready-made call centre you set up in a browser instead of buying phone hardware.
like: Renting a fully staffed reception desk with phone lines, hold music and a queue, instead of installing a switchboard in your building.
what: You get phone numbers, a drag and drop call flow builder, agent and supervisor screens, queues, routing, recording and reports, plus chat, email and outbound campaigns. It also has AI add-ons for transcription, agent assist and self service bots. It is genuinely a full contact centre, but configuring flows, routing and reporting well is real work, and reporting is often the weak point people complain about.
when: You need agents answering customer calls or chats
You want an IVR phone menu that reads from your own database
You are replacing an old on-premise phone system
nope: You just need to place or receive a few automated calls, use AWS End User Messaging voice
You need internal staff telephony and meetings, that is Teams Phone or a normal UCaaS product, not Connect
eg: A bank's caller enters a card number, a Lambda checks the account, and the call routes straight to the fraud queue with the details already on the agent's screen.
pay: Per minute of usage plus per number per day, with no per seat licence. The surprise items are the AI add-ons like Contact Lens and Amazon Q in Connect, which are charged per minute or per message on top.

name: Amazon Pinpoint APIs
one: The older set of Pinpoint APIs for customer messaging, most of which stop working in October 2026.
like: A phone line that is being switched off, with the useful calls moved to a new number.
what: Amazon Pinpoint was a service for talking to your customers by email, SMS, push and voice, with campaigns, journeys and analytics on top. AWS has announced end of support for Amazon Pinpoint on 30 October 2026. After that date the Pinpoint console and Pinpoint resources such as endpoints, segments, campaigns, journeys and analytics stop being available. The parts that survive are the sending APIs. AWS says the APIs for SMS, voice, mobile push, OTP and phone number validate are not affected, and those now live under AWS End User Messaging. So "Amazon Pinpoint APIs" today means two different things. The campaign and analytics APIs are going away. The message sending APIs continue under a new name.
when: You already have an app calling Pinpoint APIs and need to plan the move before October 2026
You want to send SMS, push, OTP or voice from your own code, in which case you use AWS End User Messaging
You are checking which of your API calls survive the end of support date
nope: Do not start a new project on Pinpoint APIs. The service has an end of support date. For SMS, push, voice and OTP use AWS End User Messaging. For email use Amazon SES.
If you only send transactional email such as receipts and password resets, Amazon SES is the better fit and always was.
If you want marketing campaigns and customer journeys with a console, AWS no longer offers that here. You will need a third party tool.
eg: A shopping app sends order updates by SMS and push. The sending calls keep working through AWS End User Messaging. The campaign that used to send a weekly offer from the Pinpoint console has to move somewhere else before October 2026.
pay: You pay per message sent, by channel, with the price depending on the country for SMS and voice. There is no charge for the API itself. Pinpoint campaign and analytics features carried their own charges, and those go away with the service.

name: Amazon Pinpoint
one: A marketing messaging service that AWS is closing down.
like: A mailroom that still delivers, but the landlord has posted the date it shuts, so nobody moves in.
what: It combined message sending with audience segments, campaigns, journeys and analytics. AWS stopped taking new customers in May 2025 and support ends on 30 October 2026, after which the console, segments, campaigns, journeys and analytics stop working. The sending channels live on as AWS End User Messaging, and confusingly the API is still named pinpoint. If you are on it, plan the move now.
when: Nothing new
Only for planning an exit if you already run campaigns on it
nope: New campaign and journey work, use Braze, Iterable, Klaviyo or Amazon Connect outbound campaigns
Plain SMS, push or voice sending, use AWS End User Messaging
Email, use Amazon SES
eg: A retailer exports its Pinpoint segments and journey definitions and rebuilds them in Braze ahead of the October 2026 cutoff.
pay: Was per targeted endpoint per month plus per message. The migration effort, not the bill, is the cost that matters now.

name: Amazon Quick
one: The new umbrella name for Amazon QuickSight plus AI agents that answer questions about your business data.
like: A business analyst who reads all your reports and answers your questions, instead of just handing you the reports.
what: On the AWS site, QuickSight is now presented as part of Amazon Quick, also written as Amazon Quick Suite. Quick is the wider product. Amazon Quick Sight is the business intelligence part inside it, the dashboards and charts that QuickSight always did. Around it, Quick adds research and automation agents, connections to many other applications, and no code app building. The pitch is answers grounded in your own business data rather than a general chatbot. This is recent, so treat the naming as still settling. The QuickSight dashboards, APIs and pricing you may already use are not gone. They sit under a new brand.
when: You already use QuickSight and want to know why the branding changed
You want people to ask questions in plain English about company data instead of reading a dashboard
You want dashboards plus an agent that can pull from other business apps in one place
nope: If you just want charts over a database and nothing more, plain QuickSight dashboards, or Athena with any BI tool, is a simpler answer.
If your data is not in AWS and not in a connected app, there is nothing for the agent to ground its answers in.
If you need an AI agent inside your own application rather than a business tool, Amazon Bedrock is the right layer.
eg: A sales head asks "why did revenue drop in the west region last month" and gets an answer built from the company's own sales data, with the chart behind it, instead of opening six dashboards.
pay: QuickSight has always charged per user per month, split between authors who build and readers who view, with a capacity option for large reader counts. The agent and automation parts of Quick are new and priced separately, so check the current pricing page before committing.

name: Amazon Simple Email Service
one: Sends email from your app, cheaply and at scale.
like: A bulk post office for letters your system writes.
what: SES sends transactional and bulk email. New accounts start in a sandbox and must be approved for real sending. You must set up SPF, DKIM and DMARC or your mail lands in spam.
when: Invoices, receipts, password resets
Newsletters
nope: A handful of manual emails a week.
pay: Per thousand emails. Very cheap.
eg: Emailing an invoice PDF the moment a payment succeeds.

name: Amazon WorkDocs SDK
one: The programming interface to Amazon WorkDocs, a file sharing service AWS has closed to new customers.
like: A key to a building that is being emptied. Useful for carrying your things out, not for moving in.
what: Amazon WorkDocs was a managed file storage and sharing service for companies, with commenting, versions, sharing controls and desktop and mobile apps. AWS documentation now carries a notice that new customer sign ups and account upgrades are no longer available for Amazon WorkDocs, and points customers at instructions for migrating their data out. The WorkDocs SDK is the set of API calls for that service, available through the normal AWS SDKs in Python, Java, Go and so on. It lets code upload documents, list folders, manage users and read comments. Because the service itself is being wound down, the SDK matters mainly for one job now, which is getting existing data out in bulk. I could not confirm a final shutdown date from an official page, so verify that before planning a migration.
when: You are an existing WorkDocs customer and need to export documents, folders and metadata in bulk
You need to list what is stored in WorkDocs before deciding where it should move to
You are auditing old code that still calls WorkDocs APIs
nope: Almost nobody needs this now. Do not build anything new on it. The service is closed to new customers.
For file storage from an application, use Amazon S3.
For shared team file storage that people use like a drive, use Amazon FSx or a non AWS product such as Google Drive, SharePoint or Dropbox.
eg: A company with ten years of documents in WorkDocs writes a script that walks every folder, downloads each file with its latest version, and writes it into an S3 bucket before the service closes.
pay: WorkDocs charged per active user per month with a storage allowance. There was no separate charge for API calls. Since sign ups are closed, pricing only matters to existing customers.

name: Amazon WorkDocs
one: Amazon's file storage and sharing service for staff, now switched off.
like: An office filing cabinet that the company has already emptied and taken away.
what: It was a Dropbox or Google Drive style service with sync clients, sharing links and commenting on documents. AWS stopped new sign-ups in April 2024 and ended support on 25 April 2025, after which data was purged. The site, the APIs and WorkDocs Drive are all gone. Listed here only so you recognise the name in old documentation.
when: Nothing, it is closed
nope: Team file sharing, use Google Drive, SharePoint, OneDrive or Dropbox
File storage for an application, use Amazon S3, or Amazon FSx or EFS for a network drive
eg: An admin ran the bulk export in early 2025 and moved the company's shared folders to SharePoint before the purge.
pay: Nothing, it is closed.

name: Amazon WorkMail
one: AWS business email and calendar. It is being shut down on 31 March 2027.
like: A company post room that is closing. It still sorts your post today, but you have been told the date it stops.
what: Amazon WorkMail is a managed business email and calendar service. It gives your staff mailboxes on your own domain, with shared calendars and contacts. People can use Microsoft Outlook on Windows or Mac, phone mail apps, IMAP clients, or a web browser. It can link to Active Directory and it encrypts mail using keys you control in AWS KMS. The important fact comes first though. AWS has said it will stop supporting Amazon WorkMail on 31 March 2027. After that date you will not be able to get into it. AWS has published migration guidance. So this is not a product to start a new business on.
when: Almost nobody should start with this now, because of the 2027 end date
Existing WorkMail customers, who should be planning a move off it
Reading up on it only to understand a system you have inherited
nope: Do not pick this for new email. It ends on 31 March 2027. Use Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace instead.
Do not use it to send bulk or app email. That is Amazon Simple Email Service, which is a different thing and is not going away.
Do not confuse it with Amazon Simple Email Service. WorkMail is staff mailboxes. SES is mail your software sends.
If you are on it today, start the migration now rather than near the date.
eg: A 30 person firm gave every person a mailbox on their own domain and used Outlook as usual. That firm now needs to move to another mail provider before March 2027.
pay: 4 US dollars per user per month, including 50 GB of storage per user. That price is still listed, but the service ends in March 2027, so the real cost to you includes a migration.

name: AWS Billing Conductor
one: It lets you send someone a different AWS bill than the one AWS actually produced.
like: A landlord who pays one electricity bill for the whole building, then works out what each flat owes, with his own rates and a service charge added.
what: You group accounts into billing groups and set your own prices, discounts or flat fees. It produces a second, made-up bill for that group, while AWS still charges you the real amount. It is for resellers, managed service providers and big companies that charge internal departments. Almost nobody else needs it.
when: You resell AWS to customers and need to bill them your own rates
You charge internal business units for their cloud use
You must hide AWS discounts from the people you invoice
nope: You only want to see which team spent what, use cost allocation tags with Cost Explorer
You just want a spending limit, use AWS Budgets
eg: An IT company hosts 12 clients in separate AWS accounts and invoices each one at list price plus 15 percent, generated automatically each month.
pay: A fee per account per month in each billing group. The surprise is that you still pay AWS the real bill in full, so this is pure extra cost on top.

name: AWS Budgets
one: It emails you when your AWS spending passes a number you picked.
like: A limit alert on your bank card. It does not stop the card, it just texts you.
what: You set a monthly amount and it warns you at thresholds, for example at 80 percent and 100 percent. It can warn on forecast spend too, so you hear about it before the month ends. Important limitation: by default it only alerts, it does not stop anything, though you can attach an action that applies a restrictive IAM policy or stops instances.
when: Your first week on AWS, before anything can run up a bill
Capping a side project or a client account
Tracking whether a team stays inside its allowance
nope: You want to understand why the bill grew, use Cost Explorer instead
You want a hard spending cap that cannot be exceeded, AWS does not really offer that, so use alerts plus tight IAM limits
eg: A student sets a 20 dollar budget and gets an email at 16 dollars, finds a forgotten NAT gateway, and deletes it.
pay: Two budgets are free. After that a few cents per budget per day. Budget actions and forecasted alerts cost a little more.

name: AWS Cost Explorer
one: Shows where your AWS money is going.
like: A bank statement with charts, so you can see what you actually spend on.
what: Cost Explorer breaks the bill down by service, tag and time, and forecasts next month. Tag everything from day one or the breakdown is useless. Set a budget alert on day one too.
when: Always. From the first day.
pay: The console view is free. The API has a small per request charge.
eg: Spotting that a forgotten test server has cost 4,000 rupees this month.

name: AWS Cost and Usage Report
one: It drops a giant spreadsheet of every line of your AWS bill into an S3 bucket.
like: An itemised phone bill, except every call is listed hour by hour, so the file is far too big to read by eye.
what: It is the most detailed billing data AWS gives you, one row per resource per hour, delivered as compressed files a few times a day. You are meant to query it with Athena or load it into a data tool, not open it. The newer version, CUR 2.0, is created through the Data Exports console and has a cleaner, more stable column layout.
when: You need exact per-resource costs for chargeback
You are building your own cost dashboard
Cost Explorer does not slice the data the way you need
nope: You just want to see where the money went, Cost Explorer already shows that with no setup
You want alerts, use AWS Budgets
eg: A finance team queries the report in Athena to find every S3 bucket that cost more than 100 dollars last month.
pay: The report itself is free. You pay for the S3 storage and for every Athena query you run against it, and the files get big fast.

name: AWS FinOps Agent
one: An AI agent that watches your AWS bill, investigates cost spikes and answers cost questions in plain English.
like: A finance person who notices the bill jumped, finds out who changed what, and tells the right engineer.
what: AWS FinOps Agent is an agent you create in your own AWS account to monitor cost, investigate anomalies and surface savings. It reads cost and usage data from AWS Cost Explorer, listens for alerts from AWS Cost Anomaly Detection, pulls recommendations from Cost Optimization Hub and Compute Optimizer, and uses AWS CloudTrail to find the change that caused a spike. It then writes an investigation summary with a likely root cause and the owner, and can open a Jira ticket or post to Slack. Engineers can also just ask it questions such as why cost went up last month. You can upload context files, for example which account belongs to which team, so it answers in your own terms. Each agent is a separate instance with its own permissions, context, memory and integrations. It is in preview and starts in the US East N. Virginia region, so expect changes.
when: A cost spike appears and nobody wants to dig through CloudTrail to find which change caused it
You want engineers to self serve cost answers instead of pinging the finance team
You want anomaly alerts to arrive as a Slack message or Jira ticket with a cause already attached, not just a number
nope: If your AWS bill is small and one person reads Cost Explorer once a month, this is more machinery than you need. Cost Explorer plus AWS Budgets is enough.
If you only want to be told when spend crosses a limit, AWS Budgets does that on its own.
It is in preview, so do not put a process that must not break on top of it yet.
eg: Cost Anomaly Detection flags a 900 dollar jump overnight. The agent correlates it with CloudTrail, finds a team launched a large GPU instance and left it running, and posts that in Slack with the owner named, by the time people log in.
pay: Preview pricing should be checked on the AWS page before use. The data sources it reads, Cost Explorer, Cost Anomaly Detection and Compute Optimizer, are largely free or low cost on their own, so the agent's own charge is what to look at.

name: Reserved Instance Reporting
one: It is the screen that tells you whether the capacity you pre-paid for is actually being used.
like: Checking a gym membership you paid for a year upfront, to see how many sessions you actually attended.
what: This is not a separate service, it is a pair of reports inside Cost Explorer: utilization, how much of what you bought you used, and coverage, how much of your usage is protected by a reservation. It covers EC2, RDS, ElastiCache, MemoryDB, OpenSearch and Redshift. You can set a target percentage and be alerted when you fall below it.
when: You bought Reserved Instances and want to know if they are wasted
Deciding whether to buy more reservations before renewal
Proving savings to finance
nope: You use Savings Plans instead of Reserved Instances, look at the Savings Plans reports
You have not committed to anything yet, start with Cost Explorer's recommendations
eg: A team sees RI utilization at 62 percent, finds an instance type was changed after buying, and modifies the reservation.
pay: The reports are free. The cost is the reservation itself, paid whether or not you use it, which is exactly what these reports expose.

name: Savings Plans
one: A pricing commitment, not a service. You promise to spend a set amount per hour for one or three years and pay less per hour.
like: A yearly train pass instead of buying a ticket each day. Cheaper per trip, but you pay for the pass whether you travel or not.
what: Savings Plans is a way of paying, not something you switch on and use. You commit to spend a fixed amount of money per hour, for one year or three years, and in return AWS charges you lower rates, up to about 72 percent below on demand. The discount is applied to your bill automatically each hour, across your accounts in AWS Organizations. There are different plans. Compute Savings Plans are the most flexible and cover Amazon EC2, AWS Lambda and AWS Fargate across instance families, sizes, operating systems and Regions. EC2 Instance Savings Plans give a bigger discount but lock you to one instance family in one Region. There are also plans for Amazon SageMaker AI. You can pay all up front, part up front, or nothing up front, with a better rate the more you pay early. Once bought, a plan cannot be cancelled or refunded.
when: You have steady baseline usage that runs all year and is not going away
You want a discount without picking exact instance types, so a Compute Savings Plan fits
You already know your lowest monthly compute spend and can commit to a part of it safely
You run Lambda or Fargate a lot, since Reserved Instances do not cover those but Compute Savings Plans do
nope: Not for short lived or spiky workloads. You pay the commitment even on quiet hours.
Not for a new workload you cannot size yet. Run on demand first, look at AWS Cost Explorer, then commit.
Not a fault tolerance or batch discount. For interruptible work, Spot Instances are cheaper.
Do not commit to 100 percent of your usage. Cover the floor, not the peak.
Do not buy one expecting to change your mind. There is no cancel and no refund.
eg: A team always runs at least 20 servers day and night. They look at Cost Explorer, commit to the spend those 20 cover for three years, and their bill for that part drops sharply. The extra servers they add in busy weeks stay on demand.
pay: There is no fee for a Savings Plan itself. You pay the hourly amount you committed to, every hour of the term, used or not. Usage above the commitment is billed at normal on demand rates. Paying more up front lowers the rate.

name: AWS App Runner
one: Give it your code or container, it runs a web service.
like: A vending machine for web apps. Put the code in, a running URL comes out.
what: App Runner builds from your repository or image, runs it, scales it and gives you HTTPS. No VPC or load balancer to configure. Less control than ECS, far less to learn.
when: A containerised web app, quickly
Small teams with no ops person
nope: Complex networking needs.
pay: Per vCPU and GB while running, with a lower idle rate.
eg: A Node API live from a GitHub repo in minutes.

name: AWS Batch
one: Runs large numbers of background jobs.
like: A night shift that works through a pile of tasks while you sleep.
what: Batch queues your jobs and starts the right amount of compute to work through them, then shuts it down. It handles dependencies and retries. Good with Spot instances for cheap compute.
when: Rendering, simulations, bulk processing
Thousands of independent jobs
nope: A few small tasks. Use Lambda.
pay: Free service. You pay for the compute it starts.
eg: Generating ten thousand certificate PDFs overnight.

name: AWS Compute Optimizer
one: Looks at how hard your servers actually work and tells you which ones are too big.
like: A friend who checks your wardrobe and says you only ever wear three of these coats.
what: It reads CloudWatch metrics from the last 14 days and rates resources as over provisioned, under provisioned or fine, with a suggested size. It covers EC2, Auto Scaling groups, EBS volumes, Lambda and ECS on Fargate. Without the CloudWatch agent it cannot see memory usage, so advice for memory heavy workloads can be wrong. It only recommends, it never changes anything.
when: Cutting a bill that grew without anyone watching
Choosing a Lambda memory setting with evidence
A quarterly right sizing review
nope: Workloads with a big monthly or seasonal peak, 14 days of data will mislead you
Deciding whether to buy Savings Plans, use Cost Explorer for that
eg: It shows 40 EC2 instances sitting under 10 percent CPU and suggests a smaller size, saving a few thousand a month.
pay: The basic recommendations are free. Enhanced infrastructure metrics, which extend the lookback to three months, carry a small per resource hourly charge that quietly applies to every resource once enabled.

name: AWS Elastic Beanstalk
one: Upload your code and AWS sets up the servers for you.
like: A serviced office. Bring your laptop, the desk and internet are ready.
what: Beanstalk takes your application and creates the EC2 servers, load balancer and scaling behind the scenes. You can still reach in and change things. It is an older service and newer options often fit better.
when: A traditional app you want online fast
You want servers without configuring them
nope: A brand new project. Look at App Runner or containers first.
pay: Free. You pay for the resources it creates.
eg: Deploying a Django app without touching a load balancer setting.

name: AWS Lambda
one: Run a small piece of code without owning a server.
like: A taxi instead of a car. You pay for the trip, not for parking it all night.
what: You upload a function. AWS runs it when something triggers it, then shuts it down. Nothing to patch, nothing running idle. It sleeps between requests, so the first call after a quiet spell can be slower.
when: Short jobs that run on an event
Traffic that comes in bursts
You do not want to manage a server at all
nope: Jobs that run longer than 15 minutes
Something that must respond instantly every single time
pay: Per request and per millisecond of run time. Nothing when idle.
eg: Someone uploads a photo, a function makes a thumbnail, then stops.

name: AWS Local Zones
one: Small AWS outposts in extra cities, so your servers sit closer to users there.
like: A corner shop your chain opens in a suburb, stocking the few items people need urgently, while the big warehouse stays across town.
what: A Local Zone is an extension of an AWS Region placed in a metro area like Los Angeles or Mumbai, giving single digit millisecond latency to users there. Only a small subset of services is available in each one, and you still lean on the parent Region for the rest. Most applications do not need this, CloudFront gets you most of the benefit for content.
when: Real time gaming or trading where a few milliseconds matter
Live video or media editing for a specific city
Data that must stay inside a particular geography
nope: General web speed, use Amazon CloudFront instead
Anything needing the full AWS service catalogue, stay in the Region
Mobile network edge latency, look at AWS Wavelength
eg: A game studio puts match servers in the Los Angeles Local Zone so local players see under 10 ms ping.
pay: EC2 in a Local Zone costs more per hour than the same instance in the parent Region, and data moving between the zone and the Region is charged.

name: AWS Nitro Enclaves
one: A sealed side room on your server where secret data can be processed and nobody, not even you, can look in.
like: A bank's night safe drop slot. Things go in through one narrow opening, nothing else reaches inside, not even the branch staff.
what: An enclave is an isolated virtual machine carved out of an EC2 instance, with no network, no persistent storage and no shell access. The only way in or out is a local secure channel from the parent instance. It can prove what code it is running through attestation, and KMS can be told to release a key only to that proven code. This is a specialist tool, most teams never need it.
when: Processing card numbers or health records where even admins must be excluded
Holding private keys for signing, with proof of the code using them
Regulated multi-party data where each side must not see the other's raw data
nope: Ordinary secret storage, use AWS Secrets Manager or Parameter Store
Just encrypting data, use KMS on its own
Any workload needing disk or direct network access, it has neither
eg: A payments firm decrypts card data only inside an enclave, so its own engineers can never read a full card number.
pay: No extra charge for the enclave. You pay for the parent EC2 instance, which must be large enough to donate CPU and memory to the sealed room, so you buy capacity you cannot otherwise use.

name: AWS Outposts family
one: AWS ships actual racks or small boxes of its own hardware to your building and runs them for you.
like: A coffee chain installing one of its own branded machines in your office lobby, still serviced by their staff, still on their system.
what: Outposts come as full 42U racks or as 1U and 2U servers. They run a subset of AWS services on your premises, managed by AWS and connected back to a Region. You need real datacentre conditions, power, cooling and a solid network link, and if that link drops your control plane goes with it. The service list is much shorter than a Region's.
when: Data legally required to stay in a specific building or country
Factory or hospital systems that need very low latency to local machines
Migrating slowly while old hardware still sits on site
nope: Just wanting things nearer users, use Local Zones or CloudFront
Short projects, these are multi-year commitments
Small offices without proper power, cooling and network
eg: A hospital runs its imaging application on an Outposts rack in its own basement so scans never leave the building.
pay: You buy or commit for one or three years, upfront or monthly, per rack. The surprise is that the commitment runs whether you use the capacity or not, plus the cost of the network link home.

name: AWS Outposts rack
one: Puts a full rack of AWS hardware inside your own building.
like: Renting a branch of the bank and having it built in your office lobby.
what: AWS ships a 42U rack, installs it in your data centre, and keeps running it. You use the same AWS console and APIs, but the machines sit on your floor. Only a subset of AWS services run on it, and you need real data centre space, power and cooling.
when: Data must stay inside your building by law
An app needs very low delay to machines on site
You are moving off a data centre slowly and want one control plane
nope: If you just want cloud servers, use amazon-ec2 in a normal Region.
If you only need a small box at a shop or factory, use AWS Outposts servers instead.
If you only need a private network link back to AWS, use aws-direct-connect.
Most companies never need this. It is for large regulated or latency bound workloads.
eg: A hospital runs its imaging app on an Outposts rack in its own basement so patient scans never leave the site.
pay: You pay per rack for a 3 year term, billed monthly, whether you use it or not. The surprise is that it is a long commitment, not pay as you go, and you still pay for data going back to the Region.

name: AWS Outposts servers
one: A single AWS server box you put in a shop, clinic or factory.
like: A vending machine AWS drops off, refills and services, but it lives in your shop.
what: This is the small version of Outposts. A 1U or 2U server arrives, you or a contractor rack it, and AWS provisions it remotely. It runs far fewer services than the rack, mainly EC2, ECS and local storage, and there is no local block storage service or database service.
when: A retail store needs compute on site when the internet drops
A factory floor needs fast local processing of sensor data
Hundreds of small sites need the same setup managed centrally
nope: If you have real data centre space and need databases or large capacity, use the Outposts rack.
If you just need to process data on a small device at the edge, aws-iot-greengrass is far cheaper and simpler.
If latency is fine, use a normal Region with amazon-ec2.
Very few teams need this.
eg: A supermarket chain puts one 1U Outposts server in each store to run checkout software that must keep working offline.
pay: Per server, on a 3 year commitment, paid up front or monthly. Capacity is fixed, so you pay the same whether the box is busy or idle.

name: AWS Parallel Cluster
one: Sets up a cluster of machines that run scientific jobs in a queue.
like: Hiring a shift manager who opens extra counters when the queue grows and closes them when it empties.
what: It is an open source command line tool, not a hosted service. You give it a config file and it builds the head node, the Slurm scheduler, the shared file system and the compute nodes. You still own and operate the cluster, including patching and upgrades.
when: Running engineering simulations or genomics pipelines
Moving an existing on-site Slurm cluster to AWS
You want machines to start only while jobs are waiting
nope: AWS Parallel Computing Service (PCS) is the newer managed Slurm option. Pick that if you do not want to run the cluster yourself.
For ordinary batch work that is not HPC, aws-batch or aws-step-functions is simpler.
If your work is containers, use amazon-elastic-kubernetes-service.
Nobody outside HPC and research computing needs this.
eg: A drug research team submits 2000 molecule simulations; the cluster grows to 500 instances, then shrinks back to zero.
pay: The tool is free. You pay for the EC2 instances, the shared storage and the network. The surprise is the head node and shared file system run 24/7 and cost money even with no jobs.

name: AWS Parallel Computing Service
one: It runs a proper scientific computing cluster for you, using the Slurm scheduler researchers already know.
like: A university workshop with a booking sheet. You write your job on the sheet, the technician assigns benches and tools, and work starts when there is room.
what: PCS is AWS's managed Slurm service, launched in 2024. It runs the controller for you and scales compute nodes up and down, so researchers keep submitting jobs with the same sbatch and squeue commands. It is for genuine HPC with many nodes working on one problem together, which is a narrow audience. It replaces the hand-built approach of ParallelCluster with something AWS operates.
when: Existing Slurm workflows you want to move to the cloud
Simulations spanning many nodes that must talk to each other
A research group wanting a cluster without an HPC admin
nope: Independent jobs that do not talk to each other, AWS Batch is simpler and cheaper
Machine learning training, use SageMaker
Full control over every cluster detail, use AWS ParallelCluster
eg: A weather research team submits a 200-node Slurm job for a regional forecast run and the cluster grows to fit, then shrinks.
pay: An hourly charge for the managed controller plus all the EC2, storage and networking underneath. The controller charge continues even when no jobs are running.

name: AWS Serverless Application Repository
one: A catalogue of ready-made small AWS apps you can deploy into your own account in a few clicks.
like: A recipe card box. You pick a card, and the whole dish gets cooked in your kitchen, with your ingredients.
what: It holds SAM templates published by AWS and third parties, mostly small Lambda based utilities. Deploying one creates the resources in your account, so you own and pay for them. It is quiet and lightly maintained, many listings are years old, and most teams now copy a template from GitHub or use CDK constructs instead. Read the template before deploying anything from a publisher you do not know.
when: Grabbing a known AWS-published helper like a log forwarder
A quick one-off utility you do not want to write
Publishing an internal template for your own organisation
nope: Anything production critical, write the template yourself with SAM or CDK
Reusable building blocks in code, use CDK constructs or Terraform modules
Trusting an unknown publisher's stale template with IAM permissions
eg: A team deploys the published Datadog log forwarder Lambda straight from the repository instead of writing one.
pay: The catalogue is free. You pay normal charges for whatever the template creates, which can include resources you did not notice in the template.

name: AWS SimSpace Weaver
one: A retired service that used to spread one huge simulated world across many servers.
like: A shop that has closed down. Worth knowing what it sold, but you cannot buy there any more.
what: SimSpace Weaver ran large spatial simulations, like a city of millions of people, by splitting the world across several machines that kept each other in step. It closed to new customers in January 2025 and support ended on 20 May 2026, so the console and resources are gone. AWS points people to AWS Batch for containerised simulation work instead. Include it only so nobody wastes time looking for it.
when: Understanding an old architecture diagram that mentions it
Planning a migration off a legacy simulation setup
nope: Any new simulation project, it no longer exists, use AWS Batch
Large agent-based models, use AWS Batch or a self-managed cluster on EC2
eg: A city planning demo once simulated a million pedestrians across several servers, work that now goes to Batch or EC2.
pay: Not applicable any more. While it ran, you paid per simulation hour and per worker instance.

name: AWS Wavelength
one: AWS servers placed inside mobile phone networks, so phone apps reach them without crossing the wider internet.
like: A first aid post inside the stadium instead of a hospital across town. Help arrives fast, but it only does a few things.
what: Wavelength Zones sit in telecom operators' 5G sites, so traffic from a phone on that network reaches your servers in very few hops. It only helps devices on that specific operator's network, availability varies by country and operator, and only a small set of services runs there. Almost nobody needs this.
when: AR or VR on phones where latency is visible to the user
Connected vehicles or drones on a specific carrier network
Live video processing from mobile devices
nope: Users on home broadband or WiFi, it does not help them, use CloudFront
General low latency in a city, use Local Zones
Anything needing the full AWS service list, stay in the Region
eg: An AR game puts its physics server in a Verizon Wavelength Zone so headset movement feels immediate.
pay: EC2 in a Wavelength Zone costs more than in the Region, plus data transfer between the zone and the Region.

name: Amazon DCV
one: Lets you use a graphics heavy desktop that is running somewhere else.
like: A very good live video link to a computer in another room, with your mouse and keyboard attached.
what: Amazon DCV is the renamed NICE DCV, the remote display protocol AWS bought in 2016. It streams the screen of a remote Linux or Windows machine to a laptop or browser. It is software you install, not a managed service, and it is the same protocol underneath WorkSpaces and AppStream.
when: A designer needs a CAD or 3D app that will not run on a laptop
Viewing simulation results that live next to the data
Giving engineers access to a shared GPU workstation
nope: If you want a finished managed desktop, use amazon-workspaces instead of building your own.
For plain server admin, SSH or Systems Manager is enough.
If the app is a normal web app, none of this is needed.
eg: An architect opens a 40 GB building model on a GPU instance in Mumbai and works on it from a thin laptop.
pay: No charge for the DCV server when it runs on an EC2 instance. You pay the normal EC2 and GPU cost. Running DCV outside AWS needs a paid licence, which catches people out.

name: Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling
one: Adds servers when busy, removes them when quiet.
like: Calling in extra staff on a festival weekend and sending them home on Monday.
what: You set a minimum, a maximum and a rule. Auto Scaling adds or removes EC2 machines to match. It also replaces any machine that fails a health check.
when: Traffic rises and falls
You want automatic recovery from a dead server
nope: Steady, predictable traffic on one machine.
pay: The feature is free. You pay for the servers it starts.
eg: Two servers normally, six during a live class, back to two after.

name: Amazon EC2 Image Builder
one: It builds your standard server image for you, on a schedule, with your software and patches baked in.
like: A bakery that makes the same loaf to the same recipe every morning, so every shop gets an identical one.
what: You define a recipe: a base OS image plus components that install software and settings. Image Builder runs it on a temporary instance, tests the result and publishes an AMI or container image to the accounts and regions you choose. It is slow, a build takes many minutes, and debugging a failed component is awkward because the test instance disappears.
when: A hardened golden AMI your organisation must use
Monthly patched images without a person doing it
Sharing one image across many accounts and regions
nope: Container images, use a Dockerfile and a normal CI pipeline
Config that changes often, use user data or a config tool at boot
One-off images, just snapshot an instance
eg: A security team publishes a patched, CIS-hardened Amazon Linux AMI on the first of every month to twelve accounts.
pay: The service is free. You pay for the temporary build instance, the snapshots and the storage of every AMI version. The surprise is dozens of old AMIs and snapshots quietly accruing storage charges.

name: Amazon EC2
one: A computer you rent in Amazon's data centre.
like: Renting a flat instead of buying a house. You pick the size, you get the keys, you install what you want.
what: EC2 gives you a full server. You choose how much CPU, memory and disk. You install the operating system and your software. You control everything, so you also maintain everything.
when: You need full control of the machine
You are moving an existing server to the cloud
Your software must run all the time
nope: You just want to run a small piece of code now and then. Use Lambda.
You do not want to patch servers. Use Fargate or App Runner.
pay: Per second the machine is on, by size. Stopped machines cost nothing for compute but the disk still costs.
eg: A shop's billing software that must run 24 hours a day on one server.

name: Amazon Elastic VMware Service
one: It runs VMware Cloud Foundation on AWS hardware, inside your own network.
like: Renting the same machinery you already know how to operate, in somebody else's factory, so none of your staff need retraining.
what: Launched in August 2025 as the AWS answer after VMware Cloud on AWS changed hands. It runs VMware Cloud Foundation on EC2 bare metal inside your VPC, so your IP addresses, vCenter habits and runbooks carry over. You bring your own VMware licence from Broadcom, and you or a partner manage the VMware layer, not AWS.
when: A data centre lease ends and you must move VMware workloads fast
You cannot change IP addresses or rewrite applications
Your team's skills and tooling are all VMware
nope: You have time to replatform, plain EC2 or containers cost less and need no VMware licence
You have a few dozen VMs, the minimum host count makes this very expensive, use Application Migration Service to move them to EC2
eg: A manufacturer moves 500 VMs out of an expiring data centre in weeks, keeping vCenter and the same addresses, and modernises later.
pay: Per bare metal host hour, plus storage and network, plus your own VMware licence from Broadcom. The surprise is the minimum number of hosts and the separate licence bill, so this is not a small monthly number.

name: Amazon Lightsail for Research
one: A simple rented desktop in the cloud with research software like RStudio or JupyterLab already installed.
like: A hotel room with the kettle and iron already there. You do not shop for anything, you just check in.
what: You pick a size and an application, and get a browser accessible virtual computer with that software set up, at a flat monthly price. It is aimed at academics and students who do not want to learn EC2. It is a niche corner of Lightsail, the software choices are few and fixed, and serious labs outgrow it quickly.
when: A student needing RStudio on a bigger machine than their laptop
A short research project with a predictable budget
Teaching, where everyone needs the same environment
nope: Multi-node or GPU heavy research computing, use EC2 or AWS Parallel Computing Service
Shared team notebooks with data governance, use Amazon SageMaker
Anything needing VPC or IAM control, it is deliberately simplified
eg: A masters student runs a month of R analysis on a 16 GB Lightsail for Research machine instead of their old laptop.
pay: Flat hourly or monthly by size, with an idle shutdown option. The surprise is being billed for a machine left running after the term ends, since flat pricing hides the waste.

name: Amazon Lightsail
one: A simple server at a fixed monthly price.
like: A prepaid mobile plan. One price, known limits, no bill shock.
what: Lightsail gives a small server, a fixed price and a simple console. It hides most of AWS. Good for learning and small sites. You outgrow it once you need real AWS features.
when: A small website or WordPress
Learning
You want a predictable bill
nope: Anything that will need to scale properly.
pay: A fixed price per month, from a few dollars.
eg: A WordPress site for a small business.

name: Bottlerocket
one: A stripped down operating system for machines that only run containers.
like: A kitchen with nothing in it but the one oven you need, so there is less to clean and less to break.
what: Bottlerocket is a free, open source Linux distribution from AWS. It has no package manager and no SSH by default, and updates are applied as one whole image that can roll back. That minimalism is the point, but it also means you cannot install agents the normal way.
when: Running EKS or ECS nodes and wanting a smaller attack surface
You want node updates that are atomic and reversible
A security team asks for a hardened container host
nope: If you run normal software on the host, not containers, use Amazon Linux.
If you use aws-fargate, there is no host to choose, so this is irrelevant.
If your tooling depends on SSH and yum, expect friction.
eg: An EKS cluster runs Bottlerocket nodes, and a bad update rolls back automatically on reboot.
pay: The OS is free. You pay only the usual EC2 charges for the instances.

name: Elastic Fabric Adapter
one: A special network card for EC2 that lets many servers talk to each other extremely fast.
like: Swapping a queue at the post office for a hatch between two adjoining rooms. The message goes straight across, no counter in between.
what: EFA is a network interface option on certain EC2 instance types. It lets applications bypass the operating system's networking and talk directly between machines, which matters for MPI and for spreading model training across GPUs. Your software has to be written for it, a normal web app gains nothing. Instances using EFA must sit in the same subnet and ideally the same placement group.
when: MPI simulations across many nodes
Distributed GPU training with NCCL
Any job where nodes exchange data constantly
nope: Ordinary application traffic, plain networking is fine
Independent jobs that never talk, it adds nothing
Instance types that do not support it, check first
eg: A 64-node fluid dynamics run finishes in a third of the time once EFA replaces standard networking.
pay: No charge for EFA itself. The cost is being forced onto larger, pricier instance types that support it, and keeping the cluster together in one placement group.

name: AWS Fargate
one: Runs containers without you owning any servers.
like: Ordering food instead of renting a kitchen. You get the meal, not the gas bill.
what: Fargate is not a separate service you visit. It is a way to run ECS or EKS where AWS supplies the machine. No patching, no capacity planning. It costs more per unit than raw EC2.
when: You want containers with no servers to manage
Uneven workloads
nope: Very heavy steady workloads where EC2 is cheaper.
pay: Per vCPU and per GB of memory, per second.
eg: A background worker that runs for ten minutes each night.

name: Amazon ECS Anywhere
one: Lets AWS run and manage containers on servers you own, not AWS servers.
like: A cleaning company that also sends staff to your own house, while still running the schedule from their office.
what: It is a feature of ECS, not a separate product. You install an agent on your own machine, it registers as an external instance, and ECS schedules containers onto it. The control plane is still in AWS, so you need a working network link to AWS, and some ECS features that depend on AWS networking or load balancers do not apply.
when: Data must stay in your own building for legal reasons
Factory or shop floor hardware that must keep working close to the machines
You want one way of deploying containers across cloud and on site
nope: Normal cloud workloads, plain ECS on Fargate is simpler and cheaper to run
Sites with no reliable internet link, the agent needs to reach AWS
eg: A retailer runs the same stock counting container in AWS and on a small server in each shop, deployed from one ECS console.
pay: A small hourly charge per registered external instance. The hardware, power and network are yours and are the bigger cost.

name: Amazon EKS Anywhere
one: Runs AWS style Kubernetes clusters on your own servers.
like: Getting the restaurant's recipe and kit so you can cook the same dish in your own kitchen.
what: EKS Anywhere is software you install on your own hardware or VMware to create and update Kubernetes clusters. AWS does not operate these clusters, you do. The control plane is not in AWS, so cluster uptime is your problem, and support is a paid add on.
when: Kubernetes must run in your own data centre
You want the same tooling on site and in AWS
Air gapped or regulated environments
nope: If the workload can run in AWS, use amazon-elastic-kubernetes-service and let AWS run the control plane.
If you only want the tested open source parts, use Amazon EKS Distro.
If you do not already run Kubernetes, do not start here.
eg: A bank runs EKS Anywhere on vSphere in its own data centre and uses the same Helm charts as its AWS clusters.
pay: The software is free. Enterprise support for it costs per cluster per year. You also pay for your own hardware.

name: Amazon EKS Distro
one: The exact Kubernetes build AWS itself runs, handed to you as open source.
like: Buying the same flour and yeast the bakery uses, then baking the bread yourself.
what: EKS Distro is a set of tested Kubernetes binaries and container images on GitHub, with AWS security patches. It is parts, not a product. It does not install, run or upgrade anything for you, and there is no console and no support ticket.
when: You already have your own cluster build process
You want versions patched after upstream support ends
Building a Kubernetes product of your own
nope: If you want clusters created and managed for you on your hardware, use EKS Anywhere.
If you want a managed cluster, use amazon-elastic-kubernetes-service.
This is for platform teams. Almost no application team should touch it.
eg: A platform team builds its own cluster images from EKS Distro so its on-site clusters match the AWS ones.
pay: Free. You pay only for wherever you run it.

name: Amazon Elastic Container Registry
one: A private store for your container images.
like: Your own locked shelf for the blueprints your factory builds from.
what: ECR keeps Docker images privately in your account. ECS, EKS and Lambda pull from it. It can scan images for known vulnerabilities.
when: You build containers and do not want them public
nope: Open source images that are fine on Docker Hub.
pay: Per GB stored, plus data transfer.
eg: Pushing a new build image, then telling ECS to use it.

name: Amazon Elastic Container Service
one: Runs your app in containers, the simple AWS way.
like: Standard shipping containers. Any port can handle them because the shape is always the same.
what: ECS runs Docker containers for you. It restarts them if they crash and can scale them. It is simpler than Kubernetes and only works on AWS.
when: You already use Docker
You want containers without learning Kubernetes
nope: You need to run the same setup on other clouds too. Use EKS.
pay: Free control plane. You pay for the EC2 or Fargate capacity underneath.
eg: A Node.js API running as three containers behind a load balancer.

name: Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service
one: Managed Kubernetes.
like: The international standard plug socket. It works the same everywhere, and the wiring is complicated.
what: EKS runs Kubernetes so you do not have to run the control plane. Kubernetes is powerful and genuinely hard. It is the right answer for large teams and the wrong answer for small ones.
when: You already know Kubernetes
You must stay portable across clouds
Large, complex systems
nope: A small team shipping one app. ECS or App Runner will hurt less.
pay: An hourly fee for each cluster, plus the compute underneath.
eg: A company running forty microservices across several teams.

name: Red Hat OpenShift Service on AWS
one: Red Hat's OpenShift, run for you inside your AWS account.
like: Renting a branded kitchen from a restaurant chain. Same fittings and rules you already trained on, but somebody else does the plumbing.
what: OpenShift is a Kubernetes platform with extra developer tools and stricter defaults. This version is installed, patched and supported jointly by AWS and Red Hat. It is mostly bought by companies that already run OpenShift in their own data centres and want the same thing in the cloud. It costs noticeably more than plain Kubernetes on AWS.
when: You already run OpenShift on premises and want a matching cloud setup
Your team's skills and tooling are OpenShift specific
You want Red Hat support included
nope: A team new to Kubernetes, EKS is cheaper and simpler
A small app that does not need Kubernetes at all, use ECS Fargate or Lambda
eg: A bank running OpenShift in its own data centre moves a few workloads to AWS without retraining its platform team.
pay: Hourly per worker node plus a control plane fee, on top of the EC2, storage and network charges. The OpenShift licence sits inside that hourly rate, so it is meaningfully pricier than EKS.

name: AWS Activate
one: Free AWS credits and help for new startups.
like: A voucher book a shopping mall hands new tenants so they try the place out.
what: A programme that gives startups AWS credits, plus some technical guidance and free support plan time. The Founders tier gives a small amount, around $1,000. The big numbers, up to $200,000 or more for AI startups, come through the Portfolio tier, which you can only reach if a VC, accelerator or partner refers you. Credits expire, usually in a year or two.
when: You are a startup under about 10 years old and new to AWS
Your investor or accelerator is an AWS Activate provider
You want to test an idea without paying the first bills
nope: You are an established business, there is no credit programme for you, ask an AWS account manager or a reseller for a discount instead
You want a big grant without a referral, applying direct gets you the small tier, go through your accelerator or VC
eg: A two person startup applies through their accelerator, gets credits, and runs their first year of EC2 and RDS bills for free.
pay: Nothing to join. The surprise is the expiry date, and the fact that credits often do not cover Marketplace software or reserved capacity, so those charges hit your card while you think you are on credits.

name: AWS IQ
one: A retired marketplace where you hired freelance AWS experts by the project.
like: A noticeboard for local handymen that the shop has now taken down.
what: AWS IQ let you post a small project and get proposals from vetted independent AWS experts, billed through your AWS account. It is being shut down. New expert sign ups stopped in May 2025, new projects stopped in August 2025, and access ends on 28 May 2026. AWS points people to AWS Marketplace Professional Services instead.
when: Basically never now, it is closing
Only relevant if you have an old engagement still running on it
nope: You need short term AWS help, use AWS Marketplace Professional Services, an AWS Partner, or hire a contractor normally
You need deep ongoing help from AWS itself, that is AWS Professional Services
eg: A small firm used to post "set up our VPC and a backup plan" and pick a freelancer for a few hundred dollars. That route no longer exists.
pay: Per project, on your AWS bill. Moot now, since you cannot start new work on it.

name: AWS Managed Services
one: You pay AWS staff to run your AWS infrastructure operations for you.
like: Hiring a managing agent for a building. They handle repairs, inspections and the fire alarm checks, you still own the building.
what: It is a service offering with people behind it, not a console feature. AWS handles patching, backups, incident response, monitoring and change requests under an agreed process. Changes usually go through a request workflow, which can feel slow to teams used to deploying themselves. It is aimed at large enterprises, often ones migrating off a data centre.
when: A large migration with no in house AWS operations team
Regulated workloads needing documented 24/7 operations
Buying time while you hire and train
nope: Small or mid sized teams, the minimum spend is large, hire or use a partner
Fast moving product teams, the change process will slow you down
eg: A bank moves its core estate to AWS and AWS engineers handle patching windows and night time incidents.
pay: A percentage of your managed AWS spend, plus the AWS resources themselves, with a substantial monthly minimum.

name: AWS Professional Services
one: AWS consultants you pay to come and build or advise on a project with you.
like: Calling in the manufacturer's own engineers to install a machine, rather than a local fitter.
what: A paid consulting team inside AWS that works alongside your staff on migrations, big architecture jobs and modernisation programmes. They are consultants, not support, so they do not answer tickets. They are usually more expensive than an AWS Partner doing the same work, and most projects run through Partners instead.
when: A large, high risk migration where you want AWS itself involved
You need expertise on a very new AWS service nobody else knows yet
An executive wants AWS accountable on the project
nope: You have a bug or an outage, that is AWS Support, not this
You want normal delivery work at a normal price, use an AWS Partner or your own contractors
eg: An airline hires ProServe for a year to help move a core booking system off a data centre.
pay: Time and materials or fixed fee, quoted per engagement, usually six figures. The surprise is that it does not come out of credits and is not included in any support plan.

name: AWS Support
one: A paid plan that lets you raise a ticket and get a human at AWS to help.
like: An extended warranty with a phone number, where the price decides how fast somebody picks up.
what: Four paid tiers above the free Basic account help. Developer is cheap and business hours only. Business gives 24/7 technical help and one hour response for a production outage. Enterprise On-Ramp and Enterprise add faster response and a named technical account manager. Support covers AWS services, not bugs in your own code.
when: You run anything in production
You need somebody to call during an outage
You want a service limit raised quickly
nope: You just want a general question answered, re:Post is free
You want somebody to write or debug your application, support will not do that, hire a Partner or Professional Services
eg: Your RDS instance fails over at midnight and you open a severity one case that gets a reply in under an hour.
pay: Developer starts around $29 a month, Business around $100 a month, but both are really a percentage of your AWS spend once it grows, which is the bit that surprises people. Enterprise On-Ramp starts around $5,500 a month and Enterprise around $15,000 a month.

name: AWS Training Certification
one: AWS courses and exams, some free, that prove you know the services.
like: Driving lessons and a driving licence. The lessons help, the licence is what employers ask to see.
what: Free digital courses on AWS Skill Builder, paid classroom and lab training, and exams such as Cloud Practitioner, Solutions Architect Associate and the specialty certs. The exams test recall of AWS specifics, so passing one is not the same as having built anything. Certifications expire after three years.
when: You are new to AWS and want a structured path
Your employer or a partner tier needs certified staff
You want the hands on labs rather than reading docs
nope: You want to actually learn to build, do a real small project alongside, certification alone does not teach you that
You want vendor neutral cloud knowledge, this is AWS specific by design
eg: A developer does the free Cloud Practitioner course in a week, then sits the exam for $100 to satisfy a client requirement.
pay: Much of Skill Builder is free. Exams cost roughly $100 to $300 depending on level. Instructor led classes and the paid Skill Builder subscription cost extra.

name: AWS rePost Private
one: A private version of the re:Post question site, just for your company. It is being shut down.
like: An internal staff noticeboard instead of a public one.
what: A private knowledge and question space for large AWS customers, where your own engineers and AWS support staff answer internal questions. It is closed to new customers and reaches end of service on 30 June 2027, after which all private spaces are removed. Very few organisations ever used it.
when: Almost never, it is closing
Only if you already have a space and need to plan an exit
nope: You want an internal knowledge base, use Confluence, Notion, SharePoint or a wiki, not a service with an end date
You want expert answers from AWS, that is your Enterprise Support plan and your technical account manager
eg: A large enterprise ran an internal space where staff asked AWS questions without going public. Those spaces now need moving elsewhere before mid 2027.
pay: Tiered, tied to Enterprise or Enterprise On-Ramp Support. Not worth pricing now given the shutdown.

name: AWS rePost
one: A free public question and answer site for AWS, run by AWS.
like: A public library help desk. Free, useful, but you wait for whoever is around to answer.
what: The replacement for the old AWS Forums. You ask a question in public and community members or AWS staff may answer. Answers are not guaranteed and not a support commitment. Quality varies, and for a specific account problem it is usually slower than a support ticket.
when: A general how do I question about a service
You want to search what others already asked
You have no paid support plan
nope: Your production system is down, open an AWS Support case, do not post in public
The question involves account numbers, billing detail or anything private, it is a public site
eg: You ask why a Lambda function times out reaching RDS, and somebody points you at the VPC subnet setup.
pay: Free.

name: AWS Database Migration Service
one: Moves a database into AWS with almost no downtime.
like: Shifting house while still living in it. Things move across one room at a time.
what: DMS copies an existing database into AWS and keeps replicating changes until you switch over. It can also change engine, for example Oracle to PostgreSQL, paired with the conversion tool.
when: Moving an on premise database to AWS
Changing database engine
nope: A small database you can dump and restore in an hour.
pay: Per replication instance hour.
eg: Moving a live MySQL server to RDS with minutes of downtime, not days.

name: Amazon Aurora
one: Amazon's faster version of MySQL and PostgreSQL.
like: The same car, tuned. It drives the same way, it just goes faster and recovers better.
what: Aurora speaks MySQL and PostgreSQL, so your code usually works unchanged. Storage grows on its own and copies data across three availability zones. Serverless versions can scale down when quiet.
when: You outgrew RDS
You need more read copies
Traffic goes up and down a lot
nope: A tiny app. Plain RDS is cheaper.
pay: Per hour, plus storage used, plus reads and writes. Serverless charges by capacity used.
eg: A growing LMS where thousands of students log in at exam time.

name: Amazon DocumentDB
one: It is a database that speaks MongoDB's language but is built and run by AWS.
like: A coffee shop that makes a drink tasting like a famous chain's, close enough for most people, not identical.
what: You point a MongoDB driver at it and store JSON-like documents, and AWS handles backups, patching and failover. It is compatible with the MongoDB API up to version 5.0, not with MongoDB itself, so some commands, aggregation stages and features are missing. Check compatibility before committing, because migrations away from it are painful.
when: Moving an existing MongoDB app onto managed AWS infrastructure
You want document storage without running database servers
You need the MongoDB query style rather than SQL
nope: You need the full modern MongoDB feature set, use MongoDB Atlas which also runs on AWS
You are starting fresh with simple key lookups, DynamoDB is cheaper and scales better
eg: A content platform moves its self-hosted MongoDB cluster to DocumentDB so nobody has to patch servers at midnight.
pay: Per instance-hour plus storage, I/O and backups. The surprise is that it runs on always-on instances, so a small idle cluster still costs over 200 dollars a month, and I/O charges can exceed the instance cost.

name: Amazon DynamoDB
one: A very fast database with no tables to join.
like: A cloakroom. You hand over a ticket, you get your coat instantly. You cannot ask it which coats are blue.
what: DynamoDB gives single digit millisecond reads at any scale. You must know how you will look data up before you design it. Queries it was not designed for are slow or impossible.
when: Huge scale, simple lookups
Sessions, carts, device data
You want zero database administration
nope: You need flexible reporting queries
Your access patterns keep changing
pay: Per read and write, or a fixed capacity. Plus storage.
eg: Storing which lesson each student is currently on, looked up by student id.

name: Amazon ElastiCache
one: Keeps frequently used data in memory so it is fast.
like: Keeping the tools you use most on the bench, not in the store room.
what: ElastiCache runs Redis or Memcached. It holds results in memory so your database is not asked the same question a thousand times. Memory is not permanent, so never keep the only copy here.
when: Slow repeated queries
Session storage
Leaderboards and counters
nope: Data you cannot afford to lose.
pay: Per node hour.
eg: Caching the course list so the database is hit once a minute, not once a click.

name: Amazon Keyspaces
one: It stores data the way Apache Cassandra does, without you running any Cassandra servers.
like: Renting a self-drive car that has the same controls you already learned, so you can drive off without lessons.
what: It accepts Cassandra CQL queries and drivers, and scales storage and throughput on its own. It is API compatible, not real Cassandra, so some features such as materialized views and certain consistency options behave differently or are missing. It is a narrow service, mainly useful if you already have Cassandra code.
when: You have a Cassandra application and do not want to operate a cluster
You need wide-row, high-write workloads with a known access pattern
Your team already knows CQL
nope: You are starting a new project on AWS with no Cassandra history, DynamoDB is the better default
You depend on Cassandra internals or unusual features, run Cassandra yourself on EC2
eg: A telecom team lifts an existing CQL-based event store off a self-managed cluster and keeps the same client code.
pay: Per read and write request plus storage, or provisioned capacity. Costs climb fast with large rows, because you are billed by data size per operation, not per row.

name: Amazon MemoryDB
one: It is a very fast in-memory store that, unlike a normal cache, does not lose your data.
like: A whiteboard that quietly photocopies itself every time you write on it, so wiping it by accident costs nothing.
what: It is compatible with Valkey and Redis, so existing clients work, but every write is also stored in a durable multi-zone log before it is acknowledged. That makes it safe to use as the main database, which plain ElastiCache is not. The trade-off is slower writes than a pure cache and a much higher bill, since everything lives in RAM.
when: You need microsecond reads and cannot lose the data
Replacing a cache plus database pair with one system
Session or leaderboard data that must survive a node failure
nope: You only need a cache in front of a real database, use ElastiCache, it is cheaper
Your data set is large or cold, RAM pricing will hurt, use DynamoDB
eg: A payments service keeps live fraud counters in MemoryDB so a node restart does not reset them.
pay: Per node-hour by memory size, plus a charge per gigabyte written to the durable log. The write charge is the part people do not expect.

name: Amazon Neptune
one: It is a database for things that are connected to other things, and for the connections themselves.
like: A family tree on a wall. The lines between the names matter as much as the names.
what: You store nodes and the relationships between them, and ask questions like who is two steps away from this person, using Gremlin, openCypher or SPARQL. There is also Neptune Analytics for running graph algorithms over a loaded data set. Graph databases are a genuinely small niche, and most problems people bring to them are better handled by SQL joins.
when: Fraud rings, recommendations or identity resolution
Knowledge graphs where relationships are the main data
Queries that would need many levels of joins in SQL
nope: Your relationships are only one or two joins deep, use RDS or Aurora
You want a graph for the sake of it, the operating cost and learning curve are real
eg: A bank finds accounts that share a phone number with an account that shares an address with a known fraudster.
pay: Per instance-hour plus storage and I/O, or serverless capacity units. There is no cheap idle mode on provisioned instances, so a test cluster left running is an expensive mistake.

name: Amazon RDS
one: A normal SQL database, run for you.
like: A rented flat with a cleaner included. It is still your flat, someone else does the chores.
what: RDS runs MySQL, PostgreSQL, MariaDB, Oracle or SQL Server. AWS handles backups, patching and standby copies. You still design the tables and write the queries.
when: You already know SQL
Normal business data: orders, users, invoices
nope: You need one database serving the whole world at once. Look at Aurora or DynamoDB.
pay: Per hour the database is on, by size, plus storage and backups.
eg: The orders table for a shop, with an automatic nightly backup.

name: Amazon Timestream
one: It stores readings that arrive with a timestamp, like sensor or metric data.
like: A logbook where every entry is stamped with the time and you mostly ask what happened between two times.
what: Read the status carefully, because the name covers two different things now. Timestream for LiveAnalytics, the original AWS-built engine, was closed to new customers on 20 June 2025, so you cannot start using it unless you already do. The version still open is Timestream for InfluxDB, which is AWS running the open source InfluxDB for you.
when: You already use InfluxDB and want it managed
IoT device readings or application metrics kept for a long time
Queries that are almost always time ranges and roll-ups
nope: You are new to AWS and want time series storage, do not plan on LiveAnalytics, it is closed to new customers
You only want dashboards and alarms on your own systems, CloudWatch already does that
eg: A solar company stores per-minute output from 5,000 inverters and charts the last 90 days.
pay: Timestream for InfluxDB bills per instance-hour and storage, like a database. Idle instances still cost money, so it is not a cheap parking spot for old data.

name: Oracle Database at AWS
one: Runs real Oracle Exadata databases inside an AWS data centre, next to your apps.
like: Oracle renting a locked room inside AWS's building, with a door straight into your office.
what: This is a joint Oracle and AWS offering, also branded Oracle AI Database@AWS. Oracle's own hardware sits in an AWS Availability Zone and you link it to your VPC over an ODB network. You create the network and infrastructure in AWS, but you manage the databases themselves in the Oracle Cloud console, so you work in two clouds.
when: You have Oracle Exadata workloads that cannot be rewritten
Apps on EC2 need very low latency to an Oracle database
You want Oracle licence benefits without your own data centre
nope: If your database is not Oracle, ignore this completely.
If you can move to PostgreSQL or MySQL, amazon-rds or Aurora is far cheaper and simpler.
For plain Oracle Database without Exadata, RDS for Oracle is the normal choice.
Buying is through a private offer, so this is enterprise only.
eg: An insurer keeps its Exadata core system in Oracle Database@AWS and points its EC2 application servers at it over a peered ODB network.
pay: Bought through AWS Marketplace as a private offer negotiated with Oracle, on committed terms. It is not pay as you go pricing, and it is expensive.

name: AWS Cloud Control API
one: One set of five commands to create, read, update, delete and list almost any AWS thing.
like: A universal remote. Instead of a different remote for the TV, the fan and the lights, one remote with the same five buttons works on all of them.
what: Normally every AWS service has its own API with its own command names. Cloud Control API puts a single CRUDL interface in front of hundreds of resource types, so tool builders write one piece of code instead of hundreds. It is mostly used by people building infrastructure tools, like the Terraform Cloud Control provider. Coverage is not total, and it can lag behind a service's own API by a while.
when: You are building a tool that manages many AWS resource types
You want new resource support without writing per service code
You already use CloudFormation resource types and want them callable directly
nope: You just want to create a few resources, use the AWS CLI or CDK
You need a service feature that is new or unusual, call that service's own API
eg: A small internal tool that can create an S3 bucket, a DynamoDB table or an SNS topic using the same function, just with a different type name.
pay: No charge for the API itself. You pay for whatever resources it creates, and those bills are easy to forget because the tool hides which service it touched.

name: AWS Cloud Development Kit
one: Write your AWS setup as normal code instead of a long config file.
like: A recipe you write in your own handwriting, which a machine then turns into the official form the kitchen requires.
what: CDK lets you describe infrastructure in TypeScript, Python, Java, Go or C#. It converts that code into a CloudFormation template and deploys it. You get loops, variables and reuse, but you still inherit CloudFormation's behaviour underneath, including slow stack updates and awkward rollbacks. The generated template is often much bigger than one a person would write.
when: Your setup repeats a lot and you want loops and functions
Your team already writes in one of the supported languages
You want sensible defaults instead of hand writing every property
