nope: A handful of resources you will rarely change, plain CloudFormation or the console is simpler
Your team already runs on Terraform, adding CDK gives you two sources of truth
eg: Ten near identical Lambda functions defined with a for loop over a list of names, rather than ten copied blocks of YAML.
pay: CDK itself is free. The surprise is the deploy bucket and the bootstrap stack it creates in every account and region, plus charges for whatever it builds.

name: AWS Cloud9
one: A code editor that ran in your browser, now closed to new customers.
like: A shared workshop that stopped taking new members. The people already inside can keep working, but nobody new gets a key.
what: Cloud9 was a browser based IDE with a terminal attached to an EC2 machine. AWS stopped accepting new customers in mid 2024 and is not adding features. Existing users still have it. If you want a browser terminal today, use CloudShell, and for a full editor use VS Code on your own machine or a remote dev environment.
when: You are an existing Cloud9 user and it still works for you
You are reading old tutorials and need to know why the button is missing
nope: You want a quick terminal in the browser, use CloudShell
You want a real IDE, use VS Code locally with the AWS Toolkit
eg: An old workshop tells you to open a Cloud9 environment, and your account has no option to create one.
pay: You paid for the EC2 instance behind it, not the editor. People were billed for idle environments they forgot to stop.

name: AWS CloudShell
one: A terminal inside the AWS website that already knows who you are.
like: A courtesy phone in a hotel lobby. It is already connected, you just pick it up and use it.
what: Click the shell icon in the AWS console and you get a Linux command line with the AWS CLI installed and your console login already applied. It gives you a small home directory that persists, around 1 GB. The machine itself resets after about 20 minutes of no use, so anything installed outside your home directory disappears.
when: You need to run one or two AWS commands without setting up keys locally
You are on a machine where you cannot install the CLI
You want to test what permissions your console role actually has
nope: You are running long builds or heavy jobs, use EC2 or CodeBuild
You need access to something inside a private VPC, it does not sit in your VPC by default
eg: Checking why an S3 bucket policy is blocking you, by running one CLI command from the console without touching your laptop.
pay: Free. The catch is the small home directory, which is deleted if you do not use that region for about 120 days.

name: AWS CodeArtifact
one: A private store for the code libraries your team installs.
like: A company stockroom. Common parts are pulled in from the outside supplier once, and your own in house parts sit on the same shelves.
what: CodeArtifact hosts private npm, pip, Maven, NuGet and similar packages, and can also mirror public registries so builds do not break when a public package vanishes. Authentication uses a token that expires, up to 12 hours, so build scripts must fetch a fresh one. It supports fewer package formats than JFrog Artifactory.
when: You publish internal libraries that must not be public
You want a cached copy of public packages so builds are repeatable
You already run builds in AWS and want package access controlled by IAM
nope: You only use public packages and builds are fine, this is extra work for nothing
You need Docker images, use ECR instead
You need a format it does not support, use Artifactory or GitHub Packages
eg: An internal Python utility library that every team installs with pip, without it ever being published to PyPI.
pay: Per GB stored, per request, and per GB transferred out of the region. The request charges add up when many build agents install the same packages repeatedly.

name: AWS CodeBuild
one: A machine AWS starts for you to compile and test your code, then throws away.
like: Hiring a kitchen by the hour. You bring the ingredients and the recipe, cook, and leave nothing behind.
what: You give CodeBuild a buildspec.yml listing the commands to run. It starts a clean container, runs them, keeps the logs and output files, then shuts down. Every build starts fresh, so dependency downloads repeat unless you turn on caching. Builds default to no VPC access, which surprises people trying to reach a private database.
when: You want CI without running your own build servers
Your build must reach AWS resources using IAM instead of stored keys
You need a specific container image or large build machine on demand
nope: Your code lives on GitHub and the team is happy there, GitHub Actions is usually simpler
You need long running or always on build agents, use EC2 or ECS
eg: On every push, install dependencies, run the test suite, build a Docker image and push it to ECR.
pay: Per build minute, by machine size. The surprise is slow builds with no cache, and ARM or GPU sizes costing far more per minute.

name: AWS CodeCommit
one: AWS's own private Git repository hosting.
like: A filing cabinet in your own office rather than a shared one down the street.
what: CodeCommit stores Git repositories inside your AWS account with IAM controlling access. AWS closed it to new customers in 2024, then reversed that in late 2025 and made it generally available again with new features planned. It has no pull request review culture, issues, or actions comparable to GitHub or GitLab, so it is a bare repository host.
when: Your rules say source code must stay inside your AWS account
You want repository access controlled by IAM roles, not separate accounts
You need a repo in a restricted region such as GovCloud
nope: You want code review, issues and a community, use GitHub or GitLab
Your CI already lives on GitHub, connecting AWS to it is easier than moving
eg: A bank keeping its deployment scripts in an account that has no route to the public internet.
pay: Free for the first five active users per month, then a flat fee per active user, with extra for storage and requests above the included amount.

name: AWS CodeDeploy
one: Puts a new version of your app onto servers gradually, and rolls back if it breaks.
like: Changing the menu in one branch of a restaurant first. If customers complain, the other branches never get the new menu.
what: CodeDeploy pushes code to EC2 or on premises servers, or shifts traffic for Lambda and ECS. You get canary and linear rollouts, and automatic rollback on a CloudWatch alarm. On EC2 it needs an agent installed and an appspec.yml with lifecycle hooks, which is the fiddly part. It moves traffic, it does not build anything.
when: You run on EC2 and want staged rollouts instead of replacing everything at once
You want an automatic rollback tied to an error alarm
You need blue green traffic shifting for ECS or Lambda
nope: You deploy containers and already use ECS rolling updates, that is often enough
Your infrastructure is defined in CDK or CloudFormation and deploys with the stack
You want the whole pipeline, that is CodePipeline
eg: Sending 10 percent of traffic to a new Lambda version for five minutes, then all of it if no errors fire.
pay: Free for Lambda and ECS deployments. On premises instance deployments cost per instance update, and EC2 deployments are free but you still pay for the instances.

name: AWS CodePipeline
one: Joins the steps from code change to live release into one automatic chain.
like: A conveyor belt. Something is placed at one end, each station does its job, and it comes out finished at the other end.
what: CodePipeline watches a source, then runs stages in order: build, test, approve, deploy. It does not do the work, it calls CodeBuild, CodeDeploy, CloudFormation and others. Version 2 added better triggers, branch filters and variables. It is rigid compared with a script, and approvals and cross account deploys take real setup.
when: You want a visible chain of stages with manual approval gates
Your deploy steps already use AWS build and deploy services
You need separate dev, staging and production accounts in one flow
nope: Everything you need is in GitHub Actions or GitLab CI, do not run two CI systems
You have one small app, a build job that deploys directly is simpler
eg: A push to main runs tests, waits for a human to click approve, then deploys the CloudFormation stack to production.
pay: A small monthly fee per active pipeline, free if unused that month. The real cost is the CodeBuild minutes each run burns.

name: AWS Command Line Interface
one: Type AWS commands in a terminal instead of clicking around the website.
like: Ordering by phone with an exact list, instead of walking every aisle of the shop.
what: The AWS CLI is one program that can call almost every AWS service. You install it, configure credentials, and run commands like aws s3 cp. Version 2 is the current one, version 1 reached end of support. Output is JSON by default, and the --query and --output flags are what make it usable. Some services have long, unfriendly command names.
when: You want to script something you do repeatedly
You need a feature the console has not exposed yet
You are debugging permissions and want the exact error
nope: You are writing an application, use the SDK for your language, not shell calls
You want repeatable infrastructure, use CloudFormation or CDK, not a pile of CLI commands
eg: Copying a folder of files to S3 with one command instead of dragging them in the browser.
pay: Free. The trap is a command like a full S3 listing or a wide CloudWatch query running up request or scan charges.

name: AWS Fault Injection Service
one: Deliberately breaks parts of your system so you can see how it copes.
like: A fire drill. You set off the alarm on purpose, on a day you choose, to find out whether people know the way out.
what: Formerly called AWS Fault Injection Simulator. It runs controlled experiments such as stopping EC2 instances, adding network latency, throttling an API, or failing over a database. You define stop conditions using CloudWatch alarms so the experiment aborts if real damage starts. This is a niche tool, useful mainly to teams that already have good monitoring and a real availability target.
when: You claim multi AZ resilience and want proof
You are preparing for a game day or a disaster recovery test
You want to check that alarms and failover actually fire
nope: You have no monitoring yet, you will break things and learn nothing, fix observability first
You want to test application logic under load, use a load testing tool
eg: Stopping every instance in one availability zone for ten minutes to confirm the load balancer keeps serving traffic.
pay: Per action minute during an experiment. The real cost is the outage you cause if you skip stop conditions, so never start in production without them.

name: AWS Infrastructure Composer
one: Draw your AWS setup on a canvas and get the config file out of it.
like: Sketching a floor plan by dragging furniture around, and the builder's drawing is produced from your sketch.
what: Renamed from AWS Application Composer in October 2024. You drag services onto a canvas in the console or in VS Code, connect them, and it writes a CloudFormation or SAM template. It also draws a diagram from an existing template, which is often the more useful direction. It covers a limited set of resource types well, and hand edits and canvas edits can fight each other.
when: You are new to CloudFormation and want to see the shape of a template
You want a diagram of a template someone else wrote
You are sketching a small serverless app before writing code
nope: Your infrastructure is large or written in CDK, this will not help
You need full control over every property, write the template by hand
eg: Dragging an API Gateway, a Lambda and a DynamoDB table onto the canvas and exporting a working SAM template.
pay: Free to use. You pay for whatever the generated template deploys, which is easy to underestimate from a picture.

name: AWS Tools and SDKs
one: The official libraries that let your program talk to AWS.
like: The set of adapters that come with an appliance, one for each country's socket.
what: This is not one service, it is the collection: SDKs for Python (boto3), JavaScript, Java, Go, .NET, Rust and more, plus IDE plugins, the SAM CLI and toolkits. They handle signing requests, retries and credential lookup so you do not write that yourself. Each SDK has its own idea of defaults, especially around retries and timeouts, so check those rather than assuming.
when: Your application needs to read or write AWS resources
You want credentials picked up automatically from a role
You want retries and request signing handled for you
nope: A one off task from your terminal, use the CLI
Managing infrastructure, use CDK or CloudFormation, not SDK calls in a script
eg: A Python Lambda using boto3 to write a record into DynamoDB, with no keys in the code because the role supplies them.
pay: Free to use. The surprise is aggressive default retries turning one failure into several billed API calls.

name: AWS X Ray
one: Follows one request through all your services and shows where the time went.
like: A parcel tracking page. You see every depot the parcel passed through and how long it sat at each one.
what: X-Ray collects traces from instrumented applications and draws a service map plus a timeline of each request. You must instrument your code or run an agent, it does not appear on its own. It samples by default, so a rare slow request may never be recorded. AWS now points new work toward OpenTelemetry and CloudWatch Application Signals, with X-Ray as the storage behind them.
when: A request is slow and you do not know which service caused it
You have several services calling each other and need a map
You want to see downstream AWS call latency per request
nope: You have one small service, logs and CloudWatch metrics are enough
You already run Datadog, Honeycomb or another tracing tool, do not double instrument
eg: Finding that a 3 second API response was actually 2.6 seconds spent on one DynamoDB query, not on your code.
pay: Per trace recorded, per trace retrieved and per trace scanned. Turning sampling up to 100 percent on a busy service is the bill shock.

name: Amazon CodeCatalyst
one: AWS's all in one place for repos, pipelines and issues, now in maintenance mode.
like: A serviced office where the desks, phones and meeting rooms all came together. The landlord has stopped refurbishing it.
what: CodeCatalyst bundled Git hosting, CI workflows, issue tracking and dev environments into one product with project blueprints. AWS has moved it to maintenance mode, meaning it still runs but is not getting new development. Do not start new projects on it. Use GitHub or GitLab for the repo and issues, with CodePipeline or GitHub Actions for the pipeline.
when: You already have projects on it and need to keep them running
You are evaluating it and need to know its status before committing
nope: You are starting a new project, use GitHub or GitLab
You want AWS native CI, use CodePipeline and CodeBuild
eg: An existing CodeCatalyst space still building an app, with a plan being written to move it to GitHub.
pay: There was a free tier, with charges for build minutes, storage and dev environment hours. The dev environments billed for uptime, not use.

name: Amazon Corretto
one: Amazon's free version of Java, which they keep patched for years.
like: A generic medicine. Same formula as the branded one, made by someone else, and cheaper to keep taking.
what: Corretto is a build of OpenJDK that Amazon supports at no cost, with long term security updates for versions 8, 11, 17, 21 and newer. It runs anywhere, not only on AWS. It is not a service, it is a download, and it behaves like standard Java because it is certified against the Java standard. Most people switch to it purely to avoid Oracle's licence terms.
when: You want free long term security patches for an old Java version
You want to avoid Oracle JDK licensing questions
You run Java on AWS and want the build AWS already tests against
nope: You need a feature only a commercial JDK offers, such as a specialist garbage collector
Your build is pinned and tested against another JDK, changing it for no reason adds risk
eg: A Java 11 service still in production, pulling Corretto 11 security updates years after Oracle's free updates stopped.
pay: Free, including the updates. No AWS account needed, and nothing appears on your bill.

name: Amazon WorkSpaces
one: Gives each person a Windows or Linux desktop they open from any device.
like: A locker at work. Your things stay in it, and you can open it from any branch.
what: AWS runs the desktop in the cloud and streams the screen to a client app or browser. The desktop keeps your files and settings between sessions. Performance depends heavily on the user's internet, and Windows licensing rules can be awkward if you bring your own.
when: Contractors need access without company laptops
Staff must work from home on a locked down machine
Data must never sit on a personal device
nope: If you only need one application, not a whole desktop, AppStream 2.0 is cheaper.
If people only need a safe browser, use WorkSpaces Secure Browser.
For developers who just need a Linux shell, an amazon-ec2 instance is simpler and cheaper.
With bad or high latency internet, this feels terrible. Do not force it.
eg: A support team of 200 contractors in another country logs into WorkSpaces each morning, and no customer data leaves AWS.
pay: Monthly per desktop, or hourly plus a smaller monthly fee. The surprise is the monthly option charges a full month even if someone logs in once, and idle desktops keep billing until you delete them.

name: AWS Amplify
one: The quickest way to put a web or mobile front end online.
like: A ready made kitchen fitted in a day, instead of building one.
what: Amplify hosts your front end, connects to GitHub and deploys on every push. It can also generate a backend with auth, API and storage. Great to start, restrictive once your needs grow.
when: React, Next.js or Vue front ends
Quick prototypes and MVPs
nope: Complex custom backends.
pay: Per build minute and per GB served, with a free tier.
eg: Pushing to GitHub and the site is live two minutes later.

name: AWS Device Farm
one: Lets you test your app on real phones and tablets sitting in an AWS data centre.
like: A shop display of a hundred different phones you can borrow one at a time, remotely.
what: You upload your app and either run automated tests on many devices at once, or take manual remote control of one device and tap through it yourself. It covers real hardware, not just simulators, which is the point. Device availability varies, and the newest handsets are not always there. Note that its desktop browser testing feature was retired, so it is now mobile devices only.
when: Checking an app on Android models you do not own
A bug that only appears on one manufacturer's phone
Automated test runs across many devices before a release
nope: Testing a website across browsers, use Playwright yourself or a browser testing service
A team with a shelf of test phones already, this adds cost and latency
Unit tests, run those in CI
eg: A release candidate is run on 25 Android models overnight and crashes on two older Samsung handsets.
pay: Per device minute, or a flat monthly fee for unlimited testing slots. Long automated suites across many devices multiply minutes quickly.

name: Amazon Location Service
one: Maps, address lookup, routes and location tracking for your app, without a Google Maps contract.
like: An A to Z street atlas with a ruler and an index, available to your app as it runs.
what: It bundles map tiles, geocoding, routing, geofences and a tracker for moving devices, using map data from Esri, HERE and others. The pricing is usually cheaper than Google Maps at volume, which is the main reason teams pick it. The map styles and place data are less rich than Google's, and the SDK ecosystem is smaller, so expect more work in the front end.
when: Showing a map or tracking vehicles in your own app
Turning addresses into coordinates in bulk
Alerting when a delivery driver enters or leaves an area
nope: Rich place details, reviews and street imagery, Google Maps is far ahead
A simple static map image on a web page, an image from a tile provider is less setup
Indoor positioning or precise asset tracking in a building, this is not built for that
eg: A delivery app draws each driver on a map and fires an alert when a van enters the customer's street.
pay: Per thousand map tile loads, geocoding requests, route calculations and tracked position updates. A map heavy screen that reloads tiles on every pan is what inflates the bill.

name: Amazon GameLift Servers
one: Runs and scales the game servers for a multiplayer game.
like: A sports centre that opens more courts as more players turn up, and closes them when people leave.
what: This is the current name for what was called Amazon GameLift. The GameLift brand now covers several products, and this one is the server hosting part. It places players into game sessions, scales fleets up and down, and includes FlexMatch matchmaking. Your game server has to be built against its SDK, so it is not a drop in.
when: A session based multiplayer game needs servers near players
Player numbers swing wildly between launch and quiet hours
You want matchmaking without writing it yourself
nope: If the game is turn based or not real time, a normal API on amazon-api-gateway and aws-lambda is much cheaper.
If you already run your own orchestration, use amazon-elastic-container-service or EKS and skip the SDK work.
Only game studios need this.
eg: A shooter launches worldwide; fleets in 12 Regions scale on player demand and FlexMatch groups players by skill and ping.
pay: Per instance hour for the fleet, plus data transfer. Spot instances cut cost a lot. The surprise is that you pay for spare capacity you keep warm for demand spikes.

name: Amazon GameLift Streams
one: Runs a game on an AWS machine and streams the video to a player's browser or device.
like: A television channel where the console is in the broadcaster's building and only the picture reaches your screen.
what: Launched in 2025. The game runs on GPU machines in AWS, and the player's device just shows the video and sends back controller input. It means a player with weak hardware can play a heavy game, and it can run in a browser with no install. It is separate from GameLift Servers, which hosts multiplayer logic rather than pictures. Streaming quality depends heavily on the player's network latency.
when: Playable demos in a browser with no download
Reaching players on low powered devices
Letting people try a PC game before buying
nope: Ordinary multiplayer hosting, that is GameLift Servers
Players on slow or high latency connections, the experience will be poor
Mobile friendly casual games that run fine on the device itself
eg: A studio puts a Try it now button on its website and the full PC game starts in the visitor's browser in seconds.
pay: Per hour of GPU streaming capacity, plus data transfer for the video. Idle capacity held ready so players start instantly is charged too, and video egress adds up fast.

name: Open 3D Engine
one: A free 3D game and simulation engine you download and build with.
like: A free workshop full of tools. Nobody charges rent, but you still have to build the furniture.
what: O3DE is not an AWS service. It is open source software under the Linux Foundation, built from the code of the retired AWS Lumberyard. AWS is one member of the foundation, not the owner. It is far less used than Unreal or Unity, so tutorials, assets and hiring are thin.
when: You want a 3D engine with no royalties and full source
Robotics simulation, where its ROS support is used
You need to change engine internals
nope: For most games, Unreal or Unity has a far bigger ecosystem. Pick those unless royalties or source access are the deciding issue.
There is nothing to buy or switch on in the AWS console.
If you need hosted game servers, that is Amazon GameLift Servers, a different thing.
eg: A robotics team simulates a warehouse robot in O3DE before running the same code on real hardware.
pay: Free, with no royalties. You pay only for whatever machines you run it on.

name: AWS Marketplace Dark
one: Not a service. It is the dark background version of the AWS Marketplace icon.
like: The white version of a company logo used on a black poster. Same logo, different sheet.
what: This is an entry from the AWS Architecture Icons set, where many icons ship in a light and a dark variant. There is no product called AWS Marketplace Dark, nothing to sign up for and nothing to pay. The real thing is AWS Marketplace, an online store for software you can buy and run on AWS, billed through your AWS account.
when: Drawing an architecture diagram on a dark slide
Building a diagram tool's icon library
nope: If you wanted the store, that is AWS Marketplace, not this icon file.
Do not put this in a service list or a cost estimate. It is an image asset.
Nobody needs to learn this.
eg: A solutions architect drops the dark Marketplace icon into a diagram that uses a black background.
pay: Nothing. It is an image. AWS Marketplace itself adds the vendor's software charges to your normal AWS bill.

name: AWS Marketplace Light
one: Not a product. It is the light-background version of the AWS Marketplace icon.
like: A shop sign printed in two colours, one for a white wall and one for a black wall.
what: This is not a service. It is an icon variant from the AWS architecture icon set, where AWS Marketplace is drawn twice, once light and once dark, so diagrams look right on either background. The real thing behind the icon is AWS Marketplace, an online store where you buy software and data from other companies and the cost lands on your AWS bill. Nothing runs when you 'use' this icon.
when: Drawing an architecture diagram on a dark slide or a light slide
Picking the correct icon file from the AWS icon pack
Showing that part of your stack is bought software, not built in-house
nope: If you actually want to buy software, go to AWS Marketplace itself, not this icon.
If you want to sell software on AWS, that is AWS Marketplace seller listings, managed through AWS Partner Central.
Nobody needs to 'learn' this. It is a picture file.
eg: You are drawing your VPC diagram in a dark theme, so you drop in the dark icon and leave the light one alone.
pay: Nothing. Icons are free. AWS Marketplace purchases themselves are charged by the seller and appear on your normal AWS bill, often as a monthly or hourly software fee on top of the EC2 cost.

name: AWS IoT Core
one: It is the front door where your gadgets connect to AWS and send messages.
like: A post office for machines. Every device has its own registered address, drops off letters, and picks up letters left for it, even if it was switched off for a while.
what: Devices connect over MQTT, WebSockets or HTTPS using certificates, and publish messages to named topics. A rules engine then forwards those messages to other AWS services like Lambda, S3 or a database. It also keeps a 'device shadow', a stored copy of each device's last known and wanted state, so your app can read or set values while the device is offline. It handles the plumbing, not your application logic, and you still have to design topics, certificates and data format yourself.
when: Many small devices sending small readings
You need per device identity and certificates
You want device data to land in AWS services automatically
nope: A handful of devices you control, where a plain HTTPS API behind API Gateway is simpler and cheaper
Phone or browser apps, use API Gateway or AppSync instead of pretending they are IoT devices
High volume telemetry that only needs to be streamed and stored, Kinesis Data Streams is a better fit
eg: Two thousand water meters each publish a reading every fifteen minutes, and a rule writes each reading into DynamoDB.
pay: Per million messages, plus separate charges for connection minutes, rules engine actions and device shadow reads and writes. The surprise is that one incoming message can be billed several times over as it passes through each part.

name: AWS IoT Device Defender
one: It watches your connected devices for signs that one has been tampered with.
like: A building security guard who knows the normal routine. If a door that opens twice a day suddenly opens forty times at three in the morning, the guard raises it.
what: It has two parts. Audit checks your AWS setup for weak settings, like certificates that are shared between devices, expiring, or policies that are too open. Detect watches device behaviour against rules or a learned baseline and alerts on odd traffic. Note that Device Defender Detect moves to maintenance and access is restricted from 31 August 2026, so do not build new work on Detect; Audit is unaffected.
when: A fleet where a stolen device could be used to attack you
You need evidence of security checks for an auditor
Certificate and policy hygiene across many devices
nope: Small fleets, where reading CloudWatch metrics yourself is enough
Account wide threat detection, that is GuardDuty
New behaviour monitoring work, since Detect is being retired, build alerting on CloudWatch and your own rules
eg: An alert when one smart lock starts opening two hundred MQTT connections an hour instead of its usual one.
pay: Per device per month for audit checks, and per behaviour metric checked for Detect. Costs grow with the number of behaviours you define, not just device count.

name: AWS IoT Device Management
one: It helps you keep track of and update a large number of devices at once.
like: A fleet manager for a delivery company. It keeps the list of every van, groups them by depot, and rolls out a change to one group at a time instead of all at once.
what: It sits on top of IoT Core and adds bulk registration, searchable device groups, over the air software update jobs, and secure tunnelling so you can open a remote shell to a device behind a firewall. Jobs can be rolled out gradually and stopped automatically if too many devices fail. It manages devices, it does not run your device software.
when: Thousands of devices in the field needing firmware updates
You need to find devices by attribute, like model or region
You need remote access to a device for support
nope: Under a hundred devices, the plain IoT Core registry and your own scripts are enough
Servers or containers, use Systems Manager instead
Devices you can physically reach to update
eg: Pushing a firmware update to five thousand vending machines, ten percent at a time, pausing if failures pass five percent.
pay: Per device registered, per bulk registration, per search query, and per minute of secure tunnelling. Tunnelling sessions left open are a common unwanted charge.

name: AWS IoT Events
one: A service, now being retired, that watched device readings and reacted when a pattern appeared.
like: A checklist on the wall that says: if the light stays red for ten minutes, ring the bell. It is being taken down.
what: IoT Events let you define a state machine in the console, for example normal, warning and fault, with the conditions that move a device between states and the actions to take, such as sending an SNS message. It is being retired. New customers were cut off on 20 May 2025 and support ends on 20 May 2026. AWS suggests rebuilding the logic with IoT Core, Lambda, DynamoDB for state, and EventBridge.
when: Nothing new, it is closing
Only if you already run it and are planning the move off it
nope: Any new alerting logic, use IoT Core rules into Lambda with state in DynamoDB
Simple threshold alarms, a CloudWatch alarm is enough
Complex workflow across steps, use Step Functions
eg: A rule that raised a ticket if a freezer stayed above minus fifteen degrees for twenty minutes now runs as a Lambda with state kept in DynamoDB.
pay: Charged per message evaluated and per detector. Becomes irrelevant after May 2026.

name: AWS IoT ExpressLink
one: A ready made connectivity chip, so a simple product can reach AWS without you writing network code.
like: A pre paid mobile dongle for a machine. You plug it in, send it plain text commands, and it handles the phone network and the security for you.
what: ExpressLink is not really a service you switch on, it is a specification that hardware makers such as Espressif and u blox build modules to. Your microcontroller talks to the module over a serial link with simple AT style commands, and the module handles Wi-Fi or cellular, TLS, certificates and the MQTT connection to IoT Core. It saves firmware effort at the cost of buying a specific module and accepting what it supports.
when: A small product team with no embedded security experience
A microcontroller too small for a full TLS and MQTT stack
You want to get a connected product to market quickly
nope: A device already running Linux, just use the AWS IoT device SDK
Anything needing unusual protocols or fine control of the connection
Cases where the extra hardware cost per unit at scale outweighs the saved development time
eg: A battery powered water leak alarm whose small chip sends one MQTT message by writing a single command line to the module.
pay: There is no AWS charge for ExpressLink itself. You pay for the module in your bill of materials and for the IoT Core messages it sends.

name: AWS IoT FleetWise
one: It collects data from vehicles, choosing what to send so you do not pay for every signal.
like: A dashcam that only saves the clip when something interesting happens, rather than filming the whole journey and posting you the tapes.
what: You describe a vehicle's signals from its CAN bus or other network, then write campaigns that say which signals to collect and under what conditions, for example brake pressure only when speed is over eighty. An agent in the vehicle applies that and uploads to AWS. It is a narrow service for carmakers and fleet operators, and it needs access to the vehicle's signal database, so most people cannot use it at all.
when: You build or operate vehicles and control their software
Mobile data costs make sending everything impossible
Engineering teams investigating faults across a model range
nope: Tracking where vehicles are, a GPS tracker into IoT Core is far cheaper
Non vehicle machinery, use IoT SiteWise
Anyone without access to the vehicle bus and signal definitions
eg: Collecting battery cell temperatures from ten thousand electric cars, but only during fast charging.
pay: Per vehicle per month plus per signal message collected. Campaigns that trigger more often than expected drive the cost up quickly.

name: AWS IoT Greengrass
one: It runs AWS style code on your own hardware, near the machines, even without internet.
like: A branch office that can keep serving customers when the phone line to head office goes down, then sends the paperwork up later.
what: You install the Greengrass runtime on a Linux device such as an industrial PC or gateway. It runs components, which can be Lambda functions, containers or plain programs, caches messages while offline, talks to nearby devices, and syncs with IoT Core when the link returns. Version 1 is being retired, so use version 2. You are responsible for the hardware, the operating system and keeping it patched.
when: Unreliable or expensive connectivity at the site
Decisions that must happen in milliseconds, locally
Data too bulky or too sensitive to send raw to the cloud
nope: Devices with a solid always on connection, plain IoT Core is far less work
Tiny microcontrollers that cannot run Linux, use FreeRTOS or ExpressLink
A single site where an ordinary local server and your own code would do
eg: A gateway on a factory floor that reads a conveyor sensor, stops the line locally on a fault, and uploads a summary each hour.
pay: Per active device per month, plus the IoT Core messages it sends. The hidden cost is the field engineering to install and maintain hundreds of edge boxes.

name: AWS IoT SiteWise
one: It collects readings from factory machines and stores them in a way that matches how the plant is laid out.
like: A meter reading book for a whole factory, where each page is a machine and each machine belongs to a line, and a line belongs to a site.
what: An edge gateway reads industrial protocols such as OPC UA and sends the values to AWS. You then model your equipment as assets with properties and hierarchies, and define metrics computed from raw readings, for example machine uptime per shift. It comes with a simple dashboard tool called Monitor. Setting up the asset model is real work and the service only pays off in a plant with a lot of equipment. The SiteWise Edge data processing pack reached end of support in October 2025.
when: Existing factory equipment speaking OPC UA or Modbus
You want equipment metrics like OEE without writing a pipeline
Many sites you want to compare on the same model
nope: Consumer or one off devices, use IoT Core and a time series database
Plain time series storage with no equipment hierarchy, Timestream is simpler
A handful of sensors, where CloudWatch metrics are enough
eg: Reading temperature and cycle count from twelve injection moulding machines and showing downtime per shift.
pay: Per message ingested, per computed metric, per data storage tier and per Monitor user. Computed metrics recalculating often is the usual bill shock.

name: AWS IoT TwinMaker
one: Builds a live 3D model of a real factory or building that updates from its sensors.
like: A doll's house of your factory where the tiny lights turn on when the real lights turn on.
what: It takes a 3D model you already have, then wires each part of it to live data from sensors, cameras and business systems. Operators see the building on screen with real readings attached. The honest limitation is that it does not create the 3D model or the sensors for you, and the viewing layer is a Grafana plugin, so you need both before it is useful.
when: Plant operators need one screen showing equipment status in physical context
You already have CAD or 3D models of a site and live sensor data
Diagnosing which machine on a line is causing a problem
nope: If you only need charts and alarms, use Amazon CloudWatch or Amazon Managed Grafana. A 3D scene is a lot of work for a line graph.
If you just need to collect and store sensor readings, use AWS IoT Core and a database.
Most companies never need this. It suits large industrial sites with existing 3D models.
eg: A cookie factory shows its oven in 3D, and the oven turns red on screen when its real temperature sensor goes out of range.
pay: You pay per query against the digital twin and per GB of data stored, plus the cost of every underlying service. The surprise is that the bill is mostly the other services, the sensors, storage and the Grafana users, not TwinMaker itself.

name: FreeRTOS
one: A tiny free operating system that runs on very small chips inside devices.
like: The brain of a washing machine, not the brain of a laptop.
what: FreeRTOS is open source software you compile into a microcontroller, the sort of chip in a thermostat or a sensor. It handles running several small tasks on time. AWS looks after the project and adds libraries for talking to AWS IoT securely. It was briefly called Amazon FreeRTOS, then renamed back to FreeRTOS. It is not a cloud service and nothing of it runs in AWS.
when: Writing firmware for a battery powered sensor or small device
You need several jobs on one small chip to run on a fixed schedule
Connecting a microcontroller to AWS IoT with TLS and over-the-air updates
nope: If your device runs Linux, such as a Raspberry Pi or a gateway, use AWS IoT Greengrass instead.
If you are not writing embedded C, this has nothing for you.
If you only want the cloud side of IoT, that is AWS IoT Core. FreeRTOS is the device side.
eg: A water meter with a small chip runs FreeRTOS, wakes hourly, reads the meter, and publishes one message to AWS IoT Core.
pay: Nothing. It is MIT licensed and free, including for commercial products. You pay only for the AWS services the device talks to, such as AWS IoT Core messages.

name: AWS AppConfig
one: Changes a setting in your running app without redeploying the code.
like: The dimmer switch on the wall. You change the brightness without rewiring the lamp.
what: You store settings, like feature flags or limits, outside your app. The app checks for the current value and picks up changes within about a minute. AppConfig can roll a change out slowly and roll it back automatically if alarms fire. It is part of AWS Systems Manager, not a separate console, which confuses people. It is for small config values, not for secrets and not for large data.
when: Turning a feature on for 5 percent of users first
Changing a timeout or rate limit without a deploy
Config changes that need a safe, staged rollout
nope: Storing passwords or API keys, use AWS Secrets Manager
Plain static settings nobody changes at runtime, a Parameter Store value or an environment variable is simpler
eg: You flip a flag to turn off a slow search feature during a traffic spike, with no deploy and no restart.
pay: Per configuration request your app makes. The surprise is polling: an app that checks every second across many instances adds up, so you cache and poll less often.

name: AWS Application Auto Scaling
one: Adds and removes capacity automatically for AWS services other than plain servers.
like: A cafe that opens extra tills when the queue gets long and closes them when it is quiet.
what: It watches a metric, like CPU or queue length, and changes how much capacity a service has. It covers things like ECS tasks, DynamoDB tables, Aurora read replicas and SageMaker endpoints. It does not scale EC2 instances, that is EC2 Auto Scaling, and the similar names cause real confusion.
when: Scaling the number of ECS or Fargate tasks
Scaling DynamoDB read and write capacity
Scaling a machine learning endpoint by traffic
nope: Scaling EC2 virtual machines, use EC2 Auto Scaling groups
Traffic that spikes in seconds, scaling takes minutes, so use a queue or serverless like AWS Lambda
eg: Your order service runs 3 containers overnight and 30 at lunchtime, with nobody touching it.
pay: The scaling itself is free. You pay for whatever capacity it turns on, which is the whole point and also the bill.

name: AWS Auto Scaling
one: One screen to set up scaling across several services at once.
like: A master thermostat for the whole house instead of one dial per room.
what: It is a front end over EC2 Auto Scaling and Application Auto Scaling. You pick an app, say whether you care more about cost or availability, and it sets scaling policies on the pieces. Most engineers skip it and configure the underlying services directly, often through infrastructure as code. It gets little attention and is easy to mistake for EC2 Auto Scaling, which is the one people actually mean.
when: A first, quick scaling setup across a small stack
Wanting one plan covering EC2 and DynamoDB together
nope: Anything defined in Terraform or CloudFormation, set the underlying policies directly
A single service, go straight to EC2 Auto Scaling or Application Auto Scaling
eg: You point it at a web app and it puts target tracking on both the EC2 group and the DynamoDB table.
pay: Free. You pay only for the capacity that gets added.

name: AWS Backint Agent
one: Backs up an SAP HANA database straight into S3 using SAP's own backup screens.
like: A plug adapter, so SAP's existing backup button works with an Amazon cupboard.
what: It is a small program you install on the EC2 machine running SAP HANA. It is certified by SAP and implements SAP's Backint interface, so backups triggered from SAP HANA Cockpit, Studio or SQL land in Amazon S3 or AWS Backup. It supports full, incremental, differential and log backups. It only works for SAP HANA. It does nothing for any other database.
when: You run SAP HANA on EC2 and want backups in S3 rather than on disk
Your SAP team wants to keep using their own backup tools and schedules
You need log backups going to durable storage continuously
nope: If your database is not SAP HANA, this is the wrong tool. Use Amazon RDS backups or AWS Backup.
If you use SAP HANA Cloud or RISE, backups are handled for you and this does not apply.
If you only want EBS volume snapshots, use AWS Backup directly and skip the agent.
eg: Your SAP admin runs the usual nightly full backup from HANA Cockpit, and the files quietly arrive in an S3 bucket instead of a local disk.
pay: The agent itself is free. You pay for S3 storage, requests and any AWS Backup charges. The surprise is log backups, which are small but constant, so request counts add up.

name: AWS Chatbot
one: Sends AWS alerts into Slack or Microsoft Teams, and lets you run some commands from the chat.
like: A pager that posts into the team group chat instead of buzzing one person.
what: It was renamed to Amazon Q Developer in chat applications in February 2025. The API, the console URL and the IAM names are still chatbot, so you will see both names. Alarms and events go to an SNS topic, and it posts them to a channel. You can also type read only AWS commands in chat. It is not a conversational bot for your customers.
when: Getting CloudWatch alarms into a team channel
Letting on-call check a resource without opening the console
Posting deploy or budget events to chat
nope: Building a chatbot for your own users, use Amazon Lex or Amazon Bedrock
Serious incident paging with escalation, use PagerDuty or similar
eg: A CloudWatch alarm on database CPU posts to the #ops Slack channel, and someone types a command there to check the instance.
pay: The service is free. You pay for the SNS messages and CloudWatch behind it, which is small.

name: AWS CloudFormation
one: Writes your whole setup as a file, so you can rebuild it exactly.
like: An IKEA instruction sheet for your infrastructure. Same sheet, same result, every time.
what: You describe what you want in YAML or JSON. CloudFormation creates it, updates it, and can delete it all cleanly. No more clicking in the console and forgetting what you did.
when: You want staging and production to match
You want a record of your infrastructure
nope: A one off experiment you will delete tomorrow.
pay: Free. You pay for what it creates.
eg: One file that builds a VPC, two servers, a load balancer and a database.

name: AWS CloudTrail
one: Records who did what in your AWS account.
like: A CCTV log of the building. Not what the machines did, what the people did.
what: CloudTrail records every API call: who, when, from where. It is how you answer 'who deleted that database'. CloudWatch watches your app. CloudTrail watches your account.
when: Always. Turn it on the first day.
Any compliance requirement
pay: One free trail of management events. Extra trails and data events cost.
eg: Finding out which user turned off a security setting last Tuesday.

name: AWS Config
one: Records how your AWS setup changes over time.
like: A logbook of every change made to the building, with the rules it must follow.
what: Config records the configuration of your resources and checks them against rules. It can tell you what changed and when, and flag anything that drifts out of policy.
when: Compliance
You need change history
Many people have access
nope: A single tiny project.
pay: Per configuration item recorded and per rule evaluation. It adds up.
eg: Alerting the moment a security group is opened to the whole internet.

name: AWS Console Mobile Application
one: The official AWS app for your phone, for checking things while away from a laptop.
like: A mobile banking app. Enough to check the balance and stop a card, not enough to run the bank.
what: It shows alarms, billing, and the status of common resources, and lets you do a few actions like restarting an instance. It covers a small slice of what the web console does. Sign in works with a device passcode or biometrics after the first setup. Most people install it, use it during one incident, then forget it.
when: Checking an alarm while you are out
Seeing current spend quickly
Restarting or stopping an instance in a pinch
nope: Real work like configuring a service, use the web console
Team incident response, chat alerts through AWS Chatbot reach more people
eg: A billing alert fires on a Sunday, you open the app and see one forgotten large instance running.
pay: Free. You only pay for whatever the underlying resources cost.

name: AWS Control Tower
one: Sets up a tidy, rule enforced group of AWS accounts for a company.
like: An estate with a gatehouse and rules. Every new house gets the same wiring, the same locks and the same inspections.
what: It creates a multi account setup with a management account, logging and audit accounts, single sign on, and guardrails that block or detect risky actions. New accounts come out of a factory already set up. It is opinionated, hard to unwind later, and it turns on AWS Config broadly, which drives cost. It is for organisations, not for one person with one account.
when: A company standardising dozens of AWS accounts
Needing audit logging and rules applied everywhere by default
Giving teams their own accounts safely
nope: One or two accounts, use AWS Organizations and service control policies directly
A setup already built in Terraform, Control Tower will fight your existing structure
eg: A new product team asks for an account and gets one within an hour, already logging to the central bucket with guardrails on.
pay: Control Tower itself is free. The surprise is AWS Config recording every resource in every account, plus CloudTrail and S3 storage, which can run to hundreds of dollars a month.

name: AWS DevOps Agent
one: An AI assistant that digs into why your system broke and suggests the fix.
like: An on-call colleague who reads all the logs before you wake up.
what: It connects to your logs, metrics, code repositories and deployment pipelines, then works out what changed and what is failing. It went generally available in March 2026 and also looks at Azure and on-premises systems. It is new, so treat its conclusions as a strong first draft, not a verdict, and it needs real access to your telemetry and code before it is any use.
when: An incident is live and nobody knows which deploy caused it
You want preventive advice from past incidents rather than a fresh guess each time
A small team has no dedicated SRE
nope: If you have no logs or metrics wired up yet, fix that first with Amazon CloudWatch. The agent has nothing to read otherwise.
If you want simple threshold alerts, a CloudWatch alarm is cheaper and more predictable.
If your rules require a human to approve every production change, keep it as an advisor and do not let it act.
eg: Latency jumps at 2am, and by morning it has pointed at a config change in yesterday's deploy and named the pull request.
pay: Charged for use, with monthly credits included depending on your AWS Support plan. The surprise is that heavy investigation of large log volumes also raises your CloudWatch and data transfer bills.

name: AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry
one: AWS's own build of the standard open source tool that collects traces and metrics from your app.
like: A generic medicine sold under a shop's own label. Same formula, packaged and supported by that shop.
what: OpenTelemetry is an industry standard for instrumenting code. ADOT is AWS's tested distribution of it, with the AWS exporters already included and AWS support behind it. It sends data to X-Ray, CloudWatch, Amazon Managed Prometheus, or to non AWS tools like Datadog. It is a packaging choice, not a new capability, and upstream OpenTelemetry works on AWS too.
when: Instrumenting apps without locking into one vendor
Sending the same telemetry to AWS and a third party tool
Wanting AWS support on your collector build
nope: A pure AWS shop happy with the CloudWatch agent and X-Ray SDK, that is less work
Just wanting logs, CloudWatch Logs is far simpler
eg: Your Kubernetes services run an ADOT collector that ships traces to X-Ray and metrics to Managed Prometheus.
pay: The distribution is free. You pay for what receives the data, and trace and custom metric ingestion in CloudWatch and X-Ray is the part that surprises people at volume.

name: AWS Health Dashboard
one: Tells you when AWS itself has a problem, including ones that affect only your account.
like: The notice board at the station. General delays for everyone, plus a message about your specific train.
what: There are two views. The public one shows broad service issues. Your account view shows events that touch your resources, such as a scheduled reboot of your instance or a certificate about to expire. The account level API and the organisation view need a Business or Enterprise support plan, so basic accounts see less. It reports, it does not fix.
when: Checking whether an outage is AWS or your code
Finding scheduled maintenance on your instances
Getting warnings about deprecations that affect you
nope: Monitoring your own application health, use CloudWatch alarms
Fast public outage news, the public dashboard is often slow, and your own metrics tell you sooner
eg: Your app slows down, and the dashboard shows raised error rates for a service in your region, so you stop hunting your own code.
pay: The dashboard is free. The Health API and organisation view require a paid support plan, which is the real cost.

name: AWS Launch Wizard
one: A guided form that builds the AWS setup for a few specific packaged applications.
like: The setup wizard on a new printer. It asks a few questions and does the fiddly bits for you.
what: You answer questions about size and availability, and it generates and deploys a CloudFormation stack sized for that application. It supports a short list, mainly SQL Server, SAP and Active Directory. It is narrow, and outside that list it is no help at all. What it produces is a normal stack you can then manage yourself.
when: A first SQL Server Always On cluster on EC2
Standing up an SAP landscape without deep AWS knowledge
nope: Anything not on its short supported list, write CloudFormation or Terraform
Infrastructure your team will keep changing, own the templates from the start
eg: A Windows admin answers ten questions and gets a highly available SQL Server cluster across two availability zones.
pay: The wizard is free. You pay for the EC2, storage and any Windows or SQL licensing it turns on, which is not small.

name: AWS License Manager
one: Keeps count of software licences you own so you do not go over what you paid for.
like: A library ticket system. Only so many copies exist, so it tracks who has one out.
what: You describe a licence rule, such as 100 Windows Server cores, and it counts usage across accounts and can block launches that would break the limit. It also manages bring your own licence hosts and user based subscriptions for things like Office on AppStream. Most people only meet it because a vendor audit or a Microsoft agreement forced them to.
when: Bringing your own Windows or Oracle licences to AWS
Proving licence compliance in an audit
Stopping teams launching more licensed instances than allowed
nope: Everything running on open source or AWS supplied licences, you do not need it
Tracking SaaS seats like Slack or Figma, it does not do that
eg: A launch of an eleventh Oracle instance is blocked because the rule says you own ten.
pay: The core tracking is free. User based subscriptions carry a per user monthly charge, and dedicated hosts for bring your own licence are the expensive part.

name: AWS Management Console
one: The AWS website where you click around to see and change your stuff.
like: The dashboard of a car. Everything is reachable, but you still need to know what each dial does.
what: It is the browser interface covering every AWS service, plus search, billing and a built in shell called CloudShell. It is the right place to learn and to look at things. It is the wrong place to build production infrastructure, because clicks are not recorded, not repeatable, and nobody can review them. Experienced teams read here and write with code.
when: Learning what a service does
Checking a resource or a bill quickly
One off emergency action during an incident
nope: Creating production infrastructure, use CloudFormation, CDK or Terraform
Anything repeated more than twice, script it with the AWS CLI or an SDK
eg: You open the S3 page to check why a bucket is bigger than expected, then fix the lifecycle rule in Terraform.
pay: Free to use. Everything you click into costs whatever that service costs, and forgotten resources created here are a classic surprise bill.

name: AWS Organizations
one: Manages many AWS accounts as one company.
like: A head office with branch offices. One policy, one bill, separate premises.
what: Organizations groups accounts under one payer, applies rules that even account admins cannot override, and keeps production separate from development. Separate accounts are the strongest blast radius control AWS offers.
when: More than one project or client
You want production isolated
nope: A single personal learning account.
pay: Free.
eg: Separate accounts for dev, staging and production, one combined bill.

name: AWS Partner Central
one: The website AWS resellers and software vendors use to manage their AWS partnership.
like: The staff entrance of a shopping centre, not a shop you buy from.
what: This is a business portal, not a technical service. Companies in the AWS Partner Network sign in here to list products on AWS Marketplace, register sales deals with AWS, claim partner benefits and get training. It has now absorbed the old AWS Marketplace Management Portal. It runs nothing and stores none of your application data.
when: Your company sells software or consulting and wants to list it on AWS Marketplace
You need to register a customer deal so AWS sales will co-sell with you
Tracking your partner tier and required certifications
nope: If you are an AWS customer rather than an AWS partner, you will never open this.
If you only want to buy software, use AWS Marketplace.
If you want technical support on a service, use AWS Support, not this portal.
eg: A consultancy logs in to register a deal with a retail client so AWS sales does not compete with them on the same account.
pay: Free to use. Some partner programmes have their own annual fees or spend requirements, and Marketplace takes a cut of what you sell through it.

name: AWS Proton
one: A way for a platform team to publish ready made deployment templates for developers, now being shut down.
like: A canteen with fixed menu sets. The kitchen decides what combinations exist, you pick one.
what: Platform engineers defined environment and service templates, developers picked one and got infrastructure plus a pipeline. AWS is discontinuing it. New customers were closed off on 7 October 2025 and support ends on 7 October 2026. It never caught on widely. Do not build on it now.
when: Only if you already run it and are planning the exit
nope: Any new platform work, use Terraform or CDK with a module library, or Backstage for the developer portal
Simple app deployment, use ECS or Lambda with a normal pipeline
eg: An existing Proton user plans migration of its service templates to CDK before the October 2026 cut off.
pay: No charge for Proton itself, you paid for the resources. Now the real cost is the migration work before support ends.

name: AWS Resilience Hub
one: Scores how well your app would survive a failure, and tells you what is missing.
like: A home safety inspection. Someone checks the smoke alarms and the fire exit, then hands you a list.
what: You describe an application and your recovery targets, how much downtime and data loss you can accept. It inspects the resources, compares them against those targets, gives a score and lists fixes such as missing backups or a single availability zone. It can also run fault injection tests. It checks your setup, it does not make your app resilient.
when: Before a compliance or disaster recovery review
Checking whether recovery targets are actually met
Finding single points of failure in a known stack
nope: Small or non critical apps, the per application charge is not worth it
Actually testing failure behaviour deeply, use AWS Fault Injection Service directly
eg: It flags that your database has no cross region backup, so your four hour recovery target is not achievable.
pay: A flat monthly charge per application assessed, around 15 dollars, which surprises teams that register dozens of small apps.

name: AWS Resource Explorer
one: Search across all your AWS resources in every region at once.
like: The search box on your phone that looks through every app instead of you opening each one.
what: You turn on an index, then search by name, tag or type and see matches across regions. Before this you had to visit each service in each region. It needs to be enabled with an aggregator region first, and results lag behind reality by minutes. Not every resource type is indexed, so an empty result is not proof something does not exist.
when: Hunting a resource when you forgot the region
Finding everything tagged with an old project name
Cleaning up before a cost review
nope: A precise inventory for audit or compliance, use AWS Config
Cross account search, it is per account, so use Config aggregators or Organizations tooling
eg: You search a project tag and find a load balancer still running in a region nobody remembered using.
pay: Free. The value is the resources you find and switch off.

name: AWS Service Catalog
one: An internal menu of approved setups that staff can deploy without free rein.
like: A vending machine in the office. Only the approved items are inside, and you press one button.
what: An admin publishes CloudFormation or Terraform products, and users launch them with a few inputs. The launch runs under a role the admin defines, so the user does not need broad permissions. It works well for standard, stable items and poorly when teams want to change templates often, because every change goes through the catalog. Mostly seen in larger, governed organisations.
when: Letting non experts create approved infrastructure safely
Enforcing tagging and standards on every new resource
Handing out sandbox or project stacks on request
nope: Engineering teams that own their own infrastructure code, it just slows them down
One team, one repository, plain CloudFormation or Terraform in a pipeline is simpler
eg: A data analyst clicks one item and gets an approved, encrypted, correctly tagged S3 bucket plus a notebook.
pay: Free for normal use. Charges apply to very heavy API usage above a monthly allowance, and you pay for whatever the products create.

name: AWS Service Management Connector
one: Retiring. It let ServiceNow or Jira users request and see AWS resources from their own ticket tool.
like: A hatch between two offices, now being bricked up.
what: This is being shut down. It closed to new customers on 31 March 2026 and support ends on 31 March 2027, after which it stops working. It was a plugin for ServiceNow, Jira Service Management and Jira Cloud that surfaced AWS Service Catalog products, AWS Config data, Security Hub findings and Support cases inside those tools. AWS now tells customers to use partner ITSM integrations or write their own with the SDK.
when: Nothing new. Existing users should be planning their exit
Understanding an old diagram or runbook that mentions it
Deciding what replaces it before March 2027
nope: Do not start a new project on it. It is being switched off. Use a partner ITSM integration or build a direct SDK integration.
If you only need a self-service catalogue inside AWS, use AWS Service Catalog on its own, which is not affected.
If you want AWS events pushed into a ticket tool, EventBridge plus a webhook does that and is not going away.
eg: A staff member used to raise a ServiceNow ticket for a test server and get an approved EC2 instance, and that path now needs rebuilding.
pay: The connector was free. You paid only for the AWS resources it created. The real cost now is the migration work before the 2027 cutoff.

name: AWS Sustainability
one: Not a service. It is AWS's environment programme, with one real tool for your carbon numbers.
like: A company's recycling policy, plus a single electricity meter you can actually read.
what: There is no service you can switch on called AWS Sustainability. The name covers AWS's own renewable energy commitments, the Sustainability pillar of the Well-Architected Framework, which is guidance, and one concrete tool, the Customer Carbon Footprint Tool in the Billing console. That tool shows estimated emissions from your AWS usage, by month, region and service.
when: Your company has to report cloud emissions for an ESG disclosure
You want to compare the carbon cost of regions before choosing one
Reviewing a design against the Well-Architected sustainability guidance
nope: If you want live, detailed, per-resource carbon data, this is too coarse. It is monthly and estimated.
If your real goal is to spend less money, use AWS Cost Explorer. Less waste usually means less carbon anyway.
Do not expect an API to call. Most of it is documents and a billing dashboard.
eg: Your finance team downloads last quarter's carbon report from the Billing console for the annual ESG statement.
pay: Free. The surprise is the delay and the coarseness. Data appears about three weeks after month end, and anything under half a kilo of CO2e shows as zero.

name: AWS Systems Manager
one: Manage all your servers from one place.
like: A facilities team with a master key and a maintenance schedule.
what: Systems Manager patches servers, runs commands on all of them at once, stores configuration in Parameter Store, and gives shell access without opening SSH to the internet.
when: More than a couple of servers
You want to stop opening port 22
nope: Fully serverless setups with no servers to manage.
pay: Most of it is free. Some advanced features are paid.
eg: Applying a security patch to twenty servers with one command.

name: AWS Telco Network Builder
one: Deploys and manages mobile network software for phone companies running 5G on AWS.
like: Assembly instructions and a crew for building a phone network, rather than a shelf.
what: Known as AWS TNB. Telecom operators package network functions in a standard telecom format called TOSCA, and TNB turns that into running infrastructure on EC2 and EKS, then handles upgrades. It is still active and still getting updates. Almost nobody needs it. If you are not a mobile network operator or a telecom vendor, this service is not for you.
when: A mobile operator running 5G core functions on AWS
A telecom vendor automating network function delivery
nope: Any normal application, use ECS, EKS or plain CloudFormation
Networking between your own VPCs, use Transit Gateway
eg: An operator rolls out a new version of its 5G core across regions from one package definition.
pay: No charge for TNB itself. You pay for the EC2, EKS and networking it creates, and 5G workloads use large instances.

name: AWS Trusted Advisor
one: Checks your account and suggests fixes.
like: A yearly service for your car. It lists what needs attention.
what: Trusted Advisor checks for wasted money, security holes, missing redundancy and hitting limits. A few checks are free on every account, the full set needs a paid support plan.
when: Regular account health checks
pay: Some checks free. Full set needs Business support or above.
eg: Flagging an S3 bucket that is open to the public.

name: AWS User Notifications
one: One place to decide which AWS events reach you, and where they land.
like: The notification settings screen on your phone, for the whole of AWS.
what: You set rules like send me EC2 state changes and CloudWatch alarms in these regions, and choose email, chat, or push to the mobile app. It gives a single inbox in the console instead of scattered per service settings. It is a router over EventBridge events, so if an event does not exist in EventBridge, it cannot notify you. It is fairly new and still thin on options.
when: Wanting one consistent place for AWS alerts
Cross region and cross account alerting without wiring each service
Push notifications to the mobile console app
nope: Notifying your own end users, use SNS or Pinpoint
Complex routing, filtering and retries, build on EventBridge and SNS directly
eg: You get one email whenever any account in the organisation has a security finding, instead of per account rules.
pay: The service is free. You pay for the underlying delivery, and a noisy rule sending high volume email is what annoys people.

name: AWS Well Architected Tool
one: A questionnaire about your system that produces a list of the risks you have not handled.
like: A building safety checklist you fill in yourself. The form does not inspect the building, it just makes sure you thought about the fire exits.
what: You answer questions across six areas such as security, cost and reliability, and it produces a scored report of high and medium risks with links to guidance. Every answer comes from you, so the output is only as honest as your answers. It is mostly used by consultants and by teams doing a formal review before a big launch.
when: A structured review before a major launch
Partner or audit work that needs a documented review
Getting a team to agree on where the weak spots are
nope: Finding real problems in a live account, use Trusted Advisor, Security Hub or Compute Optimizer which actually look at your resources
A small side project, the review takes hours and tells you little
eg: A team answers the reliability questions, realises nobody has ever tested the database restore, and logs it as a high risk.
pay: The tool is free. The cost is the time, and any consultant you pay to run the review.

name: Amazon CloudWatch
one: Watches your systems and tells you when something is wrong.
like: The dashboard of a car. Speed, fuel, engine warning light.
what: CloudWatch collects metrics, logs and alarms. An alarm can email you or trigger scaling. Log storage grows quietly, so set a retention period or the bill creeps up.
when: Always. If you cannot see it, you cannot run it.
pay: Per metric, per GB of logs, per alarm. Log retention is the usual surprise.
eg: Alert on WhatsApp when CPU stays above 80 percent for five minutes.

name: Amazon Managed Grafana
one: Runs Grafana dashboards for you so nobody has to patch a Grafana server.
like: Renting a noticeboard that someone else keeps clean and locked.
what: Grafana is popular open source dashboard software. This is AWS hosting it, with logins through your existing identity provider and ready-made connections to CloudWatch, Prometheus, OpenSearch and outside sources. You get the normal Grafana experience. You do not get full server access, so some plugins and tweaks are not possible.
when: Several teams share dashboards and you do not want to run the server
You want one dashboard mixing AWS metrics with non-AWS sources
You need single sign-on and per-team dashboard permissions
nope: If you only look at AWS metrics, CloudWatch dashboards are already there and cost less.
If you have dozens of casual viewers, self-hosting Grafana on a small EC2 instance is usually cheaper.
If you need an unusual plugin or deep server config, run your own Grafana.
eg: An on-call engineer opens one dashboard showing EKS pod health from Prometheus next to RDS metrics from CloudWatch.
pay: Per active user per workspace per month, roughly nine dollars for an editor and five for a viewer. The surprise is that anyone who logs in once in a month counts as active for the whole month, and API keys and service accounts are billed as users too.

name: Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus
one: Stores and queries Prometheus metrics for you, without running Prometheus servers.
like: A warehouse for your meter readings, instead of a filing cabinet you have to keep buying shelves for.
what: Prometheus is the standard way Kubernetes and containers expose metrics. Running it yourself means managing storage and scaling as metric volume grows. This takes the metrics in, keeps them, and answers PromQL queries. It stores and queries only. It draws no dashboards, so pair it with Grafana.
when: You run EKS or ECS and already emit Prometheus metrics
Your self-hosted Prometheus keeps running out of disk or memory
You want metrics kept longer than a local Prometheus can hold
nope: If you are not using Prometheus metrics today, use Amazon CloudWatch. Do not adopt Prometheus just to have this.
If you have a handful of containers, a single self-hosted Prometheus is simpler and cheaper.
If you want dashboards, this is not it. Add Amazon Managed Grafana.
eg: Your EKS cluster ships pod metrics here, and Grafana queries them to show memory use per service over six months.
pay: You pay per metric sample taken in, per GB stored, and per billion samples processed by queries. The surprise is the query charge. A dashboard on auto-refresh in front of a wall screen can quietly cost more than the storage.

name: AWS Deadline Cloud
one: It runs your 3D renders and other heavy creative jobs on rented computers.
like: A print shop for animation frames. You drop off the job, they run hundreds of machines overnight, you pick up the finished pictures.
what: You submit a render job from software like Maya, Blender, Houdini, Nuke or Unreal, and Deadline Cloud spreads the frames across a fleet of machines it starts and stops for you. It handles the queue, the job dependencies and the licences for some paid renderers. It is aimed at studios; the hard parts are still getting your assets and plugin versions onto the render machines, which the service does not do for you.
when: Rendering animation or VFX frames faster than your own machines can
You already use a render farm manager and want burst capacity
Studio pipelines with deadlines and many artists
nope: A single quick render, just use your own workstation
General batch computing that is not rendering, use AWS Batch instead
You want a cheap hobby farm, the per-machine-hour fee plus licence fees adds up fast
eg: A small animation studio pushes 4,000 frames of a commercial to Deadline Cloud on Friday and has them back Saturday morning.
pay: Per minute of machine time on the render workers, plus a smaller per-minute service fee per worker, plus usage-based licence charges for renderers you get through AWS. The service fee on top of the machine cost is the part people miss.

name: AWS Elemental Appliances & Software
one: It is the name for the video encoding boxes and software AWS sells you to run in your own building.
like: Buying the oven instead of ordering from the bakery. Same recipes, but it sits in your kitchen and you maintain it.
what: This is not a cloud service you switch on. It is a catalogue: physical appliances and licensed software (Live, Server, Conductor, Delta) that broadcasters install in their own machine rooms, usually to work alongside AWS video services. Almost nobody outside television and live sports operations buys this. AWS now pushes MediaLive Anywhere for new on-premises work, which runs the cloud service on your hardware with cloud control.
when: A broadcast facility that must keep video processing on site
Latency or contract rules stop you sending the feed to the cloud
You are extending an existing Elemental on-premises setup
nope: Any normal streaming need, use MediaLive or MediaConvert in the cloud
New on-premises projects, look at MediaLive Anywhere first
You do not have staff who rack and maintain hardware
eg: A national broadcaster keeps encoders in its playout centre and sends only the finished streams to AWS.
pay: You buy or license it through AWS sales, not by the hour. Support contracts and hardware refresh are the ongoing cost.

name: AWS Elemental Conductor
one: It is the control panel that manages a room full of Elemental encoders.
like: A shift supervisor on a factory floor. The machines do the work, the supervisor decides which machine gets which job and shouts when one stops.
what: Conductor sits on top of several AWS Elemental Live or Elemental Server units in your own building and gives one place to set up channels, balance work and fail over when a box dies. It is legacy on-premises broadcast software, sold with appliances, and very few organisations run it. In the cloud the equivalent controls are simply built into MediaLive and MediaConvert.
when: You already run a cluster of on-premises Elemental encoders
You need redundancy across those boxes with automatic failover
A broadcast facility with an operations team watching channels
nope: Anything cloud based, MediaLive already manages itself
A single encoder, Conductor adds cost and no benefit
New builds, prefer MediaLive Anywhere
eg: A sports network runs twelve Elemental Live boxes and uses Conductor so a failed unit is replaced by a spare without anyone going off air.
pay: Licensed with the appliance purchase, not metered. Cost sits in licences and support, not usage.

name: AWS Elemental Delta
one: It stores and hands out live video in your own building so thousands of viewers can watch it.
like: A newsagent who keeps the last hour of newspapers on the counter, so everyone arriving late can still take a copy.
what: Delta is on-premises software that packages a live feed into the formats players need, keeps a rolling window so viewers can pause or rewind, and serves it to a CDN. It is the older, self-hosted cousin of MediaPackage. It is legacy and rare; new work of this kind goes to MediaPackage in the cloud.
when: An existing on-premises broadcast chain that already uses it
Time shift and catch up recording that must stay on site
Serving your own network of viewers without cloud delivery
nope: Anything new, use MediaPackage
Video on demand files, that is MediaConvert plus S3 and CloudFront
Small audiences, a plain origin server is cheaper
eg: A cable operator lets subscribers rewind the last two hours of a channel from equipment in its own head end.
pay: Sold as software licences with appliances, not per stream. No hourly bill, but support and hardware are yours.

name: AWS Elemental Link
one: A small box you plug a camera into, and the video goes straight to AWS.
like: A prepaid postbox for video. Plug in the cable, and whatever the camera sees is posted to AWS with no settings to fiddle with.
what: Link is a piece of hardware about the size of a paperback. One end takes HDMI or SDI from a camera or vision mixer, the other takes network, and it appears as an input inside MediaLive. There is nothing to configure on the device itself; you control it from the AWS console. It only feeds MediaLive, so it is useless on its own, and if it is lost or broken you buy another.
when: Sending a camera feed to the cloud without an encoding PC
Fixed installations like a church, lecture hall or stadium
Events where you want a setup that non technical staff can plug in
nope: Streaming from software you already run, use RTMP into MediaLive directly
A one off event, hiring an encoder or using OBS is cheaper than buying hardware
You need the feed to go somewhere other than AWS
eg: A university plugs a Link into the lecture theatre camera so every session streams without an operator.
pay: A one time purchase for the device, a few hundred dollars. The video it sends is then billed by MediaLive as normal, which is the recurring cost people forget.

name: AWS Elemental Live
one: Software or a box in your building that turns a live camera feed into internet streams.
