like: A translator standing beside the camera, turning what it says into every language the audience speaks, right there in the room.
what: Elemental Live is the on-premises live encoder: it takes SDI, ST 2110 or IP feeds and produces multiple bitrates and formats for broadcast and streaming. It is the product MediaLive was built from. It is still sold for facilities that must process video on site, but for most new work AWS points people at MediaLive, or MediaLive Anywhere if the processing has to stay local.
when: Broadcast facilities with baseband SDI infrastructure
Feeds that legally or practically cannot leave the building
Very low latency contribution inside a venue
nope: Cloud streaming, use MediaLive and skip the hardware
Recorded files, that is MediaConvert or Elemental Server
Teams without broadcast engineers
eg: A stadium encodes the in-house camera feeds on site and sends only the finished streams out to the internet.
pay: Appliance or software licence bought through AWS, with a support contract. Not hourly.

name: AWS Elemental MediaConnect
one: It moves a live video feed from one place to another without losing quality.
like: A courier for a single fragile parcel. Not a shop, not a warehouse, just careful delivery from A to B, with a spare van following.
what: MediaConnect carries broadcast grade live feeds over the internet using protocols that recover lost packets, such as Zixi, SRT and RIST, and it can encrypt the stream and fan it out to several receivers. It only transports; it does not encode, package or store anything. Broadcasters use it to replace satellite links between sites.
when: Sending a live feed between studios, partners or regions
Replacing a satellite or fibre contribution link
Handing a feed to another company without giving them AWS access
nope: Delivering video to viewers, that is MediaPackage plus CloudFront
Changing resolution or format, MediaConnect does not encode
File transfer, use S3
eg: A news agency sends a reporter's live feed from a remote city into its main studio's MediaLive channel.
pay: Per hour for each flow plus per gigabyte transferred, and each extra output of a flow is billed too. Redundant flows double the cost.

name: AWS Elemental MediaConvert
one: It converts video files you already have into the formats players can stream.
like: A photo lab that takes one negative and prints it in every size the customer asked for.
what: You put a video file in S3, submit a job, and MediaConvert writes out new files: different resolutions, codecs, subtitles, thumbnails, and the playlists streaming players need. It is for files, not live feeds. Jobs are queued, so a long film takes real time to process, and getting the output settings right is fiddly the first time.
when: Preparing recorded video for a website or app
Making one upload play on phones, TVs and browsers
Adding captions, watermarks or audio tracks to a library of files
nope: Live streaming, use MediaLive
Simple, low volume conversions, a script running ffmpeg on EC2 can be cheaper
Real time conversion while a user waits, jobs are not instant
eg: A training company uploads a 2 hour recorded session and gets back three quality levels plus an HLS playlist.
pay: Per minute of output video, per output. Six renditions of one hour means six hours of billed output, which is why bills come out higher than expected. Professional tier features like HEVC and HDR cost more per minute.

name: AWS Elemental MediaLive
one: It takes a live camera or stream and turns it into something viewers can watch.
like: The control room at a TV station. The camera feed comes in, and it goes out in the shapes every screen in the country can show.
what: MediaLive is the live encoder. You point a feed at it, it produces several quality levels, inserts ad markers, adds captions and overlays, and passes the result to MediaPackage or your own destination. Channels are billed while they are running whether or not anyone is watching, and stopping a channel is a manual step people forget.
when: Live events, sport, worship services, conferences
24/7 channels that need broadcast features like ad insertion
Live feeds that must go out in several bitrates
nope: Simple low latency streaming with chat, Amazon IVS is far less work
Recorded files, use MediaConvert
Occasional casual streams, a third party service is cheaper than running a channel
eg: A football club streams home matches, with MediaLive producing 1080p, 720p and 480p versions live.
pay: Per hour of channel running time, by input and output class, plus data out. The surprise is being charged for a channel left running after the event ended.

name: AWS Elemental MediaPackage
one: It hands your live video to viewers in whatever format their player wants, and can record it.
like: A waiter who takes one dish from the kitchen and serves it on the plate each table asked for.
what: MediaPackage sits between the encoder and the viewer. It takes one incoming stream and outputs HLS, DASH or CMAF, applies content protection, and keeps a recent window so viewers can pause, rewind or start the programme again. It can also save a finished event as a video on demand asset. It does not encode, so it always needs MediaLive or a similar source in front of it.
when: Live streaming where viewers use many kinds of device
You want pause, rewind or catch up on a live channel
You need DRM applied to a live stream
nope: Static video files, use S3 with CloudFront
Low latency chat style streaming, look at Amazon IVS
If your players all take one format, you may not need the extra layer
eg: A conference stream lets someone joining an hour late rewind to the opening keynote.
pay: Per gigabyte in and out, plus storage for any recorded window. Each extra output format multiplies the outbound gigabytes.

name: AWS Elemental MediaStore
one: It was fast storage made for live video, and AWS has now shut it down.
like: A kiosk that was closed and boarded up. The nearby supermarket sells the same thing now.
what: MediaStore was storage tuned for live video origination, with lower delay than S3 had at the time. AWS discontinued it on 13 November 2025; the console and the resources are gone. S3 improved to the point where it is both faster and cheaper for this job, so AWS told customers to move to S3 or MediaPackage. Do not design anything around MediaStore.
when: Nothing, the service is retired
Only relevant if you are reading old architecture diagrams
Migrating legacy documentation that mentions it
nope: Any live origin need, use Amazon S3
Live packaging with catch up, use MediaPackage
Do not follow old tutorials that still show MediaStore containers
eg: An old 2019 reference architecture shows MediaLive writing to MediaStore; today that arrow points to S3.
pay: No longer billable. When it ran, it charged per gigabyte stored and per request, and the request charges were the expensive part for live workloads.

name: AWS Elemental MediaTailor
one: It slips adverts into a video stream so they play like part of the programme.
like: A radio presenter reading a different advert to each listener, in the same gap, without the music stopping.
what: MediaTailor stitches personalised ads into live and on demand streams on the server side, so ad blockers and player quirks do not break them, and it reports what was actually watched. It can also build a 24/7 linear channel out of a list of files. It needs an ad decision server to tell it which ad to play, which you bring yourself, and getting ad breaks to line up exactly is the hard part.
when: Making money from streaming through advertising
Free ad supported channels built from a content library
You need ads that client side blockers cannot strip out
nope: You have no advertising, it adds cost and complexity for nothing
Simple pre roll in your own player, a client side ad SDK is simpler
Small audiences, ad revenue will not cover the effort
eg: A free film channel plays a different local advert to a viewer in Mumbai and one in Manchester, in the same break.
pay: Per thousand ad requests, plus per gigabyte for the channel assembly feature. Heavy channel assembly use is the surprise line.

name: AWS Elemental Server
one: Software in your own building that converts recorded video files into streaming formats.
like: Your own photocopier in the office instead of walking to the copy shop.
what: Elemental Server is the on-premises file transcoder, the local version of what MediaConvert does in the cloud. It runs on appliances or your own servers and is used where the source files must not leave the building, or where a facility already owns the hardware. It is legacy broadcast kit, and very few new buyers pick it over MediaConvert.
when: Media archives that cannot legally leave the premises
A facility with spare hardware and steady, predictable volume
Existing Elemental installations being extended
nope: Cloud workflows, MediaConvert needs no hardware
Bursty volumes, you pay for capacity you are not using
Small teams, there is nobody to maintain it
eg: A broadcaster converts its master tapes to streaming files on machines inside its own archive facility.
pay: Licence and appliance purchase through AWS sales, plus support. Your own power, space and staff are the real running cost.

name: AWS Thinkbox Deadline
one: Free software you install yourself to manage a render farm.
like: A job board pinned up in a workshop. Everyone takes the next ticket when they are free.
what: Deadline is the long established render farm manager AWS bought with Thinkbox. You run the database and the scheduler on your own machines, and it hands frames out to whatever computers you have, including EC2 machines when you want extra. AWS made it free of charge in 2022 and put it into maintenance mode on 7 November 2025, so it gets critical fixes and DCC integration updates but no new features. Deadline Cloud is the managed successor.
when: You already own render machines and want to schedule them
An existing studio pipeline built around Deadline
You want a free scheduler and will run it yourself
nope: Starting fresh with no hardware, use AWS Deadline Cloud
You want AWS to run it for you, this one you install and maintain
Long term bets, it is in maintenance mode and will not gain features
eg: An architecture visualisation studio runs Deadline on its own 20 workstations overnight and bursts to EC2 at deadlines.
pay: The software is free. You pay for the machines it runs on, and for the EC2 capacity if you burst to the cloud.

name: AWS Thinkbox Frost
one: A 3ds Max plugin that turns clouds of particles into a solid surface you can render.
like: Taking a bowl of tiny beads and shrink wrapping them, so it looks like one smooth blob of liquid instead of beads.
what: Frost is a mesher for 3ds Max: it builds geometry around particle simulations so splashes, mud, snow or crowds of objects can be rendered. It is a niche artist tool with nothing to do with cloud computing. AWS made it free in 2022 and published the source on GitHub, but has not updated it since; a community developer maintains builds for newer 3ds Max versions. Almost nobody outside 3ds Max VFX work needs it.
when: 3ds Max artists meshing fluid or particle simulations
Scattering geometry over particle positions
Existing pipelines already built on Frost
nope: Any non 3ds Max software, use that package's own mesher such as Houdini's VDB tools
Anything to do with AWS infrastructure, it is a desktop plugin
New work, be aware AWS is not developing it
eg: An artist turns a 3ds Max water splash simulation into a renderable mesh for a drinks advert.
pay: Free, with no AWS account needed. The cost is the 3ds Max licence and the machines you render on.

name: AWS Thinkbox Krakatoa
one: Free desktop software that renders huge clouds of particles, like smoke, dust and fire.
like: A camera that can photograph every grain in a sandstorm.
what: This is desktop software, not a cloud service. AWS bought Thinkbox and now gives all Thinkbox products away at no cost, with parts of Krakatoa released as open source. It is a renderer plugin for 3ds Max, Maya, Cinema 4D and similar tools, built for scenes with billions of particles. It is effectively in maintenance. Do not expect active development.
when: Rendering dust, smoke, fire or magic effects in a film or advert
Visualising very large point cloud or particle data sets
You already work in 3ds Max or Maya and hit limits on particle counts
nope: If you are not doing 3D visual effects, this is irrelevant.
If you want rendering to run on AWS machines, that is AWS Deadline Cloud, which schedules the jobs. Krakatoa is just the renderer.
If you are starting fresh, check whether your DCC tool's own particle renderer is enough before adopting maintenance-mode software.
eg: A studio renders a collapsing building's dust cloud from a hundred million particles, spread over a render farm.
pay: Free to download and use, including the licences. You pay only for whatever machines you render on, such as EC2 instances or your own workstations.

name: AWS Thinkbox Stoke
one: Free 3ds Max plugin that simulates particles moving through fields of motion.
like: Dropping confetti into a wind tunnel and watching where it goes.
what: This is desktop software for Autodesk 3ds Max only, not a cloud service. It generates and simulates particles driven by velocity fields, and reads simulation data from FumeFX, Particle Flow, thinkingParticles and RealFlow. It is free now, along with every Thinkbox product, and is in maintenance rather than active development. It is usually used to feed Krakatoa.
when: Adding drifting debris or spray on top of an existing smoke simulation in 3ds Max
Reusing velocity field data from another simulation tool
You need particle counts beyond what 3ds Max handles natively
nope: If you use Maya, Houdini or Blender, this does not apply. It is a 3ds Max plugin.
If you need full fluid or smoke simulation, use a dedicated solver. Stoke moves particles, it does not simulate the fluid.
Almost nobody outside 3ds Max visual effects work has a use for this.
eg: An artist takes a FumeFX explosion and uses Stoke to send sparks tumbling along its motion, then renders them with Krakatoa.
pay: Free, licence included. Your only cost is the 3ds Max licence and the machines you simulate and render on.

name: AWS Thinkbox XMesh
one: Saves moving 3D animation to disk so an artist can replay it fast.
like: Recording a stage rehearsal on video, so you can watch it again without calling the actors back.
what: This is not a cloud service. It is a plugin for 3ds Max and Maya on an artist's own computer, from Thinkbox, a company AWS bought. It writes animated geometry to XMesh files that load quickly, which helps with heavy crowd or simulation scenes. AWS made all Thinkbox tools free in 2022, and the Maya version was released as open source. It is a niche visual effects tool, and almost nobody outside a VFX or animation studio will ever touch it.
when: A 3D scene is so heavy that scrubbing the timeline crawls
A studio wants to hand a baked animation to render machines without the original rig
Crowd or particle work needs to be cached once and reused
nope: You are not doing 3D animation in 3ds Max or Maya. Then this is simply not for you.
You want cloud rendering. That is Deadline plus EC2, not XMesh.
You want to store files in the cloud. Use amazon-simple-storage-service.
eg: An animator bakes a 200 million polygon crowd shot to XMesh so the scene opens in seconds.
pay: Nothing. The software is free with an AWS account, and the Maya plugin is open source.

name: Amazon Interactive Video Service
one: It gives you live streaming with chat, like a Twitch style channel, with very little setup.
like: A walkie talkie set you take out of the box and use. No wiring, no engineer.
what: IVS takes an RTMP stream from software like OBS and delivers it to viewers in a few seconds, with a player, a chat service and viewer counts included. There is a real time mode for stages where several people appear on screen together with sub second delay. You give up control: fewer broadcast features than MediaLive, and the channel types and limits are fixed by AWS.
when: Live shopping, creator streams, classes, gaming style channels
You want chat and low latency without building a video stack
Small teams with no broadcast experience
nope: Broadcast channels needing ad insertion and DRM, use MediaLive with MediaPackage and MediaTailor
Recorded video libraries, use MediaConvert with CloudFront
Very high hour counts, per hour delivery pricing gets expensive at scale
eg: A jewellery seller runs a nightly live sale where viewers ask questions in chat and buy as they watch.
pay: Per hour of input and per hour of video delivered to viewers, plus chat messages. Delivery hours multiply by audience size, which is where the bill grows.

name: AWS Application Discovery Service
one: It surveys the servers in your data centre so you know what you actually have before moving.
like: Walking through a warehouse with a clipboard and writing down every box, its size and who uses it, before you hire the removal van.
what: Collects inventory and performance data from on premises servers, either agentless through a VMware appliance or with an agent on each machine. It records CPU, memory, disk and network connections, which helps you see which servers talk to each other. It does not move anything, and the agentless mode only works properly with VMware vCenter.
when: Planning a data centre migration and you do not trust your own inventory
You need to work out which servers must move together
You want real usage data to size EC2 instances
nope: You already have a good CMDB or a small, well known server list, just export what you have
You are moving a handful of servers, the setup effort is not worth it, size them by hand
eg: Before a migration, a team runs the collector for a month and finds 40 of their 300 servers have no network traffic at all, so they are switched off instead of moved.
pay: The service is free. You pay for the data it stores in your account and for the agentless appliance running on your own hardware.

name: AWS Application Migration Service
one: It copies your existing servers, as they are, onto EC2 and lets you cut over.
like: Moving house by lifting every room exactly as it is onto the new plot, rather than repacking each cupboard.
what: Known as MGN, and the replacement for the retired CloudEndure and Server Migration Service. You install an agent on each source server, it replicates the disks continuously to AWS, then you launch a test instance and finally cut over with minutes of downtime. It is a lift and shift tool, so it copies your problems too, and it does not modernise anything.
when: Moving physical or virtual servers to EC2 with little downtime
A data centre exit with a hard deadline
You want to test the migrated server before committing
nope: The workload is a plain database, use DMS or a native restore instead of copying the whole machine
You want to end up on containers or serverless, replatform properly, a lifted server stays a server you have to patch
eg: A company replicates 60 Windows servers over three weeks, tests each one, then cuts over on a Saturday night with 15 minutes of downtime.
pay: Free for 90 days per source server, which is the trap. Replication is not free, because staging EBS volumes, snapshots and data transfer are charged from day one, and servers left replicating past 90 days start costing per server per hour.

name: AWS Data Transfer Terminal
one: Lets you drive your hard drives to an AWS building and copy them in over a very fast cable.
like: Taking a suitcase of photos to a print shop instead of emailing them one by one.
what: It is a real physical room you book by the hour. You bring your own storage device, plug into two 100 Gbps fibre links, and copy data straight into AWS. It launched in late 2024 and there are only a few sites, starting with New York and Los Angeles, so it is useless unless you can physically reach one.
when: You have tens or hundreds of terabytes and a slow office internet line
Film footage or vehicle sensor logs need to land in AWS the same day
You do not want to post a device and wait for it to be loaded
nope: There is no terminal near you. Then use aws-direct-connect or an online copy tool instead.
The data is small, a few terabytes or less. A normal internet upload is cheaper and simpler.
You need ongoing daily transfers. Book a permanent link with aws-direct-connect, not a one off visit.
eg: A film crew back from a shoot books two hours in Los Angeles and pushes 400 TB of camera files into S3.
pay: Per port per hour, roughly 300 USD for US uploads and more for cross continent. The surprise is that you also pay for travel and staff time, and you pay for the booked slot even if your copy runs slow.

name: AWS DataSync
one: It copies large amounts of files from one place to another, and checks they arrived.
like: A removals firm. They pack the boxes, drive them over, and tick each one off the list at the other end.
what: DataSync moves data between on-premises NFS, SMB, HDFS or object stores and AWS services such as S3, EFS and the FSx family, and between AWS services or other clouds. It runs much faster than a plain copy, handles retries, keeps file metadata and verifies content afterwards. For on-premises sources you deploy an agent VM. It is task-based and scheduled, so it is not continuous replication and not a live sync.
when: A one-off migration of millions of files into AWS
A nightly copy from an office NAS into S3
Moving data between S3 and EFS or FSx
nope: For continuous, near-live replication, use S3 Replication or NetApp SnapMirror
For ongoing local access to cloud storage, use Storage Gateway
For a few small files, the AWS CLI is enough
eg: A media company schedules DataSync to pull each night's camera footage from the studio NAS into S3, with verification on.
pay: Per GB copied, around 0.0125 USD. The surprise is that request and retrieval charges on the destination, and the EC2 or VMware cost of running the agent, sit on top, and re-running a task on unchanged data still scans everything.

name: AWS Mainframe Modernization
one: Tools to move old mainframe programs to AWS, either running them as they are or rewriting them into Java.
like: An old factory machine that still works. You either build a new shed around it so it keeps running, or you rebuild it from scratch in modern parts.
what: Offers two paths, replatform with Rocket Software so COBOL and JCL keep running mostly unchanged, or refactor with AWS Blu Age which converts the code to Java or .NET. The managed runtime is closed to new customers, and the self managed experience moves to maintenance status on 30 July 2026, closing to new customers. AWS now steers new mainframe work to AWS Transform. Very few organisations ever need this.
when: You already use it and are continuing an existing programme
You are studying the replatform versus refactor choice
nope: You are starting a mainframe migration now, look at AWS Transform first, this one is closing to new customers
You have an old server but not a mainframe, this is for IBM z/OS, use Application Migration Service
eg: An insurer converts decades of COBOL batch jobs into Java Spring Boot services that produce the same output, checked line by line against the old system.
pay: Charged per compute hour for the runtime plus storage. Real cost is the multi year project and the testing, not the AWS line item.

name: AWS Migration Evaluator
one: Looks at the servers you own today and estimates what they would cost on AWS.
like: A removal company walking through your house and quoting the van size before you pack.
what: You run a small collector program in your own data centre for a few weeks. It measures how busy each server really is, then AWS produces a report matching each one to an EC2 size, with a cost estimate including licences. It is an assessment report, not something that moves any workload, and the useful version comes through an AWS team rather than fully self service. It came from TSO Logic, a company AWS bought in 2019.
when: Management wants a number before approving a move to AWS
You suspect your servers are far bigger than the work needs
You need a licence cost comparison for Windows or SQL Server
nope: You only have a handful of servers. Price them by hand with aws-cost-explorer style guesses instead.
You already decided to move and want the actual migration tooling. This only produces a business case.
You want ongoing cost control after you are on AWS. Use aws-cost-explorer and aws-budgets.
eg: A company finds 300 servers averaging 8 percent CPU and the report shows a far smaller EC2 bill than expected.
pay: No charge for the assessment itself. The real cost is the weeks of data collection and the people time.

name: AWS Transfer Family
one: An SFTP server that saves files straight into S3.
like: An old style letterbox bolted onto a modern warehouse.
what: Transfer Family gives partners a normal SFTP, FTPS or AS2 endpoint, while the files actually land in S3. Useful when a bank or vendor will only send files the old way.
when: A partner insists on SFTP
Bank or government file exchange
nope: You control both ends. Use the S3 API.
pay: Per hour the endpoint exists, plus per GB. The hourly charge runs even when idle.
eg: A bank drops a daily settlement file by SFTP, it appears in S3.

name: AWS Transform
one: An AI agent that reads your old applications and rewrites them for AWS.
like: A translator who reads an old handwritten ledger and types out a modern version, then you still have to check every page.
what: An agentic AI service for large modernisation jobs, covering mainframe COBOL to Java, .NET Framework to modern .NET, and VMware workloads to EC2. It assesses the code, writes documentation, converts it and helps test. It is new, aimed at big enterprise programmes, and the output still needs human review, so treat it as a fast first draft rather than a finished migration.
when: Thousands of files of legacy code that nobody understands any more
Upgrading old .NET Framework applications at scale
You need a documented assessment before committing to a migration
nope: A handful of applications, a developer with Amazon Q or Claude will be quicker and cheaper
You expect a working system with no review, the converted code must be tested against the old system's output
eg: A team points it at a .NET Framework application and gets a ported .NET 8 version plus a list of the parts it could not convert.
pay: Varies by workload type and has been offered free for some transformation paths. The real cost is the engineering time spent checking what it produced.

name: AWS App Mesh
one: A retired traffic controller that used to sit next to each of your services.
like: A telephone switchboard operator who sat between every pair of departments in an office. The company has now removed the switchboard and told everyone to call each other directly.
what: App Mesh is being shut down. AWS stopped letting new customers sign up in September 2024, and support ends on 30 September 2026, after which the console and resources go away. It ran a small proxy (Envoy) beside every one of your services so traffic between them could be routed, retried and measured in one place. AWS points existing users to Amazon ECS Service Connect or Amazon VPC Lattice.
when: Only if you already run it and are planning the exit
Reading old blog posts or Terraform and wondering what it was
nope: Starting anything new, use Amazon VPC Lattice or ECS Service Connect
Wanting a service mesh you control yourself, use Istio or Linkerd on Kubernetes
eg: A team with forty ECS services on App Mesh spent 2026 moving them to ECS Service Connect before the cutoff.
pay: There was no charge for App Mesh itself. The cost was the Envoy sidecar on every task, which quietly added CPU and memory to every service you ran.

name: AWS Client VPN
one: Lets staff on laptops anywhere dial into your private AWS network.
like: A staff side door with a key card, for people working from home.
what: You set up an endpoint, users install an OpenVPN style client, and once connected their laptop can reach private servers as if it were in the office. It handles logins through certificates, Active Directory or a federated identity provider. It is per user remote access, and it is not cheap once you have many people online.
when: Developers need to reach a private database that has no public address
Staff work from home and need internal tools
A contractor needs limited access for a short project
nope: You are joining two networks, an office to AWS, not individual people. Use aws-site-to-site-vpn.
You just want to reach one EC2 box for admin. Session Manager needs no VPN at all.
You want per app access without a network tunnel. A zero trust proxy fits better than this.
eg: Twenty engineers connect each morning and can reach the private RDS instance from their laptops.
pay: About 10 cents per hour for the endpoint in each subnet, plus about 5 cents per connected user per hour. The surprise is the subnet charge ticks along all night even when nobody is connected.

name: AWS Cloud Map
one: A phone book your services look things up in instead of hard coding addresses.
like: An office directory on the wall. You look up "Accounts" and it tells you which room they are in today, so nobody has to memorise room numbers that keep changing.
what: You register a resource under a friendly name, and your code asks Cloud Map for the current address. It also removes entries that fail health checks. Most people never call it directly, because ECS service discovery and Kubernetes create Cloud Map records for you behind the scenes.
when: Services on ECS that need to find each other by name
Registering things DNS cannot describe well, like a queue URL or a table name
nope: Public websites and domains, use Amazon Route 53
Service to service calls where you also want auth and routing rules, use Amazon VPC Lattice
eg: An order service asks Cloud Map for "payments" and gets the IPs of the healthy payment containers running right now.
pay: Cents per registered resource per month, plus a charge per lookup. Chatty apps that look up on every single request can run up the call count, so cache the answer.

name: AWS Cloud WAN
one: One place to build and see your whole global network instead of wiring regions together by hand.
like: Managing a rail network from a single control room with one map, rather than each station agreeing its own connections with its neighbours.
what: You describe your network as a policy document, which regions connect, which sites connect, who may talk to whom, and AWS builds it. It joins AWS regions and your own offices and data centres into one network with a shared dashboard. It is aimed at large companies with many regions and many physical sites, and it is overkill and expensive for anyone smaller.
when: Many VPCs across several AWS regions plus branch offices
You want one policy file to define global connectivity
Replacing a tangle of peerings and Transit Gateways
nope: A handful of VPCs in one region, use AWS Transit Gateway
Two VPCs that need to talk, use VPC peering
eg: A retailer with stores in twelve countries defines one policy so every store reaches the regional AWS network nearest to it.
pay: A monthly charge per core network edge in each region, plus per attachment and per GB of data. The per edge fee applies whether or not traffic flows, so idle regions still cost money.

name: AWS Direct Connect
one: A private cable from your building or data centre into AWS, instead of going over the internet.
like: A private road from your warehouse to the motorway, so your lorries never sit in public traffic.
what: A dedicated fibre link between your network and AWS, ordered through a partner at a location where AWS has equipment. It gives steadier speed and lower delay than the internet, and it lowers the price of data leaving AWS. It is not encrypted by itself, and setup takes weeks or months, not minutes.
when: Moving large amounts of data in and out every day
Applications that break when latency jitters
Rules that say your traffic must not cross the public internet
nope: You need something working today, use AWS Site-to-Site VPN
Small or occasional traffic, the internet is cheaper and fine
Only want privacy, not speed, a VPN gives you that at far less cost
eg: A media firm pushes a terabyte of daily footage to S3 over a 10 Gbps Direct Connect link instead of saturating its office line.
pay: An hourly port charge whether you use it or not, plus per GB out at a reduced rate. The surprise is the separate bill from the telecom partner for the last stretch of fibre to your building, which AWS does not include.

name: AWS Global Accelerator
one: Gets users onto the AWS network early so their traffic takes a faster path to your servers.
like: A fast lane entrance that gets you onto the motorway right away, rather than crawling through town first.
what: You get two fixed IP addresses that work worldwide. A user's traffic enters AWS at the nearest edge location and then travels over the AWS network to your application, which is usually faster and steadier than the open internet. It also fails over between regions in seconds. It does not cache anything, so it helps live and dynamic traffic, not static files.
when: Games, chat, video calls, APIs where delay matters
You need fixed IP addresses that never change
Running the same app in several regions with automatic failover
nope: Websites, images and video files, use Amazon CloudFront which also caches
One region and one country of users, a load balancer alone is enough
eg: A multiplayer game gives players two static IPs, and a player in Mumbai is routed to the Singapore servers over the AWS backbone.
pay: A fixed hourly fee per accelerator, about 18 dollars a month, plus a per GB charge on top of normal data transfer. The fixed fee runs even with zero traffic, and the data premium is easy to miss.

name: AWS Interconnect
one: Orders a private cable between AWS and another cloud or your office, in a few clicks.
like: Asking the phone company for a dedicated line instead of running the wire yourself.
what: It is a newer managed connectivity service that arranges private, fixed bandwidth links from AWS to Azure, Google Cloud, Oracle Cloud, or to your own sites through a network partner. The point is that AWS handles the paperwork and router setup that used to take weeks. It is aimed at large multicloud setups, so most teams will never open it.
when: You run workloads in AWS and another cloud and want them talking privately
Setting up a cross connect by hand with a carrier is taking weeks
You need encrypted, predictable bandwidth between providers
nope: You only need AWS to your own data centre. Plain aws-direct-connect is the well worn path.
Your traffic is small or occasional. A aws-site-to-site-vpn over the internet costs far less.
You only use one cloud. Then there is nothing here for you.
eg: A bank links its AWS region to its Azure tenancy with a 10 Gbps private path instead of routing over the internet.
pay: By the link, on capacity and how long you keep it. Fixed bandwidth means you pay whether or not traffic flows.

name: AWS PrivateLink
one: Lets your private network reach an AWS service or a partner's service without touching the internet.
like: A service hatch built straight through the wall into the shop next door, so deliveries never go out onto the street.
what: It puts a private address inside your own VPC that points at a service somewhere else, an AWS service like S3, or software sold by another company, or another team's application. Traffic stays on the AWS network. The link is one way, the consumer calls the provider, and the provider cannot call back.
when: Servers with no internet access that still need to call AWS APIs
Buying SaaS that must not be reached over the internet
Exposing one internal API to another AWS account without peering
nope: Two VPCs that need full two way access, use peering or AWS Transit Gateway
Reaching your own office network, use Site-to-Site VPN or Direct Connect
eg: A database server in a private subnet writes to S3 through a VPC endpoint, with no NAT gateway and no route to the internet.
pay: An hourly charge per endpoint per availability zone, plus per GB. Teams create endpoints for a dozen services across three zones and are surprised by the hourly fees, which add up before any data moves.

name: AWS RTB Fabric
one: Carries advertising bid requests between ad companies in a few milliseconds.
like: A private courier lane between trading floors, because the public road is too slow.
what: A private network built for real time bidding, the auctions that decide which advert you see while a web page loads. Those auctions must finish in tens of milliseconds, so it connects ad platforms to partners like Amazon Ads directly. It is only useful if your business is programmatic advertising. Everyone else has no reason to look at it.
when: You run a demand side or supply side ad platform
Bid timeouts are losing you auctions
Cross network data transfer for bid traffic is a large part of your bill
nope: You buy adverts but do not run bidding infrastructure. This is not for you.
You want general low latency networking. Use amazon-virtual-private-cloud with placement groups, or amazon-cloudfront for content.
Your traffic tolerates 100 ms or more. Ordinary networking is far cheaper.
eg: An ad exchange routes bid requests to partners over the fabric and sees fewer timed out bids.
pay: Per transaction, with no upfront commitment. It is pitched as much cheaper than paying normal cross network data transfer for the same bid volume.

name: AWS Site to Site VPN
one: An encrypted tunnel over the internet joining your office network to your AWS network.
like: Sending post in a locked box through the normal postal service. Same roads as everyone else, but nobody can read what is inside.
what: You set up a tunnel between AWS and a router or firewall at your site, and the two networks can then reach each other by private address. It is quick to create and cheap. Because it rides the public internet, speed and delay vary with the day, and a single tunnel tops out around 1.25 Gbps.
when: Connecting an office or data centre to AWS this week
A backup path in case a Direct Connect link fails
Small or occasional traffic between sites
nope: Steady high throughput or predictable latency, use AWS Direct Connect
Giving individual laptops access, use AWS Client VPN or AWS Verified Access
eg: A company's finance server in its own server room reads an RDS database in AWS over a VPN tunnel.
pay: Around 5 cents per hour per connection, plus data out. The catch is that AWS gives two tunnels for redundancy but many routers are configured to use only one, so you pay for resilience you do not actually have.

name: AWS Transit Gateway
one: A central hub that connects all your networks so you stop wiring each pair together.
like: An airport hub. Instead of a direct flight between every pair of towns, everything routes through one airport.
what: You attach VPCs, VPN tunnels and Direct Connect links to one gateway, and it routes between them using route tables you control. It replaces the mess of peering connections that grows unmanageable past about five VPCs. Every packet passing through is charged, so it is a real line on the bill, not a free convenience.
when: More than a handful of VPCs that need to talk
Sharing one VPN or Direct Connect across many VPCs
You want route tables that separate environments, like prod and test
nope: Two VPCs only, VPC peering is free and simpler
Just calling a service in another VPC, use AWS PrivateLink
Many regions and physical sites, look at AWS Cloud WAN
eg: Twelve team VPCs and the office VPN all attach to one Transit Gateway, and only some route tables let teams reach the shared services VPC.
pay: An hourly fee per attachment plus a per GB charge on all traffic crossing it. Cross zone and cross region traffic is charged again on top, so a chatty app between two VPCs can cost more than the servers.

name: AWS Verified Access
one: Staff reach internal apps over the internet without a VPN, and every request is checked.
like: A doorman who checks your ID and that your coat is buttoned, every single time you walk in, instead of one lock on the front door.
what: Verified Access puts a policy in front of an internal application. Each request is evaluated against who the user is, from IAM Identity Center or an OIDC provider, and optionally the device's health from a tool like CrowdStrike or Jamf. It is AWS's take on zero trust access. It only covers applications you host inside AWS, so it does not replace a VPN that also reaches on-premise networks or non-HTTP services.
when: Replacing a VPN for internal web apps hosted in AWS
You want device posture checked on every request
Per-application access rules instead of full network access
nope: Not for public, customer-facing apps, use Cognito or your own login plus WAF
If staff need SSH, RDP or on-premise networks, keep a VPN or use Client VPN
Small teams with one internal tool will find Cognito plus a load balancer simpler
eg: A contractor opens the internal dashboard in a browser, and access is denied because their laptop disk is not encrypted.
pay: Per application per hour, plus per gigabyte of data processed. The hourly charge runs per application whether anyone uses it or not.

name: Amazon API Gateway
one: The front door for your API.
like: A reception desk. It checks who you are, stops rude visitors, then sends you to the right room.
what: API Gateway takes HTTP requests and passes them to Lambda or your servers. It handles authentication, rate limits, keys and versions. It adds a little delay and a per request cost.
when: A public API
You are building with Lambda
You need rate limiting
nope: A simple website. A load balancer is cheaper.
pay: Per million requests, plus data out.
eg: A mobile app calling /orders, which triggers a Lambda function.

name: Amazon Application Recovery Controller
one: Big red switches that move your traffic away from a broken region or zone, and checks that the backup is really ready.
like: A fire drill plus a clearly labelled master switch. Someone checks every month that the second exit actually opens, and there is one lever to send everyone that way.
what: Formerly called Amazon Route 53 Application Recovery Controller, renamed to Amazon Application Recovery Controller in late 2024. It has three parts: readiness checks that compare your standby region against production and warn when they drift, routing controls that are simple on and off switches with a safety rule so you cannot switch everything off at once, and zonal shift and autoshift, which pull traffic out of one unhealthy availability zone. Zonal shift is free and useful to many people. The routing control part is expensive and aimed at banks and similar.
when: A multi region setup where failover must work under pressure
Draining a single bad availability zone quickly
Proving to auditors that the standby is genuinely ready
nope: Simple DNS failover on health checks, plain Amazon Route 53 does that
One region only, use zonal shift and skip the rest
Backup and restore of data, use AWS Backup
eg: An availability zone starts timing out, and an operator triggers a zonal shift so the load balancer stops sending traffic there.
pay: Zonal shift and autoshift are free. Routing control costs roughly 3,000 US dollars a month per cluster, which shocks people who find it while browsing, plus per readiness check. Turn a cluster on and you pay even in a quiet month.

name: Amazon CloudFront
one: Keeps copies of your files near your users so pages load fast.
like: A local warehouse in every city instead of shipping everything from one factory.
what: CloudFront is a CDN. It caches your content at locations around the world. Users get served from the nearest one. It also absorbs traffic spikes and shields your servers.
when: Any public website
Images and video
Global audience
nope: An internal tool used by ten people in one office.
pay: Per GB delivered and per request. There is a generous free tier.
eg: A course video watched from Ahmedabad is served from an Indian location, not from Virginia.

name: Amazon Route 53
one: The phone book that turns your domain name into an address.
like: Saving a contact by name so you never memorise the number.
what: Route 53 is DNS. It points yourdomain.com to your server or CloudFront. It can also register domains, check if your site is healthy, and send users to the closest region.
when: You own a domain and it points at AWS
nope: Your DNS is already fine at GoDaddy or Cloudflare and you have no reason to move.
pay: A small monthly fee per hosted zone, plus per million queries.
eg: kwickprep.com points at CloudFront, which points at S3.

name: Amazon VPC Lattice
one: Connects your services to each other by name, with permissions and routing handled for you.
like: An office receptionist who knows every department, checks whether you are allowed to speak to them, and puts the call through. You never need their extension number.
what: You register services into a service network and they call each other by a stable name, across VPCs and AWS accounts, without peering or Transit Gateway. It applies IAM permissions per request and handles retries and traffic splitting. It is AWS's recommended replacement for App Mesh, and it is still fairly new with a smaller community than Kubernetes service meshes.
when: Services spread across several VPCs or accounts that need to call each other
You want per request authorisation between services, not just network rules
Moving off AWS App Mesh before it shuts down
nope: Everything in one VPC, a load balancer and security groups are simpler and cheaper
You need deep mesh features and portability, use Istio on EKS
eg: A checkout service in one account calls an inventory service in another, by name, with an IAM policy allowing only that caller.
pay: An hourly fee per service and per service network, plus per GB and per request. The standing hourly fees mean a network of many small services costs money before it serves a single request.

name: Amazon Virtual Private Cloud
one: Your own private section of the AWS network.
like: A gated plot inside a big township. You decide the roads, the gates and who gets in.
what: A VPC is where your servers live. You split it into subnets. Public subnets can reach the internet, private ones cannot. Security groups act as a firewall on each machine.
when: Always. Anything you run sits in a VPC.
pay: The VPC is free. NAT gateways and data transfer cost money and surprise people.
eg: Web servers in a public subnet, the database in a private one so it can never be reached from the internet.

name: Elastic Load Balancing
one: Shares incoming traffic across several servers.
like: A queue manager at a bank sending you to whichever counter is free.
what: A load balancer sits in front of your servers. If one dies, it stops sending traffic there. It also handles HTTPS so your servers do not have to.
when: More than one server
You want zero downtime deploys
You want HTTPS handled in one place
nope: A single small server with little traffic. It is an extra monthly cost.
pay: Per hour, plus a usage unit based on traffic.
eg: Three web servers behind one address. One reboots, nobody notices.

name: Amazon Braket
one: Lets you send programs to real quantum computers, or to simulators of them, and get results back.
like: Booking time on a telescope at an observatory. You submit when you want to look, and you wait your turn.
what: It gives one interface to quantum machines from several makers, plus simulators that run on ordinary AWS hardware. Today's quantum machines are small and noisy, so almost all useful work is research, learning or simulation, not production. Almost nobody needs this service for a real business problem yet, and it is honest to say so.
when: Academic or corporate research into quantum algorithms
Learning quantum programming against real hardware
Comparing results across different quantum machines
nope: Any current business workload, classical computing will be faster and far cheaper
Optimisation or machine learning problems, use normal solvers and SageMaker
Claiming quantum benefit in a product, the hardware is not there yet
eg: A university group runs the same small circuit on a simulator and on a trapped ion machine to compare error rates.
pay: Per task and per shot on real hardware, plus a per hour charge for simulators. Per shot charges on real devices climb quickly, since meaningful runs need thousands of shots.

name: AWS Ground Station
one: Rents you time on satellite dishes to talk to your satellite, by the minute.
like: A pay by the hour recording studio, except the studio is a large dish pointed at the sky.
what: AWS owns antennas at sites around the world. You book a contact window when your satellite passes overhead, and the data it sends down lands in your AWS account ready to process. This only applies if you or your customer actually operate a satellite, which is a very small group of organisations. You still need your own satellite, licences and radio approvals.
when: You operate satellites and do not want to build ground stations
Earth observation data that must be processed immediately after downlink
Extra antenna coverage on top of your own stations
nope: Anyone who does not operate a satellite, which is nearly everyone
Buying satellite imagery, buy it from a provider such as an Open Data set or a commercial vendor
GPS or location features in an app, use Amazon Location Service
eg: An imaging satellite passes over Sweden, downlinks through an AWS antenna, and the images are in S3 minutes later.
pay: Per minute of antenna contact, with different rates for narrowband and wideband, plus a monthly reserved option. Data egress and the processing instances are extra.

name: AWS Artifact
one: A self-service download page for AWS's own audit and compliance reports.
like: The filing cabinet at the back of the office where the landlord keeps the fire safety certificates. You go and take a copy when someone asks for proof.
what: Artifact holds AWS's third-party audit reports, like SOC 1, SOC 2, ISO 27001 and PCI, plus agreements such as the HIPAA BAA and GDPR terms. You download them and hand them to your auditor or customer. The thing people get wrong: these reports cover AWS's side of the line only. They say nothing about whether your own setup is secure or compliant.
when: An auditor or enterprise customer asks for AWS compliance evidence
You need to accept a legal agreement like a HIPAA BAA
Filling in a security questionnaire
nope: Do not use it to prove YOUR system is compliant, that is Audit Manager or Security Hub CSPM
Not a place to store your own documents, use S3
eg: A hospital asks your startup for proof AWS is HIPAA eligible. You open Artifact, accept the BAA, and download the SOC 2 report.
pay: Free. No charge at all.

name: AWS Audit Manager
one: It collects evidence about your AWS setup automatically so an audit is less painful.
like: A clerk who quietly photocopies every receipt all year, so at tax time the shoebox is already sorted into folders.
what: Audit Manager runs against a framework, like SOC 2, PCI DSS or HIPAA, and keeps pulling evidence from CloudTrail, Config and Security Hub into an assessment you can export. It gathers and organises evidence. It does not decide you passed, and it does not fix anything. A human auditor still reads the report, and plenty of controls still need manual evidence you upload yourself.
when: You are going through a real, repeated compliance audit
You need a paper trail of control evidence over time
Many accounts and you cannot collect evidence by hand
nope: Not for finding or fixing security problems, use Security Hub CSPM and Inspector
Overkill if you have no actual audit coming, it costs money and attention for nothing
Not proof of AWS's own compliance, that is Artifact
eg: A fintech enables the PCI DSS framework, and a year of evidence for each control is ready when the assessor arrives.
pay: Charged per resource assessment, so cost rises with how many resources each control touches. Enabling many frameworks at once across a big account is the surprise.

name: AWS Certificate Manager
one: Free HTTPS certificates that renew themselves.
like: A licence that renews automatically so it never expires on you.
what: ACM issues and renews TLS certificates at no cost for use with CloudFront, load balancers and API Gateway. Automatic renewal removes the classic outage of a certificate expiring at midnight.
when: Any site with HTTPS on AWS
nope: You need the certificate file to install on your own server. ACM public certs cannot be exported.
pay: Free for public certificates used with AWS services.
eg: HTTPS on your domain through CloudFront, renewing itself forever.

name: AWS CloudHSM
one: A dedicated tamper-proof box that holds your encryption keys, and only you can open it.
like: Renting the actual safe deposit box at the bank, with the only key, instead of asking the bank to look after your valuables.
what: CloudHSM gives you single-tenant hardware security modules, FIPS 140-3 Level 3 validated, where you control the keys completely. AWS cannot see or recover them. That last part is the real point and the real danger: lose your credentials and the keys are gone, with no AWS support ticket that gets them back. Most people who think they need CloudHSM actually need KMS. It exists for regulators who demand sole custody of keys.
when: A regulator or contract demands you hold the keys with no cloud provider access
You need an HSM for a specific standard KMS does not meet
Running your own certificate authority or custom crypto offload
nope: For almost all encryption, use KMS instead, it is far cheaper and simpler
Do not use it for payment card PIN and EMV work, use Payment Cryptography
eg: A bank keeps its signing keys in a CloudHSM cluster because the regulator will not accept a shared service.
pay: Per HSM, per hour, and you are told to run at least two or three for reliability. That runs into thousands of dollars a month whether you use it or not.

name: AWS Directory Service
one: It runs Microsoft Active Directory for you, or connects AWS to the one you already have.
like: The office staff list that decides whose badge opens which door. This is AWS running that list for you.
what: There are three quite different things under one name. AWS Managed Microsoft AD is a real Active Directory that AWS patches and backs up. AD Connector is a pass-through to your existing on-premise AD, storing nothing. Simple AD is a small Samba-based stand-in and is the weakest option. You pick one by what you need, and mixing them up is the usual mistake.
when: Windows servers, SQL Server or file shares on EC2 that need domain join
Amazon WorkSpaces or RDS SQL Server with Windows authentication
You want AWS to reach your existing corporate AD
nope: Not for signing in to the AWS console, that is IAM Identity Center
Not for your app's own user accounts, use Cognito
If you have no Windows or AD in the picture, you do not need this at all
eg: A company joins its EC2 Windows file servers to AWS Managed Microsoft AD so staff use the same office login.
pay: Per hour, per directory, always on. A Managed Microsoft AD standard edition runs a few hundred dollars a month even if idle, and you need two of them for a second region.

name: AWS Firewall Manager
one: It pushes the same firewall rules to every account in your company automatically.
like: A head office rule that every branch must lock the back door, applied centrally so a new branch is locked on day one.
what: Firewall Manager sits above WAF, Shield Advanced, Network Firewall, Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall and security groups, and applies your policies across all accounts in an AWS Organization, including accounts created later. It is a policy distributor, not a firewall itself. It needs AWS Organizations, a nominated admin account and, for some policies, Shield Advanced, so it is useless to a single-account setup.
when: Many AWS accounts under an Organization
You must guarantee a new account cannot ship without WAF
Auditing for stray, overly open security groups across accounts
nope: Pointless with one or two accounts, just configure WAF or Network Firewall directly
It does not inspect traffic itself, the underlying services do that and bill separately
eg: Security mandates that every public ALB in the company has the managed WAF rule set, and Firewall Manager applies it to accounts opened next month too.
pay: A monthly fee per policy, per region, on top of the full cost of every WAF, Network Firewall or Shield resource it creates. The underlying services are the big number.

name: AWS IAM Identity Center
one: One login that gets your staff into all your AWS accounts, with the right permissions.
like: A single office badge that opens the doors you are allowed through, instead of a separate key for every room.
what: Formerly AWS Single Sign-On, and still called that in older docs. It gives each person one sign-in, often from Okta, Entra ID or Google Workspace, and hands out short-lived credentials for each AWS account and role. This is the current recommended way for humans to access AWS. Long-lived IAM users with access keys are the old way and are discouraged.
when: More than one AWS account, or more than about two people
You want to stop creating IAM users and access keys
You already have a company identity provider to plug in
nope: Not for applications or servers, they should use IAM roles
Not for your product's end users, use Cognito
Not a replacement for IAM policies, it hands them out, it does not define what they mean
eg: A new engineer is added to one group in Okta and instantly has read-only access to production and admin in the sandbox account.
pay: Free. You pay for nothing here, which is why there is no excuse not to use it.

name: AWS Identity and Access Management
one: Decides who can do what in your AWS account.
like: Keys for a building. The cleaner's key opens the store room, not the safe.
what: IAM holds users, roles and policies. A policy is a list of allowed actions. Give the least access that still works. Never use the root account for daily work, and turn on MFA.
when: Always. From day one.
pay: Free.
eg: A role that lets one Lambda function read one S3 bucket and nothing else.

name: AWS Key Management Service
one: Creates and guards the keys that encrypt your data.
like: The master key cutting machine, kept in a locked room. You can use the keys, you can never take them out.
what: KMS holds encryption keys. S3, RDS, EBS and others call it to encrypt your data. The key never leaves KMS. Every use is logged in CloudTrail.
when: Encrypting anything
Compliance requirements
pay: Per key per month, plus per request.
eg: All backups encrypted with a key only two roles may use.

name: AWS Network Firewall
one: A firewall that inspects traffic going in and out of your private network in AWS.
like: A guard at the estate gate who checks where each van is going, not just whether it has a pass.
what: Network Firewall is a managed, stateful firewall for a VPC. It can filter by domain name, match Suricata intrusion detection rules, and block outbound traffic to places you did not approve. Security groups and network ACLs already do simple allow and deny far more cheaply, so this earns its place mainly when you need deep inspection or outbound domain control. Getting the routing right, with traffic forced through firewall endpoints, is the hard part.
when: You must control which domains your servers can reach outbound
A compliance rule demands intrusion detection on network traffic
A central inspection VPC for many accounts
nope: For ordinary port and source rules, security groups are free and enough
For filtering HTTP attacks on a public web app, use WAF
For blocking DNS lookups only, Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall is much cheaper
eg: A regulated workload may only call api.stripe.com outbound, and Network Firewall drops every other destination.
pay: An hourly charge per firewall endpoint in each availability zone, plus a charge per gigabyte inspected. The per-zone hourly fee adds up before you pass any traffic.

name: AWS Payment Cryptography
one: It does the card-industry encryption work that bank payment systems need.
like: The sealed machine in a bank branch that turns a typed PIN into something nobody can read, rented by the hour instead of bought.
what: A very narrow service for payment processors, card issuers, acquirers and banks. It handles PIN translation, card verification values, EMV and key exchange under PCI PIN and PCI P2PE rules, replacing the physical payment HSMs those firms used to rack in a data centre. Almost nobody needs this. If you are not personally handling raw card PINs or issuing cards, it is not for you.
when: You process or translate card PINs yourself
You issue cards and need EMV key handling
You are replacing physical payment HSMs in a colocation cage
nope: Taking card payments on a website does not need it, use Stripe or a payment provider
For general encryption keys, use KMS
For your own custom crypto with sole key custody, use CloudHSM
eg: A card issuer verifies an ATM PIN block without ever having the clear PIN in its own application.
pay: Per API call plus per active key, per hour. Keys you created and forgot keep billing.

name: AWS Private Certificate Authority
one: It lets you issue your own certificates for things inside your own network.
like: Printing your own staff ID cards. They work everywhere inside your building, and mean nothing outside it.
what: Private CA, formerly ACM Private CA, runs a certificate authority you own, so you can issue TLS certificates for internal services, containers, devices and users. Browsers and the public internet will not trust these unless you install your root on every machine, which is the point people miss. It is the right tool for mutual TLS between services and for IoT fleets.
when: Mutual TLS between internal services or in a service mesh
Certificates for IoT devices or company laptops
An internal domain a public CA will not issue for
nope: Never for a public website, use ACM public certificates, which are free
Small setups can often self-sign or use cert-manager instead, this is expensive for a handful of certs
eg: A Kubernetes cluster issues short-lived certificates to each pod so services only talk to each other over verified TLS.
pay: A few hundred dollars per month for each CA, whether idle or not, plus a per-certificate charge. Spinning up a CA to try it and leaving it running is the classic bill shock.

name: AWS Resource Access Manager
one: Lets one AWS account share a specific resource with another account.
like: Giving a neighbour a key to your garage. They can use that one space, not the whole house.
what: Known as RAM. It shares certain resource types across accounts, most often VPC subnets, Transit Gateways, Route 53 resolver rules and License Manager configurations. The other account uses the resource as if it were theirs, while you keep ownership and pay for it. Only some resource types can be shared, and it works best inside one AWS Organization.
when: Many accounts using one shared network
Sharing a Transit Gateway across the company
Central DNS resolver rules for every account
nope: Sharing files or data, use an S3 bucket policy
Giving someone access to act in your account, use an IAM cross account role
eg: The network account shares its private subnets, so each team's account launches workloads into the shared VPC.
pay: Free. The owning account keeps paying for the shared resource, which is the part that catches out billing.

name: AWS Secrets Manager
one: A safe for passwords and API keys.
like: A bank locker. Only the right person gets in, and there is a record of every visit.
what: Secrets Manager stores database passwords and keys encrypted. Your app fetches them at runtime instead of keeping them in code. It can rotate database passwords automatically.
when: Any password or key
Anything you would hate to see on GitHub
nope: Plain non secret settings. Parameter Store is cheaper.
pay: Per secret per month, plus API calls.
eg: The database password is fetched at startup, never written in the repo.

name: AWS Security Agent
one: An AI helper that attacks and reviews your own application to find holes.
like: Hiring someone to try the locks on your house and write you a list.
what: A very new AI agent, now presented under AWS Continuum. It does on demand penetration testing, which is generally available, plus code scanning and threat modelling which are still in preview. Because parts are preview and it is so recent, treat its findings as a first pass, not as a replacement for a human security review or a compliance audit.
when: You want a security check before a release without booking a testing firm
You need a threat model drafted for a new design
You want repeated cheap scans between real audits
nope: You need a signed penetration test report for a customer or auditor. Use an accredited human firm.
You want to find threats in your running account, like odd API calls. That is GuardDuty and aws-cloudtrail.
You want to manage who can access what. That is aws-identity-and-access-management.
eg: A team runs it against a new API and gets a list of injection risks in hours instead of weeks.
pay: Not clearly published. Expect usage based charging, and expect preview features to change or be priced later.

name: AWS Security Hub
one: One screen that gathers security problems from all your AWS security tools.
like: A hospital nurses' station where every ward's alarms come to one desk, instead of ringing in rooms nobody is standing in.
what: Careful, the name moved. In 2025 the original service was renamed Security Hub CSPM, which runs best-practice checks against standards like CIS and AWS Foundational Security Best Practices. A newer service took the plain name Security Hub and focuses on correlating findings into prioritised exposures using the OCSF format. Both pull in findings from GuardDuty, Inspector, Macie and partners. Older blog posts and docs saying just Security Hub usually mean the CSPM one.
when: More than one AWS security service switched on and too many alerts
You need a compliance score against CIS or PCI controls
Sending security findings to a ticketing system or SIEM
nope: It does not detect threats itself, GuardDuty and Inspector do that
It does not fix anything, you still need automation or people
With one tiny account and no compliance need, the check charges may not be worth it
eg: GuardDuty, Inspector and Macie findings for twelve accounts land in one place, and a critical one opens a Jira ticket automatically.
pay: Per security check run and per finding ingested. Turning on every standard across many accounts multiplies the check count quickly.

name: AWS Security Incident Response
one: AWS security experts help you handle a breach, and the service triages alerts in between.
like: A plumber on retainer. Day to day they check the meter, and when a pipe bursts at midnight you have a number that answers.
what: Launched at re:Invent 2024. It does two things: automatic triage of GuardDuty and Security Hub findings to cut noise, and, when something real happens, access to the AWS Customer Incident Response Team with a case workflow and communications. It is help with an AWS-side incident. It is not a full managed security operations centre, and it does not cover your code, your laptops or your SaaS.
when: You have no security team of your own and AWS is where your risk lives
You want a defined path to AWS experts before an incident, not during
GuardDuty noise nobody triages
nope: Not a replacement for detection, you still need GuardDuty switched on
If you already have a mature SOC or an MDR vendor, this overlaps
Not for non-AWS incidents like a compromised laptop
eg: GuardDuty flags credentials used from an unusual country, and the service escalates a real case to AWS responders instead of it sitting unread.
pay: Originally a large monthly subscription with a high minimum. It now bills per finding ingested, with the first 10,000 a month free, and it is included with Enterprise Support.

name: AWS Shield
one: Protection against attacks that try to flood your site.
like: Flood barriers around the building.
what: Shield Standard is automatic and free on CloudFront and load balancers. Shield Advanced is a paid tier with a response team and bill protection. Most small projects only ever need Standard.
when: You are a likely target
You need the bill protection
nope: A small site. Standard is already on and free.
pay: Standard is free. Advanced is a large fixed monthly fee.
eg: A flood of fake traffic is absorbed before it reaches your servers.

name: AWS Signer
one: It digitally signs your code so the thing running it can check nobody tampered with it.
like: A wax seal on a letter. If the seal is broken when it arrives, you do not read it.
what: Signer manages the signing keys and certificates, and produces signatures for Lambda deployment packages, container images in ECR using Notation, and IoT and FreeRTOS firmware. The runtime, such as Lambda's code signing configuration, is what actually refuses unsigned code. Signer only makes the signature, so on its own it enforces nothing until you turn on enforcement at the other end.
when: A rule says only approved, signed Lambda code may run
Signing container images so a cluster rejects unsigned ones
Firmware updates to devices in the field
nope: Not for signing documents or emails, that is a different world entirely
Not needed for ordinary app deploys where your pipeline is already the only way in
It does not scan code for problems, use Inspector or a SAST tool
eg: A Lambda function is configured to reject any package that was not signed by the release pipeline's signing profile.
pay: No charge for the signing service itself. You pay for the underlying storage and, where used, a Private CA.

name: AWS WAF
one: A filter that blocks bad web traffic before it reaches you.
like: A security guard at the gate who turns away known troublemakers.
what: WAF sits in front of CloudFront, a load balancer or API Gateway. It blocks SQL injection attempts, bad bots and abusive IPs, and can rate limit. It is a filter, not a fix for insecure code.
when: Any public site
Login pages being attacked
nope: Internal tools behind a VPN.
pay: Per rule per month, plus per million requests.
eg: Blocking an IP that tries two hundred logins a minute.

name: Amazon Cloud Directory
one: Stores objects like people and devices in several overlapping trees at once.
like: A staff list you can view by manager, by office, or by project, from one set of records.
what: Closed to new customers and it reaches end of support on 24 July 2027. Do not start anything on it. It was a directory store where one object could sit in many hierarchies at the same time, useful for device registries and product catalogues. AWS points people to amazon-dynamodb or Neptune instead. It was never a login directory for IT admins.
when: Nothing new. It is on its way out
Only relevant if you already run it and need an exit plan before 2027
nope: You are building anything new. Use amazon-dynamodb, or a graph database, from the start.
You want staff logins and Active Directory. That is AWS Directory Service or IAM Identity Center.
You want app permissions. Use amazon-verified-permissions.
eg: An existing customer plans a move of its device registry from Cloud Directory to DynamoDB before the 2027 cutoff.
pay: Per gigabyte stored and per request, but the real cost now is the migration you must fund before support ends.

name: Amazon Cognito
one: Sign up and log in for your app's users, ready made.
like: Hiring a receptionist who checks ID, instead of building your own front desk.
what: Cognito handles user sign up, login, password reset, MFA and Google or Apple login. Your app gets a token. Do not confuse it with IAM. IAM is for your team, Cognito is for your customers.
when: Your app needs customer accounts
You do not want to store passwords yourself
nope: You only need internal staff access. Use IAM Identity Center.
pay: Per monthly active user, with a free tier.
eg: Students logging into a learning app with email or Google.

name: Amazon Detective
one: After an alert, it shows you the story of what actually happened.
like: CCTV footage you scrub back through after the alarm goes off, to see who came in and where they went.
what: Detective pulls CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs and GuardDuty findings into a linked graph, so you can follow a suspicious role or IP across time and accounts without writing queries. It is for investigating, not detecting: it finds nothing on its own and is only useful once GuardDuty or Security Hub has raised something. Teams that never investigate alerts get no value from it.
when: You get GuardDuty findings and have to work out the blast radius
Tracing what one compromised role touched across accounts
You do not want to hand-write Athena queries over CloudTrail
nope: Useless without GuardDuty, turn that on first
If nobody investigates alerts, this is money for a screen nobody opens
For ad hoc log searching across many sources, Security Lake plus Athena is more flexible
eg: An EC2 instance is flagged for talking to a known bad IP, and Detective shows it also assumed a role and listed every S3 bucket.
pay: Per gigabyte of log data ingested per account, per month. Chatty accounts with high VPC flow log volume drive it.

name: Amazon GuardDuty
one: Watches for signs that someone has broken in.
like: A burglar alarm that has learned what normal looks like in your house.
what: GuardDuty reads your logs and flags suspicious activity: a key used from a strange country, a server talking to a known bad address, crypto mining. It only tells you, it does not block.
when: Any account holding real data
You want intrusion detection without effort
nope: A throwaway learning account, unless you want to see how it works.
pay: By the volume of logs analysed. Watch this one.
eg: An alert that your access key is suddenly being used from another continent.

name: Amazon Inspector
one: It keeps checking your servers, containers and functions for known security holes.
like: A building inspector who comes back every time you change something, not once a year.
what: Inspector scans EC2 instances, ECR container images, Lambda functions and code for known vulnerabilities, and scores them by whether they are actually reachable. It runs continuously rather than on a schedule you start. Note the name confusion: the old Amazon Inspector Classic is a different, retired product, and AWS ends support for it on 20 May 2026. Anything new is the current Inspector.
when: You run EC2, containers or Lambda and need CVE scanning
Blocking a vulnerable image before it reaches production
A compliance requirement for vulnerability management
nope: Not for misconfiguration like a public S3 bucket, that is Security Hub CSPM or Config
Not for active threats and intrusions, that is GuardDuty
If you build images in a pipeline that already scans them, this may duplicate what you have
eg: A base image in ECR is flagged for a critical OpenSSL flaw, and the build pipeline refuses to promote it.
pay: Per EC2 instance per month, per container image scan, and per Lambda function. Rebuilding images many times a day multiplies the image scan charges.

name: Amazon Macie
one: It looks through your S3 buckets for personal data you did not know was there.
like: Someone going through every filing cabinet in the office looking for stray photocopies of passports.
what: Macie uses pattern matching and machine learning to find sensitive data such as card numbers, passport numbers and credentials in S3 objects, and reports which buckets are public or unencrypted. It only covers S3, not databases, not EBS, not other stores. Its bucket inventory is cheap, but the actual content scanning is priced per gigabyte, so scanning everything blindly is the mistake.
when: You suspect personal data has leaked into log or export buckets
A privacy law makes you prove you know where personal data sits
Before opening a bucket more widely
nope: Does not cover RDS, DynamoDB or anything outside S3, use Glue plus custom checks there
If you already know exactly what is in each bucket, you are paying to be told
For encryption and access control problems only, S3 Block Public Access and Config are free or cheaper
eg: Macie finds full card numbers sitting in a debug log bucket that an old application wrote three years ago.
pay: A per-bucket monthly charge for inventory, plus per gigabyte of objects actually inspected. Pointing it at a multi-terabyte data lake is the expensive mistake.

name: Amazon Security Lake
one: It puts all your security logs in one place, in one standard format.
like: Everyone in the company finally agreeing to write dates the same way, so the records can actually be read together.
what: Security Lake collects CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, Route 53 logs, findings and third-party sources into your own S3 bucket, converted to the OCSF standard schema and stored as Parquet. The value is the normalisation, since you can then query everything with Athena or feed one clean feed to Splunk or OpenSearch. It is plumbing. It shows you no dashboards and raises no alerts by itself.
when: Many accounts and several log sources you cannot join today
Feeding a SIEM without building a converter per source
Keeping years of security logs cheaply for investigations
nope: Not a detection tool, use GuardDuty and Security Hub for that
Not worth it for one or two accounts, just query CloudTrail with Athena
If your SIEM already ingests everything happily, this adds a layer for nothing
eg: A responder runs one Athena query across three years of flow logs and CloudTrail from forty accounts, without joining formats by hand.
pay: Per gigabyte of data converted and ingested, plus the ongoing S3 storage and Athena query costs you would pay anyway. Flow logs are usually the biggest volume.

name: Amazon Verified Permissions
one: Decides whether a user is allowed to do a thing in your app, so you do not code it yourself.
like: A doorman with the guest list, instead of every room checking names itself.
what: You write the rules in a language called Cedar, store them here, and your app asks a yes or no question for each action. It keeps permission rules out of your application code, so they can be changed and reviewed on their own. It is for permissions inside your own application, not for who can touch AWS resources.
when: A SaaS app where each customer sets their own sharing rules
Rules keep changing and you are tired of editing if statements
Auditors want to see the permission rules written down in one place
nope: You want to control access to AWS itself, like who may stop an EC2 instance. That is aws-identity-and-access-management.
Your app has three simple roles. A table in your own database is simpler and free.
You cannot afford an extra network call in a hot path. Cache decisions or check locally instead.
eg: A document app asks whether Priya may share a folder, and the answer comes back from a Cedar rule, not app code.
pay: Per authorization call, fractions of a cent each. The surprise is volume. If you check permissions on every item in a list, calls multiply fast, so use the batch call.

name: AWS Backup
one: One place to schedule backups of everything.
