like: One alarm clock for the whole house instead of one in every room.
what: AWS Backup sets backup rules across EBS, RDS, DynamoDB, EFS and more, from a single policy. It handles retention and can copy backups to another region. A backup you have never restored is not a backup.
when: More than one thing needs backing up
Any compliance rule
nope: A single database whose own backups are enough.
pay: Per GB of backup stored.
eg: Daily backups kept 30 days, monthly kept a year, copied to Mumbai.

name: AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery
one: It keeps a live copy of your servers in AWS so you can start them if the originals die.
like: A spare car kept fuelled in the garage. It is not driven every day, but you can turn the key and go.
what: An agent on each server copies disk changes continuously into cheap staging storage in AWS. When you declare a disaster, it boots real EC2 instances from that data, usually in minutes, and can roll back to a point in time from before the problem. It replaces CloudEndure Disaster Recovery, which AWS retired. It protects whole machines, not application state, so databases still need their own consistency thinking, and you must run drills or you will not know it works.
when: On-premises or other-cloud servers that need a cloud fallback
Recovery time measured in minutes, not hours
Ransomware rollback to a point in time before the infection
nope: For serverless or container apps, deploy the same stack in a second region instead
For long-term archival copies, use AWS Backup, this is not a backup archive
For a one-off move to AWS, AWS Application Migration Service is the matching tool
eg: A hospital's 40 on-premises Windows servers replicate to AWS, and a quarterly drill boots them all in a test VPC in about 15 minutes.
pay: A flat fee per source server per hour, about 0.028 USD. The surprise is everything underneath, the staging EC2 instances, EBS volumes and snapshots are billed separately at normal rates.

name: AWS Snowball Edge
one: A rugged box AWS posts you, which you fill with data and post back.
like: Posting a hard drive instead of uploading over a slow line.
what: No longer available to new customers. AWS now points new users to DataSync for online copies, aws-data-transfer-terminal for physical drop off, and aws-outposts-family for edge computing. The device held large amounts of data, could run EC2 instances and Kubernetes offline, and shipped with an E Ink label. It is still supported for existing customers, but it is not something to plan around.
when: Nothing new. New sign ups are closed
Existing users finishing an in flight migration or edge deployment
nope: You are a new customer with a bulk transfer. Use aws-data-transfer-terminal or an online copy service.
You need compute at a remote site. Use aws-outposts-family.
You want normal cloud storage. Use amazon-simple-storage-service.
eg: A ship at sea collected sensor data on a device and the box was posted ashore on arrival.
pay: A per job device fee plus daily rental after a free window, plus shipping. The classic surprise was the daily charge while the device sat unused on a loading dock.

name: AWS Snowball
one: AWS posts you a rugged box, you copy data onto it and post it back.
like: Posting a hard drive instead of emailing a huge file, because the post office is faster than your broadband.
what: Snowball Edge devices hold tens of terabytes and also run EC2 and Lambda locally, which made them useful at ships, mines and army bases. The family is closing down. Snowmobile, the truck, is gone, Snowcone was discontinued in 2024, and as of late 2025 Snowball Edge is open only to existing customers, with support ending in commercial regions on 31 December 2026. Treat it as retired and do not plan new work on it.
when: Almost never now, the service is being withdrawn
Only if you already have devices under an existing arrangement
nope: For bulk transfer over a network, use AWS DataSync
For a permanent fast private link, use AWS Direct Connect
For edge compute in a remote site, use AWS Outposts servers or ordinary hardware
eg: A research ship used to fill a Snowball Edge with sonar data at sea and ship it home at port. Today that team would plan for DataSync over satellite or a Direct Connect at dock.
pay: Historically a per job fee plus per day device rental, with shipping. Moot now, since new orders are closed.

name: AWS Storage Gateway
one: A small piece of software in your office that makes AWS storage look like a local drive.
like: A post box on your street. You drop letters in as if it were local, and the van takes them to the sorting office.
what: You run a virtual appliance on-premises. It presents an NFS or SMB share, an iSCSI disk, or a virtual tape drive, keeps recent data cached locally, and stores everything in S3, EBS snapshots or Glacier behind the scenes. Reads of cached data are fast, reads of anything else go over your internet link and feel slow. The Tape Gateway variant is popular because it lets old backup software keep thinking it has a tape library.
when: Old backup software that only understands tape
An office file share that should live in S3
Slowly retiring a NAS without changing how users work
nope: For applications running inside AWS, mount Amazon EFS or FSx directly, a gateway adds nothing
For one-time or scheduled bulk copying, AWS DataSync is faster and simpler
For low latency shared storage across an office, keep a local NAS
eg: An accounting firm points its Veeam backups at a Tape Gateway, and the tapes quietly become objects in Glacier Deep Archive.
pay: Per gateway per month, plus the underlying S3 or Glacier storage, plus request charges. The surprise is retrieval, pulling old virtual tapes back out of Deep Archive costs real money and takes hours.

name: Amazon EFS
one: A shared folder that many servers can read and write at the same time.
like: A filing cabinet in the middle of an office. Anyone can open a drawer, and everyone sees the same papers.
what: EFS is managed NFS storage. It grows and shrinks on its own, spans multiple availability zones, and mounts on EC2, ECS, EKS and Lambda. It is a network file system, so per file latency is higher than a local disk, and small random writes are noticeably slower. It is Linux only, there is no SMB support.
when: Several machines need the same files, such as uploads or shared config
A web app you cannot rewrite that expects a normal filesystem
Lambda functions needing more than the small temp space
nope: For a single machine's fast disk, use EBS, it is cheaper and quicker
For Windows and SMB shares, use FSx for Windows File Server
For storing objects an app fetches by key, S3 costs far less
eg: Three WordPress servers behind a load balancer all mount the same EFS volume so an image uploaded on one appears on the others.
pay: Per GB stored per month, with a standard and a cheaper infrequent access tier. The surprises are the per GB charge for reading infrequent access data, and Elastic throughput mode billing per GB transferred.

name: Amazon Elastic Block Store
one: The hard disk attached to your EC2 server.
like: The hard drive inside a computer, except you can unplug it and attach it to another computer.
what: EBS is a disk volume for one EC2 instance. It survives when the instance stops. You can take snapshots for backup. Type gp3 is the sensible default.
when: Any EC2 server needs a disk
Databases running on EC2
nope: Sharing one disk across many servers. Use EFS.
Storing files for a website. Use S3.
pay: Per GB per month, whether or not you use the space. Snapshots cost extra.
eg: A 100 GB disk holding the application and its data.

name: Amazon FSx for Lustre
one: A file system built for hundreds of machines reading the same data very fast.
like: A motorway with fifty lanes. Useless for one car, excellent when a whole city leaves at once.
what: Lustre is the parallel filesystem used in scientific supercomputing, and FSx runs it for you. It can link to an S3 bucket, so objects appear as files and new files can be written back to S3. Throughput scales with the size you provision, into hundreds of GB per second. It is POSIX and Linux only, and it is tuned for large sequential reads, not for lots of tiny files or long-lived general storage.
when: Machine learning training reading a large dataset from many GPUs
Genomics, seismic or simulation workloads
You need S3 data to look like files with high throughput
nope: For general shared files, use EFS, Lustre is costly and specialised
For Windows or SMB clients, use FSx for Windows File Server
For long-term storage, keep the data in S3 and create the Lustre filesystem only while a job runs
eg: A training job on 64 GPU instances mounts an FSx for Lustre filesystem linked to the S3 bucket holding 20 TB of images, then the filesystem is deleted when training ends.
pay: Per GB per month by deployment type, with throughput tied to size. An Intelligent-Tiering class now exists on Persistent_2. The surprise is provisioning capacity you do not need just to reach the throughput you do need.

name: Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP
one: Real NetApp storage, run by AWS, with the same tools your storage team already knows.
like: Moving house but taking your own kitchen with you, so you still know where everything is.
what: This is genuine ONTAP software running as a managed service, so you get NFS, SMB and iSCSI at once, plus NetApp features like snapshots, cloning, deduplication, compression and SnapMirror replication from an on-premises NetApp. Cold data tiers automatically to cheaper capacity storage. It is the most feature-rich and the most complex of the FSx types, and it really pays off only if you already use NetApp or need those features.
when: An existing NetApp estate moving to AWS with SnapMirror
You need NFS and SMB against the same data
Instant zero-copy clones of large volumes for test environments
nope: If you have never used NetApp, FSx for OpenZFS or EFS is far less to learn
For pure Windows shares, FSx for Windows File Server is simpler
For extreme parallel throughput, use FSx for Lustre
eg: A bank mirrors volumes from its on-premises NetApp into FSx for ONTAP nightly, then clones one instantly to give developers a full-size test copy.
pay: Per GB of SSD capacity, per GB of capacity pool storage, plus provisioned throughput capacity per hour. The surprise is the throughput capacity charge, which is a separate line from storage and is easy to over-provision.

name: Amazon FSx for OpenZFS
one: A fast Linux file share with snapshots, run by AWS.
like: A notebook with carbon copies. Every time you change a page, you can still flip back to yesterday's version.
what: This runs the OpenZFS filesystem as a managed service over NFS. It gives very low latency, cheap instant snapshots and clones, plus compression, and is the simplest way to lift an on-premises ZFS or general NFS server into AWS. It speaks NFS only, so Windows clients are not the target. A single-AZ filesystem is not protected against a zone failure, you choose Multi-AZ for that.
when: Replacing a Linux NFS server with something managed
Databases or build servers needing sub-millisecond file latency
You want frequent cheap snapshots and instant test clones
nope: If you do not need snapshots or low latency, EFS grows on its own and needs less thought
For SMB and Active Directory, use FSx for Windows File Server
For hundreds of parallel readers, use FSx for Lustre
eg: A CI system stores its build workspace on FSx for OpenZFS and clones a snapshot per pull request so each build starts from a clean tree in seconds.
pay: Per GB provisioned, plus provisioned IOPS and throughput. An Intelligent-Tiering class exists for Multi-AZ. The surprise is that snapshots consume the same provisioned capacity, so heavy snapshot retention forces you to buy more space.

name: Amazon FSx for WFS
one: A Windows file share, the kind with drive letters, run by AWS.
like: The shared drive at work that everyone calls the P drive, except nobody has to look after the server.
what: It gives you SMB shares with real Windows behaviour, NTFS permissions, Active Directory integration, shadow copies for user self-restore, and DFS namespaces. It is the natural home for Windows workloads and for file shares users map from their laptops. It is Windows-protocol first, Linux clients can mount SMB but it is not the smooth path, and it needs an AD directory, either your own or AWS Managed Microsoft AD.
when: Moving an on-premises Windows file server to AWS
SharePoint, SQL Server or .NET apps wanting an SMB share
User home directories and department shares
nope: For Linux workloads, use EFS or FSx for OpenZFS
If you have no Active Directory and do not want one, this is heavy going
For app data accessed by key, S3 costs much less
eg: A 300-person firm retires its old file server and maps P: to an FSx for Windows share joined to their existing Active Directory.
pay: Per GB provisioned, SSD or cheaper HDD, plus provisioned throughput capacity per MBps and backup storage. The surprise is the separate throughput charge and the fact that HDD has a minimum size.

name: Amazon FSx
one: The family name for AWS's managed versions of four real file systems.
like: A shop that sells four brands of filing cabinet. FSx is the shop, not the cabinet.
what: FSx is not one product you buy. It is the umbrella over FSx for Windows File Server, FSx for Lustre, FSx for NetApp ONTAP and FSx for OpenZFS. AWS runs the servers, backups and patching, and you pick the type by the protocol and features you need. Choosing wrongly is the common mistake, since you cannot convert one type into another later, you migrate the data.
when: You need a specific filesystem's behaviour, not generic storage
Moving an existing NetApp, Windows or ZFS estate to AWS
Workloads needing SMB, NFS with snapshots, or parallel throughput
nope: If you have no strong requirement, EFS is simpler and cheaper for Linux sharing
For object storage accessed by key, use S3
For one server's disk, use EBS
eg: A team lists its needs, SMB shares plus Active Directory, and that answer points them at FSx for Windows File Server rather than the other three.
pay: Each type bills differently, generally per GB of provisioned capacity plus provisioned throughput. The surprise across all of them is that capacity is provisioned in advance, so you pay for empty space.

name: Amazon File Cache
one: A temporary fast copy of files that actually live somewhere slower.
like: Bringing a few library books to your desk for the week, instead of walking to the shelves each time you need a page.
what: File Cache links to an S3 bucket or an NFS server and presents those files as one high speed filesystem inside AWS, built on Lustre. Files are pulled in the first time they are read and dropped when unused. It is a cache, not a home for data, so you size it for the working set, not the whole dataset. Very few teams need it, it exists for heavy compute bursts reading from on-premises or S3 data.
when: A big compute job in AWS reading data that lives on-premises
Bursty rendering or simulation that reads the same files repeatedly
You need one namespace over several scattered data sources
nope: If the data already lives in S3 and the job is in one region, FSx for Lustre linked to S3 does the same job for a steady workload
For everyday shared files, use EFS
For a permanent store, use S3 or FSx, a cache is not durable storage
eg: A visual effects studio bursts 500 render nodes into AWS and points them at a File Cache backed by the NFS server in the London office.
pay: Per GB of cache capacity per hour while it exists, and it is expensive. The surprise is that you pay for the cache even on idle days, so it is meant to be created and deleted around a job.

name: Amazon S3 on Outposts
one: Gives you S3 buckets on AWS hardware sitting in your own building.
like: Having the same brand of filing cabinet at home as the one at head office.
what: It is S3 buckets running on an Outposts rack in your data centre, so the data never leaves your premises. Your code uses the normal S3 API through an access point. The limits matter, there is only one storage class, capacity is fixed by the hardware you bought, and features like versioning and cross region replication are not the same as in a Region.
when: A law or contract says the data must stay in your building
An application on the Outpost needs local storage with very low latency
You want one S3 style codebase across cloud and on premises
nope: You have no regulatory or latency reason to keep data local. Plain amazon-simple-storage-service is cheaper and has far more features.
You need shared file access rather than object storage. Use amazon-efs style file storage on the Outpost.
You just want a one off bulk transfer. That is not what this is.
eg: A hospital keeps scan images in an S3 bucket on an Outpost rack in its own basement.
pay: You pay for the Outpost rack up front or over a term, and the storage capacity is bought with it. The surprise is that you pay for the whole capacity whether or not you fill it.

name: Amazon Simple Storage Service Glacier
one: Very cheap storage for files you almost never open.
like: A deep basement archive. Cheap to keep things, slow to fetch them.
what: Glacier classes store data at a fraction of normal S3 cost. Retrieval can take minutes or hours depending on the tier, and costs extra. It is for archives, not for anything you serve live.
when: Records you must keep for years
Old backups
nope: Anything a user might open today.
pay: Very low per GB per month. You pay to retrieve.
eg: Seven years of invoices kept for audit.

name: Amazon Simple Storage Service
one: A place to keep files, as many as you want.
like: An unlimited cupboard. You put a file in, you get a link to it.
what: S3 stores files, called objects, in buckets. It is built for very high durability. It is not a disk you can mount and edit in place. You put a whole file and get a whole file.
when: Images, videos, PDFs, backups
Website files
Data before you analyse it
nope: A database. It cannot search inside your data.
A file share your server edits live. Use EFS.
pay: Per GB stored per month, plus requests, plus data going out.
eg: All product photos for an online shop, served through CloudFront.
